added: Home Meet Dr.
Vick Issues Events News Voter Information Contact Photos 🗺️ Drive 95: The 95-County Listening Tour Headline: Faith First.
Tennessee Always.
Coming to YOUR County!
My campaign is not about Nashville or big-city politics—it is about the heart of Tennessee, and the heart of Tennessee beats in all 95 counties .
I made a promise to lead as a true servant, and to do that, I must hear directly from every community.
That is why I am launching Drive 95 , a mission to visit every single corner of our great state between now and the November 3, 2026, election.
Why Drive 95 Matters As a Christian Independent and a 40-year veteran of Tennessee public education, I know that real solutions are found on the ground, not in a capital building.

I want to look you in the eye, listen to your concerns about Mental Health , Homelessness/Poverty , and Education , and other issues that face our state and discuss how we can bring New Results to our communities.
This is a low-budget, grassroots campaign relying on the spirit and hospitality of Tennesseans.
Every stop is a chance for fellowship, listening, and prayer.
Dr Vick's prayer is simple: "May God Stir Your Heart to Vote for Dr.
Vick for Tennessee." 🗓️ Get Ready: Check Back for the Schedule!
Our full schedule will be posted here soon!
We are diligently working to finalize locations in all 95 counties.

title.after: Building an Economy That Works for Everyone

added: VOTE - November 3rd 2026 Early Voting Begins October 22, 2026 Home About Ayanna Volunteer Blog More Home About Ayanna Volunteer Blog Home About Ayanna Volunteer Blog My Blog All Posts Building an Economy That Works for Everyone July 14, 2026 | News Ayanna Khan-Flowers at Legislative Hall Building an Economy That Works for Everyone: Why Delaware's Future Depends on Inclusive Growth By Ayanna Khan-Flowers For much of my career, I have worked alongside entrepreneurs, nonprofit leaders, small business owners, and community advocates who share a common goal: creating opportunities that improve lives and strengthen our communities.
From helping businesses launch and grow to supporting organizations that serve Delaware families, I have seen firsthand the innovation, resilience, and determination that exist throughout our state.
I have also witnessed the challenges that too many people face when trying to access opportunities that should be within reach.
Those experiences have shaped my belief that Delaware's future depends on building an economy that works for everyone.
An inclusive economy is not about choosing one community over another.
It is about recognizing that when more people have access to opportunity, our entire state benefits.
Strong economies are built when entrepreneurs can start businesses, workers can access quality jobs, families can achieve financial stability, and communities have the resources they need to thrive.
The question is not whether Delaware can achieve this vision.
The question is whether we are willing to make the investments and policy decisions necessary to get there.
Throughout my work supporting businesses across Delaware, I have met entrepreneurs with innovative ideas who struggled to access capital.
I have met small business owners eager to expand but overwhelmed by regulatory barriers.
I have spoken with workers seeking career advancement opportunities and employers searching for skilled talent.
I have met families doing everything right yet still struggling to keep up with the rising cost of living.
These are not isolated challenges.
They are interconnected issues that require thoughtful, practical policy solutions.
I believe Delaware must continue to be one of the best places in the nation to start, grow, and sustain a business.
Small businesses are the backbone of our economy.
They create jobs, support local communities, and drive innovation.
Yet too often, entrepreneurs face obstacles that make success more difficult than it should be.

That is why I support policies that expand access to capital, strengthen technical assistance programs, reduce unnecessary barriers to business growth, and create pathways for entrepreneurs from all backgrounds to participate in our economy.
Economic development should not be measured solely by the number of large projects we attract.
It should also be measured by the number of small businesses that succeed, the number of local jobs that are created, and the number of families that achieve economic stability.
We must also recognize that workforce development and economic growth go hand in hand.
Businesses cannot thrive without a skilled workforce, and workers cannot succeed without access to education, training, and career pathways.

Delaware must continue investing in workforce development programs that connect people to high-demand industries, support lifelong learning, and prepare the next generation for the jobs of the future.
At the same time, we must address the barriers that prevent too many Delawareans from fully participating in our economy.
Access to affordable housing, reliable transportation, quality childcare, healthcare, and broadband connectivity are not separate issues from economic development.
They are economic development issues.
When families cannot access these essentials, businesses struggle to attract talent, workers face obstacles to employment, and communities are left behind.
Building an inclusive economy means understanding that prosperity must be shared.
It means creating opportunities in every community, not just a select few.
It means ensuring that urban, suburban, and rural communities all have access to investment and growth.

It means supporting minority-owned businesses, women-owned businesses, veteran-owned businesses, and entrepreneurs who have historically faced barriers to success - not as a matter of charity, but because Delaware benefits when all talent has the opportunity to flourish.
The strongest economies are those that harness the full potential of their people.
This philosophy also applies to how we approach public policy.
Policy should be informed by the people who live with its consequences every day.
Business owners, educators, healthcare providers, nonprofit leaders, workers, and families all have valuable perspectives that should help shape decisions.
Effective leadership begins with listening and continues with collaboration.
The future of Delaware will not be determined by government alone.
It will be shaped by partnerships between the public, private, and nonprofit sectors.

It will be built by entrepreneurs willing to take risks, workers striving to build better futures, community organizations addressing local challenges, and leaders committed to finding solutions rather than assigning blame.
I remain optimistic because I have seen what Delaware is capable of achieving when we work together.
I have seen small businesses transform neighborhoods.
I have seen nonprofit organizations create life-changing opportunities.
I have seen communities come together to solve difficult problems.
And I have seen people from different backgrounds unite around a shared belief that Delaware's best days are ahead.
Our challenge now is to ensure that our policies match that vision.

We need policies that encourage entrepreneurship, support small business growth, strengthen workforce development, invest in families, and expand economic opportunity across every community in our state.
Most importantly, we need policies that recognize a simple truth: when more Delawareans succeed, Delaware succeeds.
Building an economy that works for everyone is not simply an economic goal.
It is a commitment to creating a stronger, more prosperous, and more inclusive future for our state.
That is the Delaware I believe in, and it is the Delaware we should continue building together.

added: #YourIndependentVoice brad@electbarnhill.net 702-613-2576 Nevada Secretary of State close menu close menu Home About Independent Endorsements News Announcements Commentary Policy Events Contact Donate Volunteer no Election Transparency in Nevada Means Showing the Work electbarnhill Oct 09, 2026 0 Comments A Nevada voter shouldn’t need to be an elections lawyer, a computer expert, or a party insider to understand how a ballot is handled.
Confidence doesn’t come from asking people to take the system on faith.
It comes from showing the work.
I try to hold myself to that standard.
In my federal case over Nevada’s voter rolls, I publish my filings and every development on this site so you can read them yourself ( the latest is here ).

When the Secretary of State’s office closed my complaint about 9,607 Nevadans with duplicate active registrations, it didn’t dispute the data, and voters still haven’t gotten a public accounting of those records.
That’s the habit I want to change.
I’ve laid out the foundations (paper records, audits, one standard for every county, and quarterly public reports) in Public Trust Starts With Elections Done Right .
Transparency is what makes those foundations believable.
Here’s what it should look like in practice.
Publish the rules before anyone votes Election-night totals are the last page of a long process.
Voters deserve to see the first pages too.

For every election, the Secretary of State’s office should publish one plain-language page that is the same for every county: registration deadlines, identification requirements, voting locations, ballot-return options, signature-cure deadlines, the audit schedule, and the certification date.
If a county does something differently, it should say so and explain why.
When information is buried, late, or inconsistent, voters are left guessing.
Good administration replaces guessing with answers.
(Start by checking your own registration .) Open records, private voters Citizens have a right to inspect how public elections are run.
They shouldn’t have to give up their home address, birth date, or other personal information to prove the system is accountable.
Records about procedures, testing, audits, and results should be open.
Sensitive personal data should stay protected, and Nevada’s voter data should stay in Nevada’s hands .
Observation with clear rules Nevadans should be able to watch key parts of the process without disrupting the people doing the work.
Observers should know ahead of time where they may stand, what they may document, whom they may ask, and how to raise a concern through the proper channel.
Election workers should get the same written guidance, so the rules apply the same way whatever party an observer belongs to.
Observation isn’t confrontation.
It’s accountability through visibility, and a well-organized process protects election workers as much as it reassures voters.
Report what’s working, and what isn’t The quarterly public reports I’ve committed to should include numbers with context, not just raw data.
For voter-roll maintenance: address updates, inactive-status changes, voters contacted, and duplicate or outdated records found and resolved.
For Voter ID: how many voters asked for help getting identification, where problems clustered, and what was fixed before the next election.
When voters can see the rolls being maintained carefully, they’re less likely to be surprised at the polls, and more likely to trust that the work is being done.
Facts fast when something goes wrong Transparency doesn’t mean publishing security details that would make systems easier to attack.
But after an incident or a significant technical problem, voters deserve prompt, factual communication: what happened, what information or services were affected, and what’s being done about it.
Silence leaves room for rumor.
Clear facts, shared quickly and responsibly, let the public judge the situation on evidence.
(More in my election cybersecurity plan .) Results, Not Noise An audit isn’t an accusation.
An observer isn’t an adversary.
A public report isn’t an admission of failure.
They’re how a government that answers to its citizens shows its work.
Nevada needs finality after lawful review, and that finality is stronger when every voter can see the checks actually happened.
I’ve put my plans in writing and taken the fight for clean voter rolls to federal court.
Is your candidate for Nevada Secretary of State fighting this hard to protect your vote?
If not, it’s time to take a closer look.
Get to know me · Join the campaign · Donate · See all policy positions I’m not asking you to trust a party on any of this.
I’m asking you to hold the office accountable for solving real problems.

That’s the job, and I intend to do it. — Brad Lee Barnhill Independent American Party of Nevada Candidate for Nevada Secretary of State #YourIndependentVoice — Results, Not Noise Share: Categories: Policy Positions Post navigation Next Next post: The Court Asked Who Has a Stake in My Lawsuit.

added: Home News Latest News 60 Seconds With John Ley About Me Donate Issues Two Governors Agree: Washington Doesn’t Have a Revenue Problem—Olympia Has a Spending Addiction October 9, 2026 by John Ley State spending grew at 3 times the rate of personal income When a state budget grows three times faster than average family paychecks, working households inevitably get squeezed.
Across Washington State, families are cutting back, balancing household budgets, and prioritizing essential needs over extra spending.
Unfortunately, state leaders in Olympia have taken the exact opposite approach.
Even former Washington governors have warned that the state’s fiscal trajectory is fundamentally unsustainable.

Bipartisan agreement — Washington does not have a revenue problem; Olympia has a spending addiction. $17 Billion in New Taxes: Squeezed at Every Turn Over the last two legislative sessions alone, Olympia Democrats increased taxes on Washington citizens and businesses by approximately $17 billion .
This massive influx of revenue hasn’t brought lower costs or simpler government.
Instead, it has driven up the cost of living statewide—making everyday essentials like gas, housing, energy, and groceries increasingly unaffordable for families across the 18th Legislative District.
Despite mounting pressure on working families, the current administration refused to veto these tax increases or cut state spending in any meaningful way to offer tax relief.
Fighting on the House Floor: 84 Amendments, 24.5 Hours Fiscal discipline isn’t built on rhetoric; it’s proven through action.

During the legislative session, Representative John Ley and House Republicans stood up for taxpayers in an exhaustive floor fight: 24.5 Hours of Debate: House Republicans spent over a full day and night on the House floor fighting against runaway state spending and new tax burdens.
80 Common-Sense Amendments Offered: Proposals were put forward to lower tax bills, reduce regressive taxes, and cut unnecessary administrative spending.

Protecting the No-Income-Tax Tradition: Representative Ley voted firmly against state income tax proposals, offering key amendments designed to prevent tax creep from harming working families and job creators.
Regrettably, the majority party in Olympia refused to accept these amendments, choosing instead to push forward with unchecked state budget growth.

The Path to Fiscal Sanity in Washington Restoring affordability to Washington requires structural budget discipline, accountability, and a firm commitment to stopping tax hikes: Cap Budget Growth: Mandate that state budget increases never outpace the median growth of family paychecks.
Stop Income Tax Expansion: Defend Washington’s traditional no-personal-income-tax status and block progressive tax schemes.
Prioritize Essential Services: Demand that Olympia spend existing revenue more wisely before asking taxpayers for another dime.
A Message from Rep.
John Ley “Two former Washington governors agree with me: Washington State has a spending problem.

They have an addiction to your money… I fought with House Republicans for 24 and a half hours on the floor of the House trying to offer 80 amendments that would lower your tax bill… I’m fighting for you, but I need your help.

I need your vote in November to stop expanding the size and scope of government, and to spend your money more wisely.” — WA State Representative John Ley (LD18) Re-Elect John Ley | WA State Representative, 18th Legislative District Fighting for Fiscal Responsibility, Public Safety, and Working Families.

added: Please ensure Javascript is enabled for purposes of website accessibility Skip to content Chip in now to stand with Team Ossoff and a Stronger Georgia Donate to Join Team Ossoff If you've saved your information with ActBlue Express, your donation will go through immediately. $# $# $# $# $# $# $# $# $# $# Other Amount Other Amount Home About Jon News Shop Volunteer Home About Jon News Shop Volunteer Facebook X-twitter Instagram Youtube Donate Donate Donate Donate BIO Jon Ossoff Born and raised in Atlanta, Jon Ossoff represents Georgia in the United States Senate.
Jon has established a reputation as a legislative workhorse and a relentless investigator exposing corruption and the abuse of power.
Investigating Corruption Before his election to the Senate, Jon was an investigative journalist.
His small business produced award-winning investigations of corruption and war crimes for international news organizations.
Their investigations exposed serious crimes including human trafficking, judicial corruption, bribery, and sexual slavery.

In the Senate, Jon has applied those skills to expose corruption and abuse in government, including the abuse of children in Georgia’s foster care system, mistreatment of military families by private housing contractors, and civil rights abuses in the federal prison system.
Reforming a Broken System Jon is one of few United States Senators whose campaigns refuse to accept campaign contributions from corporate PACs or federal lobbyists.

Jon has introduced legislation to ban corporate PACs altogether and is leading the charge to ban stock trading by Members of Congress, helping pass a Congressional stock trading ban through a major Senate Committee for the first time.

A Legislative Workhorse Senator Ossoff has relentlessly delivered for the state of Georgia – fighting to: Cap insulin prices for seniors at $35/month Lower housing prices Expose abuses in Georgia’s foster care system Crack down on online exploitation of children Strengthen border security Upgrade health care for pregnant women, babies, and children Expose civil rights abuses and corruption in prisons and jails Defend women’s freedom of choice in reproductive health care Ban Members of Congress from trading stocks Help Georgia farmers and growers export more Georgia-grown products Strengthen public safety and tackle the opioid epidemic Deliver record funding for Georgia’s HBCUs Expand mental health care for veterans Expand and help build new health care facilities across the state Expand Medicaid in Georgia Upgrade infrastructure and expand high-speed internet access statewide Hold the U.S.

Postal Service accountable for service delays Expand job training programs Attract thousands of manufacturing jobs to Georgia Protect Social Security and Medicare and strengthen Social Security benefits for public servants Georgia Roots Jon grew up in Metro Atlanta.
He studied diplomacy at Georgetown University and received his Master of Science degree from the London School of Economics.
He lives in Atlanta with his wife, Dr.
Alisha Kramer, and their daughters Eva and Lila.

Mentored by civil rights icon Congressman John Lewis, civil and human rights have been at the core of Jon’s work throughout his career — whether exposing human trafficking and war crimes as an investigative journalist, or exposing the abuse of foster kids as a United States Senator.

added: 0 Skip to Content HOME WHY I'M RUNNING ISSUES EVENTS Donate Open Menu Close Menu Donate HOME WHY I'M RUNNING ISSUES EVENTS Open Menu Close Menu HOME WHY I'M RUNNING ISSUES EVENTS Donate < Back Affordability As a working 33-year-old, I am intimately aware of how the cost-of-living crisis is affecting younger generations.

I too am struggling; despite maintaining consistent employment, I have regularly needed the support of family, friends, and state services in order to have shelter, keep my car on the road, and receive medical care.
For my part, I don’t mind working hard.
But it shouldn’t be this hard to survive in PA.
My experience is far from unique.
The majority of Americans do not possess assets, and wages have not kept up with inflation and rising prices.
Until we address the underlying policies causing increasing economic disparity in our region, this will continue to be a critical problem.
While many of our economic hurdles are being created at the national level, there are proposals we can employ to better position Pennsylvanians for success.

Support the Affordability Action Plan Senate democrats have rolled out a legislative slate which seeks to improve the wellfare of Pennsylvanians by: Raising the minimum wage to $15/hour by 2029 ( HB 2189 & SB 19 ).
Expanding the Child Care Contribution Tax Credit .
Universal free school breakfast and lunch ( SB 180 ).
Protecting and expanding access to healthcare ( SB 322 ).
Build more housing, reduce costs, and create opportunities through Governor Shapiro’s Housing Action Plan , and Lightning Plan s.
Aid first-time homebuyers with financial assistance through the Put Down Roots PA Pilot Program ( SB 753 ).
These are all hugely important initiatives, and I very much support their implementation.

Tie Legislators' Cost of Living Adjustments to the Minimum wage While Pennsylvania legislators have received an automatic cost of living adjustment since 1995, the minimum wage here in Pennsylvania has remained fixed at $7.25 since 2009, when the federal minimum wage was first implemented.
We tie for last with 19 other states for having the lowest minimum wage in the nation.
It is manifestly unfair for elected officials to give themselves an annual cost of living adjustment without doing the same for the poorest wage earners in the state.
If we can’t afford to pay our poorest workers a living wage, then we can’t afford to pay more for leaders who already have it too good.
I will propose legislation requiring any legislative cost of living adjustments to be applied to the minimum wage.
This legislation isn’t going to solve wage stagnation on its own - it’s going to take a lot more than that to get them where they need to be.

What it will do is incentivize legislators to actually attend to the problem - it provides a strong personal motivator to make the minimum wage as high as the General Assembly can square with their constituency.
Improve Ratepayer Protections Utility bills are a real problem right now - the unlawful war in Iran and the encroachment of data centers are ramping up the price of fuel and the demands on our grid.
Energy costs were already too high - now they are intolerable.
Fortunately, there is some important legislation in the works which I stand behind.
House Bill 2333 – the Return to Ratepayer Protection Act – improves on what’s worked for decades to protect consumers.
The act would make sure: Ratepayers aren’t charged more to offset delinquent accounts.
Delinquent ratepayers working with utilities on payment plans are protected from shutoffs, and winter shutoffs are remain prohibited.
Account holders behind on payments will get better information, earlier information, and will be notified using multiple methods.
Lower-income households will have more flexible payment options, and fees will better reflect what people can afford.
Water, Sewer, and Gas authorities will have better tools to keep services running while working with customers on payments.
Rep.
Heather Boyd and Rep.

Liz Fiedler’s House Bill 2131– the Fairness in Retail Electricity Act – protects consumers who took part in the state’s Electric Choice program but ended up paying higher rates than if they had stayed with their default “home” utility and were unknowingly reenrolled with higher rate providers when their contract ended.
Customers like you paid more than $2 billion you didn’t have to pay.
The Fairness in Retail Electricity Act would: Return customers to the local default service provider when a contract with an outside provider ends.
Prevent retail energy sellers from automatically enrolling customers into a month-to-month variable plan.
Make sure customers can still choose to shop for electricity.
Prioritize Government Reform as an answer to Income Inequality Our country struggles with inequitable wages, and South Central Pennsylvania is no exception.
Economists frequently measure inequality using the Gini coefficient, a scale from 0 to 1 where 0 means perfect equality and 1 means all wealth sits with one person.
PA’s 34th districts trail the national average of 0.49, which is very high relative to other developed nations.

As identified by the World Happiness Report , prosperous countries with low Gini coefficients share a common approach: they use progressive tax systems and crack down on tax avoidance, ensure fair wages and safe working conditions, guarantee broad access to healthcare and social services, invest in anti‑poverty programs, and build governments that are diverse, transparent, and trusted.
These are exactly the areas where Pennsylvania must do better.

If we want South Central PA to be a place where everyone - not just the corporate elite - can build a secure life, we need to commit to the same principles that make more equitable societies possible.
Invest in Public Transportation Recent global instability has underscored a hard truth: America’s transportation system remains highly dependent on global oil markets and fragile supply chains.
As a result, many of us are hurting both at the gas pump and the auto shop.
But the real problem goes beyond rising costs.
South Central Pennsylvania functions as a regional infrastructure hub, yet it lacks the modern transportation network needed to support that role.

Overreliance on personal vehicles forces households to shoulder rising vehicular expenses while leaving many residents (especially those without access to a car) bereft of reliable ways to get to work, school, or essential services.
This is especially threatening for people who require frequent medical treatment.
I’m very interested Pennsylvania directing construction towards the development of better transportation infrastructure.
In particular, I am eager to explore the platform proposed by Transit For All PA .
Summarily, it seeks to: Generate $1.65 billion annually, replacing Act 89’s transit funding Expand and maintain transit while allowing local governments to add (but not replace) funding.
Promote flexible spending.
Expand public ownership of infrastructure.
Build using union labor.
Transition to clean, electrified fleets that support good jobs.
Create equitable access and community development by funding low-income fare programs.
Invest in bike and pedestrian connections.
Promote affordable housing near transit.
This is a forward-looking investment in mobility, economic resilience, and public health.
By strengthening transit in this way, we can reduce household transportation costs, improve access to essential services, and build communities that are more connected, sustainable, and fair.

Affordable High Speed Internet for Rural Communities Rural communities oftentimes have limited access to high-speed internet, which is important for remote work, education, and overall quality of life.
Under President Biden, federal grant programs were sought to support the installation of fiber-optic cable, which is the fastest and most reliable technology.
Satellite connections have lower upfront costs, but can be more expensive for customers and can’t offer the same maximum speeds as fiber.
Nevertheless, Donald Trump overhauled the federal program , reducing our future grants and doubling the number of locations Elon Musk’s SpaceX satellites will cover.

As a result of the latest changes to the grant awards, Pennsylvania anticipates spending $711 million on connecting nearly 130,000 homes to high speed internet - a far cry from the $1.1 billion originally allocated to the commonwealth for the task.
The president’s decision is cronyism at its most glaring and is not in keeping with the objectives of Pennsylvania.

In my cursory research, I wasn’t able to find any resources detailing what state funds Pennsylvania contributes to providing high speed internet to rural areas - we seemingly exclusively use federal funds.
The reduction in those grants has caused some contractors have started turning down work in Pennsylvania due to a poor calculated return on investment.
Without additional federal funding, installing fiberoptic cable competes with other commonwealth appropriation budgetary items.

We must advocate for the restoration of that funding. “ Be the change you want to see happen. ” — Diane Kennedy Pike other inquiries: Committee to Elect Nathan Wood 361 Pine Hill Road Carlisle, PA 17013 email: admin@electnathanwood.com call: 717.683.7065 © # Committee to Elect Nathan Wood.

added: 0 Skip to Content HOME WHY I'M RUNNING ISSUES EVENTS Donate Open Menu Close Menu Donate HOME WHY I'M RUNNING ISSUES EVENTS Open Menu Close Menu HOME WHY I'M RUNNING ISSUES EVENTS Donate < Back Anti- Corruption & Legislative Reform The needs of everyday Pennsylvanians are getting sidelined because of legislative corruption and rules that make it easy to do nothing.
Despite being richly compensated for their full-time work, Pennsylvania’s General Assembly passed a mere 65 bills last year - one of the least productive sessions in decades.

In part, this is because PA majority leaders and committee chairpersons have enormous discretion over legislative agendas and can effectively block legislation by never scheduling it for consideration.
Many good proposals die simply because our legislators refuse to debate them.
Add to that opaque financial practices, unlimited campaign contributions and gifts, and corporate lobbying, and you have a recipe for disaster.

We can’t possibly expect our legislature to negotiate hard issues like affordability, housing, healthcare, or the proliferation of AI so long as its members are being bought by dark money and shielded from having to make tough decisions.
I want to shake up the status-quo.
We need to make it harder for the General Assembly to duck hard choices and incentivize accountability and reciprocity.
To that end, here are some reforms I support: Mirror the Colorado G.A.V.E.L.

Amendment I advocate Pennsylvania renders its own version of Colorado’s GAVEL Amendment (Give A Vote to Every Legislator), which requires that every bill introduced must be assigned to a committee, receive a public hearing, and be voted on by the committee members.
This effectively eliminates pocket vetoes where a committee chair can kill bills by never scheduling them.

The amendment was approved by 72% of Colorado voters in 1988 and led to a massive increase in legislative visibility and productivity, although it isn’t directly correlated with a significant increase in legislative enactment.
Procedural changes such as this will force our elected officials to take positions on legislative proposals, making them more answerable to us.
Given the PA General Assembly’s tendency to gridlock on partisan lines, I believe this type of reform is necessary to making real progress.
Ban gifts and business interests for sitting legislators As taxpayers, we are paying full-time premiums for part-time effort from many of our elected leaders.
Pennsylvania is one of 10 full-time legislatures in the United States and has the 3rd highest paid legislature in the nation.
But despite their generous salaries, benefits, and pensions, many PA legislators want more.
There are no limits on gifts legislators may receive and the provisions allowing them to avoid reporting it are libera (see HGOC report, page 27 ).
Further, approximately half of the 50-member Senate and a fourth of the 203-member House of Representatives maintain other business activities in addition to their legislative duties.
Unlimited gifts and private business interests bias elected officials’ decisions and distract them from the important work they have been elected (and richly compensated) to perform.

For my part, I don’t mind working hard.
But it shouldn’t be this hard to survive in PA.
My experience is far from unique.
The majority of Americans do not possess assets, and wages have not kept up with inflation and rising prices.
Until we address the underlying policies causing increasing economic disparity in our region, this will continue to be a critical problem.
While many of our economic hurdles are being created at the national level, there are proposals we can employ to better position Pennsylvanians for success.

Support the Affordability Action Plan Senate democrats have rolled out a legislative slate which seeks to improve the wellfare of Pennsylvanians by: Raising the minimum wage to $15/hour by 2029 ( HB 2189 & SB 19 ).
Expanding the Child Care Contribution Tax Credit .
Universal free school breakfast and lunch ( SB 180 ).
Protecting and expanding access to healthcare ( SB 322 ).
Build more housing, reduce costs, and create opportunities through Governor Shapiro’s Housing Action Plan , and Lightning Plan s.
Aid first-time homebuyers with financial assistance through the Put Down Roots PA Pilot Program ( SB 753 ).
These are all hugely important initiatives, and I very much support their implementation.

Tie Legislators' Cost of Living Adjustments to the Minimum wage While Pennsylvania legislators have received an automatic cost of living adjustment since 1995, the minimum wage here in Pennsylvania has remained fixed at $7.25 since 2009, when the federal minimum wage was first implemented.
We tie for last with 19 other states for having the lowest minimum wage in the nation.
It is manifestly unfair for elected officials to give themselves an annual cost of living adjustment without doing the same for the poorest wage earners in the state.
If we can’t afford to pay our poorest workers a living wage, then we can’t afford to pay more for leaders who already have it too good.
I will propose legislation requiring any legislative cost of living adjustments to be applied to the minimum wage.
This legislation isn’t going to solve wage stagnation on its own - it’s going to take a lot more than that to get them where they need to be.

What it will do is incentivize legislators to actually attend to the problem - it provides a strong personal motivator to make the minimum wage as high as the General Assembly can square with their constituency.
Improve Ratepayer Protections Utility bills are a real problem right now - the unlawful war in Iran and the encroachment of data centers are ramping up the price of fuel and the demands on our grid.
Energy costs were already too high - now they are intolerable.
Fortunately, there is some important legislation in the works which I stand behind.
House Bill 2333 – the Return to Ratepayer Protection Act – improves on what’s worked for decades to protect consumers.
The act would make sure: Ratepayers aren’t charged more to offset delinquent accounts.
Delinquent ratepayers working with utilities on payment plans are protected from shutoffs, and winter shutoffs are remain prohibited.
Account holders behind on payments will get better information, earlier information, and will be notified using multiple methods.
Lower-income households will have more flexible payment options, and fees will better reflect what people can afford.
Water, Sewer, and Gas authorities will have better tools to keep services running while working with customers on payments.
Rep.
Heather Boyd and Rep.

Liz Fiedler’s House Bill 2131– the Fairness in Retail Electricity Act – protects consumers who took part in the state’s Electric Choice program but ended up paying higher rates than if they had stayed with their default “home” utility and were unknowingly reenrolled with higher rate providers when their contract ended.
Customers like you paid more than $2 billion you didn’t have to pay.
The Fairness in Retail Electricity Act would: Return customers to the local default service provider when a contract with an outside provider ends.
Prevent retail energy sellers from automatically enrolling customers into a month-to-month variable plan.
Make sure customers can still choose to shop for electricity.

Economists frequently measure inequality using the Gini coefficient, a scale from 0 to 1 where 0 means perfect equality and 1 means all wealth sits with one person.
PA’s 34th districts trail the national average of 0.49, which is very high relative to other developed nations.

As identified by the World Happiness Report , prosperous countries with low Gini coefficients share a common approach: they use progressive tax systems and crack down on tax avoidance, ensure fair wages and safe working conditions, guarantee broad access to healthcare and social services, invest in anti‑poverty programs, and build governments that are diverse, transparent, and trusted.
These are exactly the areas where Pennsylvania must do better.

If we want South Central PA to be a place where everyone - not just the corporate elite - can build a secure life, we need to commit to the same principles that make more equitable societies possible.
Invest in Public Transportation Recent global instability has underscored a hard truth: America’s transportation system remains highly dependent on global oil markets and fragile supply chains.
As a result, many of us are hurting both at the gas pump and the auto shop.
But the real problem goes beyond rising costs.
South Central Pennsylvania functions as a regional infrastructure hub, yet it lacks the modern transportation network needed to support that role.

Overreliance on personal vehicles forces households to shoulder rising vehicular expenses while leaving many residents (especially those without access to a car) bereft of reliable ways to get to work, school, or essential services.
This is especially threatening for people who require frequent medical treatment.
I’m very interested Pennsylvania directing construction towards the development of better transportation infrastructure.
In particular, I am eager to explore the platform proposed by Transit For All PA .
Summarily, it seeks to: Generate $1.65 billion annually, replacing Act 89’s transit funding Expand and maintain transit while allowing local governments to add (but not replace) funding.
Promote flexible spending.
Expand public ownership of infrastructure.
Build using union labor.
Transition to clean, electrified fleets that support good jobs.
Create equitable access and community development by funding low-income fare programs.
Invest in bike and pedestrian connections.
Promote affordable housing near transit.
This is a forward-looking investment in mobility, economic resilience, and public health.
By strengthening transit in this way, we can reduce household transportation costs, improve access to essential services, and build communities that are more connected, sustainable, and fair.

Affordable High Speed Internet for Rural Communities Rural communities oftentimes have limited access to high-speed internet, which is important for remote work, education, and overall quality of life.
Under President Biden, federal grant programs were sought to support the installation of fiber-optic cable, which is the fastest and most reliable technology.
Satellite connections have lower upfront costs, but can be more expensive for customers and can’t offer the same maximum speeds as fiber.
Nevertheless, Donald Trump overhauled the federal program , reducing our future grants and doubling the number of locations Elon Musk’s SpaceX satellites will cover.

As a result of the latest changes to the grant awards, Pennsylvania anticipates spending $711 million on connecting nearly 130,000 homes to high speed internet - a far cry from the $1.1 billion originally allocated to the commonwealth for the task.
The president’s decision is cronyism at its most glaring and is not in keeping with the objectives of Pennsylvania.

In my cursory research, I wasn’t able to find any resources detailing what state funds Pennsylvania contributes to providing high speed internet to rural areas - we seemingly exclusively use federal funds.
The reduction in those grants has caused some contractors have started turning down work in Pennsylvania due to a poor calculated return on investment.
Without additional federal funding, installing fiberoptic cable competes with other commonwealth appropriation budgetary items.
We must advocate for the restoration of that funding. “ Be the change you want to see happen. ” — Diane Kennedy Pike Data centers Your running dishwasher registers around 65-70 decibels.

We use the Fair Funding formula, and algorithm which directs state money equalizing funding for places with lower property taxes.
Senator Rothman did not effectively advocate for Cumberland Valley’s financing through this formula, whereupon the school was subsequently excluded from the algorithm and receives no supplement.
This matters - it’s one of the reasons we need accountability in this district.

Governor Josh Shapiro’s latest budget proposal for the 2026-27 fiscal year includes a $565 million increase directed through the adequacy formula, which would help to alleviate some of the burden experienced by districts with less property tax revenue.
I support this and will endeavor to see our schools receive the funding they so critically require.
Fund PA State System of Higher Education (PASSHE) The Pennsylvania State System of Higher Education (PASSHE) exists to keep college within reach for everyday Pennsylvanians.
Schools like Shippensburg University and West Chester University give students (especially first-generation and working-class ones) an affordable path to a degree.
When PASSHE is strong, tuition stays lower and Pennsylvanians have more opportunities to gain the education they need to thrive.
When it’s underfunded, students pay more and communities lose out.
Supporting PASSHE is more than an investment in education - it is an investment in economic growth, local communities, and equal opportunity across the state.

HB2370 would standardize cyber charter school tuition at $8,000 per student, which will save traditional districts an estimated $530 million.

In response, Governor Josh Shapiro’s latest budget proposal for the 2026-27 fiscal year includes $565 million increase in education spending directed through the adequacy formula, a mathematical plan to redistribute resources equitably to poorly-funded districts.
This is a necessary step in the right direction. “ Genius without education is like silver in the mine. ” — Benjamin Franklin FAQ Where do you stand on ICE?

ICE may indeed have legally authorized duties within our government - kidnapping children, violently suppressing peaceful protesters, performing arrests and raiding homes without warrants, torturing detainees, and murdering civilians are not among them.
I condemn those illegal, cruel, wicked activities and anyone who participates in them, and I encourage you to join me in peacefully doing likewise.
In the immortal words of Edmund Burke: “All that is necessary for the triumph of evil is for good men to do nothing.” What do you think of PA's Election Integrity?

While working at the 87th legislative district office in the leadup to the 2020 election, I spoke with numerous constituents and non-constituents alike who insisted there was widespread election fraud.
Every one of those claims I heard was entirely unevidenced .
I never spoke with anyone who witnessed fraud themselves, knew someone who had, provided proof of fraud, or who was willing to speak with the FBI, attorney general, or local bureau of elections.
They merely repeated unsubstantiated claims that fraud had occurred.

I don’t normally feel comfortable speaking in absolute terms, but I can say with near-total confidence that fears of widespread election fraud in Pennsylvania elections, both then and now, are unfounded.
Don’t believe me - believe the staggering 43 court victories upholding the results of that election.
So long as they retain demonstrable veracity, I commit to upholding the results of free and fair elections here in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, regardless of their outcomes.
Do you support the Legalization of Marijuana?
Legalizing marijuana for individuals over 21 would not only act as a source of tax revenue, but would remove significant barriers to getting help.

According to research on treatment barriers , fears surrounding the illegality of cannabis - including potential legal, professional, and social consequences - act as a significant barrier for individuals seeking assistance for cannabis use disorder.
We can simultaneously remove that barrier and fund high-priority public services with one decision.
Do you support Reproductive Rights?

While it is a tremendous sadness whenever an abortion is deemed necessary, it remains a medical (and in some cases financial) imperative, and consequently I support its continued availability and coverage.
What is your position on LGBTQ+ Issues?
I am often asked this question in broad terms.
Succinctly, I think LGBTQ+ people deserve a life of visibility and dignity, the same as anyone.

Regarding marriage contracts, the role of the state is to create and enforce practical legal requirements and regulations (such as age and consent), and to adjudicate matters of taxation, inheritance, spousal rights, and separation.

I support the state rendering those same services towards LGBTQ+ couples. “ ...Then they came for me And there was no one left to speak out for me. ” — Pastor Martin Niemöller other inquiries: Committee to Elect Nathan Wood 361 Pine Hill Road Carlisle, PA 17013 email: admin@electnathanwood.com call: 717.683.7065 © # Committee to Elect Nathan Wood.

added: 0 Skip to Content HOME WHY I'M RUNNING ISSUES EVENTS Donate Open Menu Close Menu Donate HOME WHY I'M RUNNING ISSUES EVENTS Open Menu Close Menu HOME WHY I'M RUNNING ISSUES EVENTS Donate < Back Education A 2023 court ruling found Pennsylvania’s school funding system unconstitutional due to inequities, resulting in a $5.1 billion shortfall in high-need districts.
We use the Fair Funding formula, and algorithm which directs state money equalizing funding for places with lower property taxes.
Senator Rothman did not effectively advocate for Cumberland Valley’s financing through this formula, whereupon the school was subsequently excluded from the algorithm and receives no supplement.
This matters - it’s one of the reasons we need accountability in this district.

Governor Josh Shapiro’s latest budget proposal for the 2026-27 fiscal year includes a $565 million increase directed through the adequacy formula, which would help to alleviate some of the burden experienced by districts with less property tax revenue.
I support this and will endeavor to see our schools receive the funding they so critically require.
Fund PA State System of Higher Education (PASSHE) The Pennsylvania State System of Higher Education (PASSHE) exists to keep college within reach for everyday Pennsylvanians.
Schools like Shippensburg University and West Chester University give students (especially first-generation and working-class ones) an affordable path to a degree.
When PASSHE is strong, tuition stays lower and Pennsylvanians have more opportunities to gain the education they need to thrive.
When it’s underfunded, students pay more and communities lose out.
Supporting PASSHE is more than an investment in education - it is an investment in economic growth, local communities, and equal opportunity across the state.
Stratify Cyber Charter School Tuition Pennsylvania law requires districts to pay tuition to cyber charter schools for each resident student enrolled.
These payments are based on district expenditures rather than the actual cost of providing online education, leading to significant financial impacts on local taxpayers and budgets.
Currently, costs fluctuate between $7,000 to $25,000 per cyber charter student, and more than double that for special education students.
HB2370 would standardize cyber charter school tuition at $8,000 per student, which will save traditional districts an estimated $530 million.

Support Josh Shapiro's Education Budget A 2023 court ruling found Pennsylvania’s school funding system unconstitutional due to inequities, resulting in a $5.1 billion shortfall in high-need districts.

In response, Governor Josh Shapiro’s latest budget proposal for the 2026-27 fiscal year includes $565 million increase in education spending directed through the adequacy formula, a mathematical plan to redistribute resources equitably to poorly-funded districts.

This is a necessary step in the right direction. “ Genius without education is like silver in the mine. ” — Benjamin Franklin other inquiries: Committee to Elect Nathan Wood 361 Pine Hill Road Carlisle, PA 17013 email: admin@electnathanwood.com call: 717.683.7065 © # Committee to Elect Nathan Wood.

While working at the 87th legislative district office in the leadup to the 2020 election, I spoke with numerous constituents and non-constituents alike who insisted there was widespread election fraud.
Every one of those claims I heard was entirely unevidenced .
I never spoke with anyone who witnessed fraud themselves, knew someone who had, provided proof of fraud, or who was willing to speak with the FBI, attorney general, or local bureau of elections.

Don’t believe me - believe the staggering 43 court victories upholding the results of that election.

added: Proven Results for Our District Meaningful solutions for a stronger community.
Actions speak louder than promises.
In public service, good intentions aren’t good enough.
Results matter and the achievements below demonstrate legislative solutions that directly benefit the people.
These real-world examples show Senator Webber’s experience working independently and across the aisle to deliver practical outcomes for our community.
Instead of promises, he brings a proven record of bipartisan, common-sense results that put local needs ahead of party politics.

Scroll to Explore Sound Solutions: Addressing Noise Pollution And Improving Government Efficiency Senator Michael Webber secured millions of dollars in state funding to improve the quality of life for residents in his district.
To help future projects avoid the same challenges he introduced thoughtful reforms to simplify the process.

Read Case Study Protecting Michigan’s Most Vulnerable: Oversight and reform for children’s mental health services The Hawthorn Center, Michigan’s only state-run psychiatric hospital for children, faced scrutiny after reports of neglect, mistreatment, and safety concerns.
Senator Webber called for oversight hearings and an audit to assess the issues and hold the state accountable.
Senator Webber introduced a package of bills to address the audit findings, focusing on improving oversight, accountability, and safeguarding patient rights within the state’s mental health services.

Read Case Study Promises Kept: Securing and Protecting the Rochester Community House Investment Senator Webber contributed to the city of Rochester’s efforts to acquire funding for a major renovation to the Rochester Community House.
He helped secure state budget funds for the much-needed renovations.
When debates over state spending threatened the appropriation, persistent legislative advocacy preserved the promised funds.
Read Case Study THANK YOU FOR YOUR SUPPORT!

Diehl says Oregon has enough tax momey For Diehl,Oregon needs to do a way better job of prioritizing its spending, not seeking new taxes The following is from state Representative Ed Diehl, writing about Oregon government's lack of competence and its inability to deliver on programs and not being able to prioritize its spending, and its continual lack of fiscal discipline and its continually looking for taxpayers to bail it out: Friend, Sometimes one person's story can expose everything that is wrong with a government system.
The Oregonian recently told the story of a formerly homeless Oregon woman who suffers from serious mental illness.
Her story is ultimately one of hope.
She found stability.
She found housing.
She is working.
But buried inside her story are three remarkable admissions about the systems that were supposed to help her.
She believes some people suffering from serious mental illness need a level of care they cannot obtain on their own.
“I think we should reinstate institutions to care for people who need more,” she said.
She also limits how much she works because earning too much could jeopardize the government health and disability benefits she depends upon.
And all of this is happening while Portland-area governments say they don't have enough money to keep hundreds of shelter beds open.
Put those three things together and you begin to see Oregon's real problem.
We don't necessarily lack money.
We lack priorities.
Hundreds of millions for climate programs.
Not enough for shelter beds.
Portland is reducing shelter spending as it deals with its budget shortfall.
At the same time, the Portland Clean Energy Community Benefits Fund is projected to begin FY 2026-27 with a fund balance of approximately $698 million.
Think about the scale of that number.

Nearly $700 million accumulated in a government climate fund while people suffering from serious mental illness are sleeping on Portland's streets and the city says it cannot afford existing shelter capacity.
That doesn't mean every dollar of that $698 million is uncommitted or can legally be transferred to shelters tomorrow.
Much of it is dedicated to grants, contracts and future expenditures.
But government created those priorities.
And Portland has already demonstrated that the wall around this money isn't absolute.
This year the city transferred approximately $27 million of PCEF interest earnings into its General Fund.
Apparently dedicated money can become flexible when elected officials decide it needs to be.
The question isn't whether we should empty the climate fund tomorrow.

The question is simpler: How did we create a government where accumulating hundreds of millions for future climate programs takes precedence over keeping vulnerable human beings off the streets today?
More than half a billion dollars saved for future preschool expansion Cross the governmental boundary from the City of Portland to Multnomah County and the numbers are just as extraordinary.

Multnomah County's Preschool for All program has accumulated approximately $514 million in "Dedicated Savings." Add approximately $47 million in contingency and reserves and the number exceeds $560 million.
Again, that money isn't an accounting accident.
It is intentional.
Multnomah County designed the program to collect more taxes than it currently needs and bank the excess to pay for preschool expansion in future years.
There may be arguments for doing that.
But there is also a moral question that shouldn't be ignored.

Should government collect taxes today and warehouse more than half a billion dollars for services it plans to provide years from now while cutting shelter capacity for desperate people who need help tonight?
You don't have to oppose preschool to believe the answer is no.
Government is about priorities.
And budgets reveal those priorities better than speeches ever will.
Then there's the money that was actually supposed to solve homelessness The third pot of money may be the most troubling.
Metro's Supportive Housing Services tax was specifically created to address homelessness.
During its first three fiscal years, the program collected approximately $592 million.
Yet Metro's auditor found that only about 40% of the tax revenue collected during those years had been spent.
The result?
An accumulated fund balance of approximately $354 million.
To be clear, that is a historical figure, not the current balance.
Governments have subsequently spent down much of that accumulated money.
But that raises an entirely different question.
How does a region collect so much money specifically for homelessness that it accumulates $354 million it cannot deploy — and then, just a few years later, find itself closing shelter beds?
That's not a revenue problem.
That's a management problem.
It's a priorities problem.
And ultimately it's an accountability problem.
Then listen to the woman we're supposedly trying to help The most powerful part of this story isn't actually the money.
It's what this woman says about mental illness.

After living through serious mental illness and homelessness herself, she recognizes something Oregon policymakers have been reluctant to acknowledge: Some people are simply too sick to seek the treatment they need on their own.
For decades, the dominant philosophy has been deinstitutionalization and community-based treatment.
Organizations such as Disability Rights Oregon continue to make preventing institutionalization an explicit priority.
Community treatment absolutely should be the first choice for people capable of succeeding with it.
But what about the person experiencing psychosis who doesn't believe he is sick?
What about the woman incapable of keeping an appointment, taking her medication or even recognizing that she needs help?
What about the person cycling endlessly between a sidewalk, an emergency room, a jail cell and back to the sidewalk?
Calling that "freedom" isn't compassionate.
Sometimes compassion means intervening.
Even NAMI has begun to recognize that This debate has changed substantially in just a few years.
I know because I've been part of it.
In 2023, I tried working with NAMI Oregon on civil-commitment reforms.
At that time, there was substantial resistance to expanding involuntary treatment, including from organizations within the mental-health advocacy community.
NAMI's position has since evolved.
By late 2024, NAMI Oregon publicly acknowledged how difficult this issue had been within its own membership.
Executive Director Chris Bouneff described civil commitment as a "tightrope" and said it wasn't an issue on which he originally wanted NAMI to lead.
But NAMI also acknowledged the reality staring Oregon in the face: Our current system often waits until someone suffering from serious mental illness commits a crime before government intervenes.
So in 2025 NAMI Oregon did something significant.
It sponsored legislation to lower Oregon's criteria for civil commitment.
That evolution shows that experience is forcing people across the ideological spectrum to reconsider the assumptions behind Oregon's mental-health system.
We don't need to recreate the horrific institutions of generations past.
We need a continuum of care.
Community treatment whenever possible.
Intensive outpatient treatment when necessary.
Secure residential treatment for those who need it.
Adequate psychiatric hospital beds.

And, for the relatively small number of people whose illness has rendered them incapable of recognizing their own condition or caring for themselves, a humane civil-commitment system that allows us to intervene before they end up in jail, dead or living under a tarp.
That isn't abandoning civil liberties.
It's recognizing that serious mental illness can sometimes rob a person of the ability to exercise those liberties meaningfully.
And then government tells her not to work too much Finally, consider what happens when someone actually makes it through this broken system.
This woman got stable.
She found housing.
She began working.
That's exactly the outcome taxpayers should want.
And then she encountered another government-created problem.
If she earns too much, she risks losing health coverage and disability benefits she depends upon.
So she limits her work.
She's responding rationally to the incentives government created.
Think about how backwards that is.
We spend enormous sums trying to move someone from homelessness toward stability.
Then, when she succeeds, we create a financial incentive for her not to become fully independent.
A rational safety net should work in the opposite direction.
Benefits should phase out gradually as someone's income rises.
Working another hour should always leave a person better off, not threaten the medical care or stability that allowed her to work in the first place.
Government should provide a ladder.
We've built a cliff.
Put people before programs That's what makes this woman's story so important.
She isn't a line item in a government budget.
She's the person all of these programs supposedly exist to help.
And look at what we've built around her.
A city cutting shelter capacity while its climate program carries an enormous accumulated balance.
A county cutting homelessness services while deliberately saving more than half a billion dollars for future preschool expansion.
A regional homelessness program that once accumulated $354 million because government couldn't deploy the money fast enough.
A mental-health system that too often waits for someone to deteriorate until the criminal-justice system intervenes.
And a disability system that can punish someone financially for working more after she finally gets back on her feet.
Oregon taxpayers are extraordinarily generous.
The answer cannot always be another tax.
Before government asks working families for another dollar, we should demand that it put first things first.
Keep emergency shelters available for people who need them.
Build enough psychiatric and secure residential capacity to treat people with serious mental illness.
Fix Oregon's civil-commitment laws so families don't have to wait for a loved one to commit a crime before getting meaningful help.
Reform benefit cliffs so work and independence are rewarded rather than punished.
And take a hard look at the hundreds of millions of dollars accumulating in dedicated government accounts while basic human needs go unmet.
We don't need to choose between compassion and fiscal responsibility.
Real compassion demands fiscal responsibility.
Because every dollar government warehouses, wastes or spends on a lower priority is a dollar that isn't available for the person sleeping outside tonight.
This woman's story proves there is hope.
Now Oregon government needs to get its priorities straight.
Thank you for taking the time to read and stay engaged.
I’ll continue working to bring common sense, accountability, and transparency to Salem, and I’ll keep you informed about the issues that matter to our communities and our state.
Thank you for the opportunity to serve you.
In Liberty (posted by Elvis Clark on October 9, 2026) Powered by

added: Skip to content Donate to Eric Conroy for Congress Home Meet Eric Issues Close Issues Open Issues Border Security Cryptocurrency and Blockchain Education Jobs and the Economy National Defense Protecting Women's Sports Safe Neighborhoods Small Business Social Security and Medicare Transportation and Infrastructure Veterans Media Center Close Media Center Open Media Center In the News Press Kit Action Center Close Action Center Open Action Center Endorse Eric Volunteer for Eric Contact Facebook X-twitter Instagram Youtube Donate News CINCINNATI, OH — Republican candidate for Congress, Eric Conroy launches his third ad ahead of the general election in November. “ Chili Bar ” highlights his ties to Cincinnati.
Growing up in a westside family, he learned what it means to always put ‘service before self’.
Eric knows what it means to work hard, serve his community, and put others before himself.
His opponent Greg Landsman only serves himself and is the posterboy for corruption.
From tripling his net worth in less than four years in office, violating the STOCK Act with insider trading and disclosure laws, to appeasing lobbyists, he serves himself.
Conroy knows what it means to put his community first, and that is why he is running for Congress, to continue his life of service and represent Southwest Ohio with honor and integrity.
“Growing up in a westside family, I understand what it means to be part of a tight-knit community.
I have always appreciated service to others, and putting country first.

Per the report, when Landsman first ran for Congress in 2022, he reported just six stock holdings worth between $90,000 and $300,000.

His amended disclosure, filed almost three years after the original, shows he actually held 54 stock positions worth as much as $1.5 million, generating stock income at least 18 times higher than originally disclosed.
His net worth rose to as much as $3.5 million, tripling what it was before he entered office less than #ago.
This is not the first time Landsman’s financial hypocrisy has been exposed.
In 2024, Landsman was busted for failing to report more than 87 stock transactions within the legally required window, violating the STOCK Act.
The report comes on the heels of Landsman’s recent TV ad on ‘ fighting corruption ’ where he says, “No member of Congress should trade stocks.
So I led by example and got rid of my stocks” “The hypocrisy and arrogance of Greg Landsman know no bounds.

He has run his campaign talking about stopping corruption and claiming he is leading the charge to end congressional stock trading, while covering up his own stock trading and voting against legislation to stop the corrupt practice .
Landsman promises that he will clean up Washington, but in less than 4 years in Washington, he has become a corrupt politician entrenched in the swamp,” Conroy said.
“When you run ads blatantly lying to voters, it shows not only dishonesty but total contempt for the people you represent.
This district and its voters deserve a representative who’s honest with them, not one who lies to them while lining his own pockets.” ### Conroy for Congress 2692 Madison Rd.

added: Skip to content Donate to Eric Conroy for Congress Home Meet Eric Issues Close Issues Open Issues Border Security Cryptocurrency and Blockchain Education Jobs and the Economy National Defense Protecting Women's Sports Safe Neighborhoods Small Business Social Security and Medicare Transportation and Infrastructure Veterans Media Center Close Media Center Open Media Center In the News Press Kit Action Center Close Action Center Open Action Center Endorse Eric Volunteer for Eric Contact Facebook X-twitter Instagram Youtube Donate News Release: On Stock Trading, Greg Landsman is a Liar October 9, 2026 CINCINNATI, OH — Today, Conroy for Congress released the following statement after Greg Landsman’s latest bald-faced lie to voters about his stock-trading corruption.
In a recent interview with WCPO9, Landsman says, “Yeah, I sold my stocks…I put my money where my mouth is.” But he doesn’t remotely tell the full story.
The Truth: Tripling his net worth: Landsman’s first personal financial disclosure filed April 5, 2022, listed six stock holdings worth 90,000 – 300,000 in related income.
On January 24, 2025, nearly 3 years later, and four months after trading first drew coverage.
He filed an amended 2022 Personal Financial Disclosure listing 56 holdings worth $ 466,052- $1.8 million.
The top of his disclosed range grew by roughly $1.5 million.
Landsman also opened his general election with a TV ad claiming he’s outraged by congressional stock trading and got rid of his stocks.
His own filings with the House Clerk tell a different story, and most of that paper trail hasn’t been reported.
The Truth: 87 late transactions.
His August 2024 periodic transaction report covered 91 trades.
87 of those trades fell outside the required 45-day window and covered more than $1.4 million.
Craig Holman of Public Citizen called it a STOCK Act violation.
Todd Zinser, the former Commerce Department Inspector General, filed an ethics complaint .
Landsman said it was a mistake and that he doesn’t handle his own trades.

On May 13, 2025, Landsman issued a release: “Landsman complies with The TRUST In Congress Act before it becomes law.” The Truth: The day of both a victory lap and the violation: The same day he filed a PTR disclosing an Exxon Mobil transaction 327 days past the deadline – a second STOCK Act violation- filed the day he declared himself clean.
Greg Landsman claims to be an ethics warrior, but he is really the worst of Washington: corrupt and dishonest.
The Truth: On July 22, 2026, Landsman voted “Nay” on the “ Stop Insider Trading Act .” “Greg Landsman continues to display a total arrogance and contempt for the voters he represents.
He claims that he is cleaning up stock trading corruption, but only after he tripled his net worth in office.
This corrupt liar has no place representing the people of Southwest Ohio.” – Collin Wojcik, Campaign Manager, Conroy for Congress.

DONATE PRATT PLAYBOOK AFFORDABILITY ACCOUNTABILITY SAFE COMMUNITITES Residents want everyday purchases to be affordable, bad actors to be held accountable, and for their reps to lead with common sense.
The President is not popular, so all messaging should be focused on local politics and needs.
AFFORDABILITY: Housing: Lower the Cost of Building a Home: Housing costs rise when it takes too long and costs too much to build.
Eric will work to streamline federal permitting, expand the American supply of building materials, and encourage more young people to pursue good-paying careers in the skilled trades.
Increasing supply and reducing unnecessary barriers can help bring housing costs down and keep more money in families’ pockets.
Social Security: Protect the Promise.
Strengthen the Future.
Eric believes seniors who paid into Social Security should receive the benefits they earned and keep more of that money.
He supports eliminating the federal income tax on Social Security benefits and increasing the taxable income cap to help strengthen the program.
But we need to be honest.
The social security program is not sustainable under the current qualifications.
For younger generations, Eric supports giving workers a choice.
Those who remain in Social Security should understand that, as Americans live and work longer, the full retirement age may need to gradually increase.

Younger workers should also have the option to opt out and take responsibility for building their own retirement through options such as 401(k)s, 403(b)s, traditional IRAs, Roth IRAs, and other tax-advantaged investments.
We need to support all options for Americans to take control of their investment opportunities, not just one government-controlled option.
Child Tax Credit: Put More Money Back in Families’ Pockets Eric believes families should be able to keep more of what they earn.
In the Minnesota Senate, he authored legislation creating a $3,000 refundable child tax credit for young children and has continued supporting efforts to expand child tax relief.
MN Revisor's Office.

In Congress, Eric would support expanding the federal Child Tax Credit to provide up to $3,000 per child for families who need the help most, giving parents more breathing room for groceries, childcare, housing, and the everyday costs of raising a family. ​ Jobs: Build a Pro-Growth Economy Eric believes good-paying jobs are built by growing the economy, not growing government.
He supports policies that encourage innovation and investment here in the United States, expand reliable and affordable domestic energy, and prepare American workers for the jobs of tomorrow.
That means strengthening career and technical education, apprenticeships, and workforce training so more people can build successful careers right here at home.
The goal is a pro-growth economy that creates opportunity, raises wages, and keeps America competitive.

Eric is proud to be endorsed by the National Federation of Independent Businesses (NFIB), as well as union (like the MN Pipe Fitters) and non-union employers representing thousands of small businesses and hard-working employees across the state.
Agriculture: Support Farmers.
Keep Food Affordable.
Eric believes keeping food affordable starts with keeping Minnesota agriculture strong.
Farmers face many of the same rising costs as families—from energy and equipment to labor and transportation.

Eric supports reliable and affordable energy, fair trade, strong infrastructure, and practical federal policies that give farmers and agricultural businesses the certainty they need to invest, grow, and plan for the next generation.
Eric is proud to have earned the endorsement of the Minnesota Farm Bureau PAC and will make sure farmers, producers, and rural communities have a strong voice in Washington.
Agriculture is more than an industry—it supports families, small businesses, communities, and a way of life that has shaped Minnesota for generations. ​ Healthcare: Lower Costs.
Protect Choice.
Eric believes healthcare reform should focus on bending the cost curve and making coverage more affordable without taking choices away from patients and families.
If someone likes the insurance they receive through their employer, they should be able to keep it.
Eric does not support replacing private and employer-sponsored coverage with a single government-run healthcare system.

Instead, he supports practical reforms that increase competition, improve transparency, reduce unnecessary administrative costs, and address the role of pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) so patients can better understand what they are paying and more of the savings negotiated in the prescription-drug system can benefit them.
Eric’s goal is clear: lower healthcare costs, make healthcare more transparent, and offer more choices, not fewer.
ACCOUNTABILITY: Program Integrity: Stop Fraud Before the Money Is Gone Eric spent more than 30 years in banking and finance, including leadership roles at Target and U.S.
Bank, where he worked in risk management and fraud prevention.

In Congress, Eric would bring that same prevention-first mindset to government by creating an independent Office of Program Integrity focused on identifying fraud, waste, abuse, and weak controls before losses reach billions of dollars.
Like a fraud-prevention team at a major financial institution, it would use audits, data analysis, and cross-agency information to flag problems early and protect taxpayer dollars.
The goal is simple: Build the guardrails before the money is gone.
Make Sure Help Reaches the People Who Need It the Most Federal programs only work when the rules are followed.
Eric supports stronger accountability for states that administer federal dollars, including clear eligibility standards, regular oversight, and swift correction when safeguards fail.
When states ignore established rules, taxpayers lose confidence and people who genuinely need assistance can be pushed aside.
In Congress, Eric will work to make sure states are accountable for how federal dollars are spent so help reaches the people it was intended to serve.
Stronger Penalties: Make Fraud Cost More Than It Pays Fraud against federal programs steals from taxpayers and from the people those programs are meant to help.
Eric supports stronger penalties for individuals and organizations that knowingly defraud the government, especially in cases involving large-scale or repeat offenses.
Families are tired of “rules for thee but not for me”.
They work hard and want assurance that everyone is held to the same standards they follow every day.

Accountability should be clear: if you deliberately steal taxpayer dollars, the consequences should be serious enough to deter the next person from trying. ​ Common Sense Representation: Accessible, Accountable, and Focused on CD2 Eric’s dad always said “you’d think common sense would be more common” .
Eric has taken that and is working toward what he calls Minnesota Common Sense.
Here’s what that looks like: Eric believes representation starts with listening.

In Congress, he will stay connected to the people of the Second District through regular community meetings and Chat With Pratt events, giving families, businesses, local leaders, and community organizations a seat at the table.
Every stakeholder deserves to be heard, and Eric will remain accessible and responsive to the needs of the district.

His guiding question will remain simple: “What is best for Minnesota families?” Government should work for the people it serves, not political agendas, special interests, or the insiders who benefit from a broken system.

Eric will bring common sense, accountability, and practical problem-solving to Congress while never forgetting how he was raised or who he works for: the families and communities of Minnesota’s Second District.
SAFER COMMUNITIES: Work Together to Keep Communities Safe Public safety works best when law enforcement agencies communicate and cooperate.

Eric supports stronger coordination between federal, state, and local law enforcement so information is shared, resources are used effectively, and dangerous individuals do not fall through the cracks because agencies are working in silos.

Give Communities and Officers the Resources to Stay Safe Safe communities require both strong law enforcement and the resources necessary to prevent crime, respond to emergencies, and protect the people who answer the call.
Eric will work to ensure departments have the tools, training, technology, and resources they need to keep residents and officers safe.
The Second District is home to a significant law-enforcement community, making public safety especially personal to many families here.
Eric’s priority is straightforward: families should feel safe in their communities, and the men and women protecting them should make it home safely to their families every night.
He’s proud to have the endorsement of the Minnesota Police & Peace Officers Association because of these strong policy stances.
School Safety: Establish a Common Standard for Protecting Our Children Parents should be able to send their children to school knowing reasonable safety measures are in place.

Just as we establish basic standards to protect students from fires and other emergencies, Eric supports developing clear federal school-safety standards to help schools prepare for and respond to threats.
Those standards should focus on practical safeguards, emergency planning, communication, and coordination with local first responders while giving communities flexibility in how they meet them.
Every child, teacher, and staff member deserves a safe place to learn and work.
