A review of the public record behind a taxpayer-funded billboard, checked through October 8, 2026.
Fact-checking Lateefah Simon's claims and billboard In short: the public record does not show that Lateefah Simon delivered $833 million in federal funding to the East Bay.
It shows her delivering $11.2 million.
"I've delivered $833 million in federal funding to the East Bay" Clear Channel billboard, downtown Oakland.
"Paid for by official funds authorized by the House of Representatives." Date posted: not established.
Rep.

Lateefah Simon's office has stated a running total of federal money it has "secured," "delivered" or "brought home" to California's 12th District at every recorded town hall since May 29, 2025, in a series of press releases, on the office website and on a billboard.
This page sets out what we collected, how we tried to match her figures to federal award records, what each dollar we could trace turned out to be, and where the public record runs out.
It is a review of public records, not an audit: only her office, which has never published an award list, or the agencies, can settle what the $833 million consists of.
Sources are linked where they are used, and every one is listed at the bottom of the page.

Watch the video: Jamie Joyce on Lateefah Simon's $833 million claim (YouTube) Summary The claim What we collected Method Where the $833M sits Formula Disaster and airport Renewals Competitive Her appropriations Not itemized Second-guessing Her documented actions Conclusions If she provides the audit Limits Check it yourself All sources Summary: the record does not show Lateefah Simon delivered $833 million Our finding The public record does not show that Rep.
Simon delivered $833 million.
It shows her delivering $11.2M , which is 1.3% of the billboard figure: fifteen local projects she chose, written into law with her name on them.
The billboard is not the end of it.

Since she first gave the $833 million figure at a town hall on July 28, 2026, her office's website now says "$1.15B+ announced in grants for the district." Nothing on the site itemizes that number, and it is about $630 million more than everything her office has ever itemized in writing.
Every finding below concerns the $833 million; the larger figure rests on even less.
That leaves $821.8M , 98.7% of the billboard figure, that the record does not show her delivering.
Of that, $639.6M could be plausibly identified by matching government records with her claims in press releases and at town halls.
It is real federal money that came to the district, or to the state and regional agencies that serve it.

We are more confident of some of these matches than others: for $219.2M of it her office named the program and the recipient; for $150.2M it named the agency and the amount and we found the records; for $258.9M it gave only a category total and we inferred which records it must mean; and $11.3M is an award her office never stated at all, counted because it went to an organization she did name (the Method section shows which is which).
But all of it looks like it came through programs that pay a fixed amount to the same recipients whoever holds the seat, or through competitions the recipients entered and won on their own.
Her office announced this money; the agencies decided it.
We found no record of her office causing any of it.
In two categories the records that fit her description add up to more than the figure she gave; the "Not itemized by her office" section explains this and gives the more conservative count.

The remaining $182.2M was never itemized: for most of it, nothing her office has said in any release or at any town hall describes it by program, recipient or amount, so there is nothing to match a government record to; for the rest (a year-end research total and a few small lines), her words were not specific enough to identify an award.
We looked and could not find what it is.
We have some ideas, set out under "Not itemized by her office" below, and we have asked her for an audit of every number.

To get this far we worked through 1,121 source documents and records, listed at the bottom of this page: 19 of her office's press releases and 11 town hall recordings, quoted verbatim; 845 federal award pages; the enacted appropriations tables; her bills, amendments and roll-call votes; the court orders behind every restoration; and the news, agency and local-government documents that bear on each claim.

We cannot be certain of any of this without that audit.

How federal money reaches a district, in plain terms Most people assume that when a member of Congress announces federal money, the member brought it.
Usually that is not how it works.
Federal money reaches a district in five main ways, and only one of them involves the member choosing where it goes.
How the money arrives Who decides the amount Example from her totals Could she have changed it?
Formula money A formula in a law, applied by the agency: population, ridership, number of vouchers BART's transit grants, Oakland's housing vouchers, the city block grants It doesn't look like it.
The same amount goes to the same recipient whoever holds the seat.

Members vote on the overall bill, often among hundreds of items Disaster relief and entitlement A disaster declaration, or airport passenger counts The $88.89 million in storm repairs; the Oakland airport grants It doesn't look like it Renewals The agency, as the annual payment on a grant the recipient won years earlier The health centers' annual Health Center Program payments (awards made in 2018), BART's 2020 grant agreement It doesn't look like it.

The competition was decided before she took office Competitive grants The agency scores applications on merit and picks winners The Port of Oakland's $35.5 million port grant, UC Berkeley's research awards Not directly.
A member may write a support letter.
None from her office is on record, and no program we checked gives points for one.

For research grants in particular, a letter from a representative outside the scientific field should not affect a merit review and is not meant to; it is a gesture Community Project Funding (earmarks) The member requests a named project and amount; Congress writes it into the law Her fifteen FY2026 projects, $11,216,000 Yes.
This is the one place her name appears in the law She does not sit on the House Appropriations Committee, which writes the spending bills; her committees are Small Business and Oversight.

How we matched her figures to the record Fix her words.
Every funding sentence in a release or transcript was copied verbatim with its date and URL.
Verbs were logged separately ("announced," "welcomed," "secured," "delivered," "brought home"), because announcing a grant and delivering one are different claims.
Find the record.

For each line, search USASpending.gov by recipient, program and date window; where no single award page exists (block-grant allocations, FTA apportionments, enacted earmark tables), use the agency's published table.
Record the award ID, amount, date signed, period of performance and place of performance as the API returned them.
Count one amount per line.
The amount counted is the obligation in the claim window (the annual installment for a continuation award, not the multi-year total), so that nothing is counted twice across her cumulative figures.
Classify by mechanism, using the government's own label.
USASpending's assistance type (formula grant, project grant, direct payment, cooperative agreement), the program's statute, and the award's first date decide the category.
A continuation on an award first competed in 2018 is a renewal, not a win.
Test against the full district universe.
Pull every award and transaction with a CA-12 place of performance for the period and ask, for each of her lines, whether a different record fits as well or better.
Where more than one fits, say so.
Check for disruption.

Cross every matched award, and every district award, against the Grant Witness tracker, agency cancellation lists, court dockets and obligation timing, to see whether anything she counted was frozen, cut or restored, and by whom.
Re-verify live on a stated date, and grade confidence.
Figures were re-checked against their primary records on September 14 and October 7, 2026.
Confidence grades High: directly supported by a primary government record or her office's own words, re-checked live.
Medium-High: a primary record checked once that could not be re-fetched on the second date, or a record plus one inference the text states.
Medium: supported but resting on an inference or a single source.
Low: not supported, or supported only by the absence of evidence.
The Limits section lists the items rated below High on source grounds; the match-confidence tiers below cover the inference risk.
Uniqueness grades A match is Unique when her line names an amount and recipient that one record, or one obvious pair of records, fits.
It is Either/or, clarification requested when more than one record, or more than one set of records, fits her words, and the release gives no list to settle it.

In every either/or case on this page, whichever record is meant, the money is formula, renewal, entitlement or competitive, never money she designated, so the conclusion is the same; what differs is which award page to cite.
Unmatched lines have no record we could find.
Her figure, taken as stated marks the one amount we could not test against a record at all.

Included by us, not stated by her marks an award counted under one of her year-end totals that no release or transcript names; the one such case is flagged so it can be moved to the remainder if her office says it was not counted.

Agency and amount named; record inferred (19 items, $150.2M): her office named the agency, the purpose and the size ("over $110 million from HUD" for affordable housing; "$22.7 million" in SBIR awards) and we identified the records of that kind in the district; the match is reasonable but her office has not confirmed it.

Category total only; record inferred (10 items, $258.9M): her December 19, 2025 release says "Infrastructure projects in CA-12, including at the Oakland International Airport, have received over $193 million," names nothing else, and the airport grants are $44.3 million; the BART, Caltrans and port records in the tables are the infrastructure money of that size in the district, and we inferred that they are what the figure refers to.

What we can say about it, what is probably in it, and what would resolve it What "itemized" means on this page.
Money counts as itemized when her office described it in a release or at a town hall by program and recipient, specifically enough to be matched to a government record.
The $650.8M traced is all money of that kind; the $182.2M is money her office has either never described at all or described too loosely to identify an award.
This is a different measure from the sum of her written running totals ($520 million: $344 million for 2025 and $176 million for 2026 through June 18), which is smaller than the traced amount.

The two differ because the billboard's $833 million is a spoken total that grew well past the written ones with no release behind the growth, and because her category lines are open-ended: her December 19, 2025 release says "over $193 million" for infrastructure, and the BART, Caltrans, airport, port and Core Capacity records that fit it total about $303 million; her May 12, 2026 release says "over $110 million" from HUD, and the housing records that fit it total about $146 million.
"Over" is not contradicted by more.
We kept every fitting record in the tables so each candidate is visible.

A reader who instead caps each category at the minimum her office stated would put the traced total near $500 million and the undescribed remainder near $330 million; the category of every traced dollar, and the conclusion, are the same either way.
What we can say about it.

Her office's 2025 category totals (December 19, 2025 release) sum to about $333 million of the $344 million headline; her two 2026 releases itemize about $119 million of $142 million (May 12) and the health-center, DOJ, UC Berkeley, Alameda Health System, Kaiser and NEA lines of $176 million (June 18).
The office has never published an award list.
The spoken figures run ahead of everything itemized in writing by then ($520 million): by about $256 million on July 7, 2026 ($776 million) and about $313 million on July 28 ($833 million).

What is probably in it, based on the uniqueness test: the untraced part of the $37.9 million and $76.5 million research lines (UC Berkeley received $118.5M in competitive research obligations in the eight weeks before her September 2025 release alone, so almost any amount could be found there), the difference between multi-year award totals and the annual payments actually made (her AmeriCorps line, for example, matches the multi-year totals of three 2024 awards, not the 2025 payments), the SBIR and STTR awards beyond the three we found (suspected: $24.2 million was obligated to district firms in 2025 and her line says $22.7 million, but her office has not said which awards it counted), and the NeighborWorks, crime-lab and small health items that have no federal award record under the descriptions given.
All of those, if confirmed, would be competitive or continuation money.

Barbara Lee, in FY2022 to FY2024 (HRSA and SAMHSA "congressional directives" to West Oakland Health Council and other district health providers, $3.57 million in all) were still paying out during her term and may also sit inside her totals; they are member-directed money, but not hers.

What would resolve it: the audit her office has agreed to provide and has not.
Until then the right label is unexplained, not false.

Conclusions: Lateefah Simon's claim to have delivered $833 million is not supported by the public record Everything below is what the public record supports as of October 8, 2026.
None of it is certain without an audit.
Jamie Joyce has asked Rep.
Simon multiple times for an audit of the $833 million; she has agreed on video more than once and has not delivered one.
That accounting would let every line be re-checked; the agencies' answers to the Freedom of Information Act requests would settle whether her office wrote in support of the awards asked about.
Not shown by the record "I've delivered $833 million in federal funding to the East Bay." The record shows her delivering $11.2M, the fifteen projects she chose.

The other 98.7% of the figure is either money that arrived through formulas, declarations, renewals or competitions she had no documented hand in ($639.6M), or money her office has never identified ($182.2M).
Shown by the record Fifteen projects requested, fifteen funded, $11.2 million.
The total and the count match the enacted tables (one per-project figure differs; see Her appropriations).
This is the part of her record that "delivered" describes.

So is her statement at the Albany town hall (July 7, 2026, 19:14) that the Children's Hospital sickle cell lab got "a million dollars" through her: we read that as her $1,031,000 FY2026 project for the Pediatric Blood Disorder Research Center at UCSF Benioff Children's Hospital Oakland.

Not shown by the record "We got the $40 million back"; "we stood shoulder to shoulder... to keep that lab open." UC Berkeley did report losing about $40 million across campus (August 2026), and much of the terminated research money came back.
It came back by court order and agency reinstatement, in a case brought by six researchers.
The lab she names reports no lost or restored award.
Her documented contact with it is a visit and two letters about a different action.
The record shows advocacy; it does not show her office getting any dollar back.

Not shown by the record "Their funding was frozen... we helped to push to get some of that liquidated"; "their grant... was cut in half." No record of a freeze at a named East Bay clinic, no record of a halved grant, no record of her office's involvement.
A payment hold inside the government's payment system would not show in public data, so the proof could exist and not be public.
Not shown by the record "Clawed back $870 million." Nothing in the record shows $870 million, or any amount near it, clawed back from anyone.
The sum of her itemized figures is money agencies awarded in the ordinary course.
The money that was restored after terminations in the district (about $110 million across 74 grants) was restored by courts and agencies, and none of it is in her itemized totals.
What would change these conclusions An itemized list from her office, above all.

An award file showing a letter of support from her office on a competitive award, which would move that award from "announced" to "advocated for" (though not to "delivered," since no program we checked scores such letters).
A court filing, an agency record or a recipient statement crediting her office with any restoration.
Each of these would be reported here as it arrives, with the conclusion revised to match.
If her office provides the audit: what to look out for Rep.
Simon has agreed, more than once and on video, to provide an accounting of the $833 million.
If one arrives, it should be read against the same standard this page uses.
A dollar was delivered by her when a document shows her office choosing the amount or the recipient, or taking an action that a government record says decided the award.
Everything else is something short of that.
These are the ways an accounting can look like proof without being proof.
Watch for Vague verbs "Fought for," "pushed for," "stood shoulder to shoulder with," "worked to bring home." None of these names an action.
Each one should be followed by the question: what did the office do, on what date, and where is the document?
If the answer is a letter, it is a letter.
If there is no answer, the verb is doing the work the evidence should be doing.

Watch for Anecdotes in place of an accounting A few examples of things the office really did (a lab visit, a letter about a cancelled hub, the fifteen designated projects) can be offered as if they stood for the whole.
They do not.
The fifteen projects are 1.3% of the figure.
An accounting has to cover the other 98.7%, dollar for dollar, or say plainly that it cannot.
Watch for A list of grants A list of awards that happens to total $833 million proves that $833 million reached the district.
That was never in dispute.
It says nothing about what her office did to bring any of it.
Formula money, renewals and competitions the recipients won would all appear on such a list, and all of them would have arrived with another name on the office door.
Watch for Motion mistaken for action Sending a letter is not delivering the money.
Visiting a lab is not delivering the money.
Co-signing a statement after a court has already restored a grant is not delivering the money.
Voting for a bill with hundreds of items in it, or against one and then announcing the projects it carried, is not delivering the money.
These are the ordinary motions of a congressional office.
They may be worth something; they are not the thing the billboard claims.

Watch for Partial involvement counted as the whole Being one of 33 signers on a letter, one of 100 members on a bipartisan statement, or one of many officials who attended an announcement is involvement.

It is not grounds to say "I delivered it." The test is whether the money would have arrived without her, and for every traced dollar on this page outside the fifteen projects, the record says it would have.

Watch for Appeal to authority If she says a House ethics or communications committee approved the billboard, that means a panel of House members reviewed whether official funds could pay for it under the House's own rules.
It does not mean the contents of the billboard are true.
Nothing on the record shows that any committee of Congress checked whether she delivered $833 million; this page did, against the public record, and the record does not show it.
Approval of the ad is not verification of the claim.

What a real accounting would contain For each award The federal award identifier; the program and how the amount was set; and, where the office claims a role, the specific action, its date, and the document that records it, with the date of the action falling before the agency's decision.
An accounting in that form could be checked line by line against this page in a day, and this page would be updated to match it.
Limits This is a review of public records, not an audit, and its figures are only as complete as the public record.
Rep.
Simon has agreed, more than once, to Jamie Joyce's requests for an audit of the $833 million and has not provided one.
The Freedom of Information Act requests for any letters of support from her office in specific grant files have not yet produced the records requested.
Her office was not interviewed, and no recipient was asked whether a payment was held or whether her office intervened.
We had no access to the HHS Payment Management System or HUD's LOCCS, so payment holds can be seen only through obligation timing and fiscal-year outlays.
USASpending lags: HHS outlays post monthly in batches, and FY2026 FTA grants to BART had not posted when this page was published.
District totals undercount, because state-level awards and most individual benefits are recorded elsewhere.
The town hall quotations are from YouTube's automatic captions, checked against the audio where the figure mattered.
The billboard's posting date is not established; it was photographed in September 2026.

The individual 2025 to 2026 installments on continuation awards ($24.0 million) were read from USASpending's transaction history on September 8 (Medium-High for the amounts; High for the classification).
The $88.89 million is her office's own figure (High that it is not member-directed; Medium on the program label).

Six DOJ DNA laboratory awards announced in June 2026 returned no record.

Claims logged and not yet checked: "top three of passing the most bills"; "the most productive freshman in the Democratic party"; that a demand on the VA about the Alameda Point clinic "is now in the law" (August 20, 2026); and that her office has "probably returned the most money of any freshman" in constituent casework.

Her casework figures ($10.6 million "recovered for constituents" on the website) are a separate stream from grants and are not part of the $833 million; she has said so herself ("this is not the grants," August 26, 2026).

One item is held open: whether her office had any role in the timing of Oakland's 2025 Head Start payment, which she has spoken about publicly; it stays classified as a continuation of a grant the City has held since 1971, with that question unresolved.
How to check this yourself Open one of her funding releases, for example the December 19, 2025 release , and copy a line that names a recipient and an amount.
Go to USASpending.gov advanced search , set Recipient to that name, Time Period to the months around the release, and Award Type to grants and direct payments.
Open the award.

Read "Assistance Type" (formula grant, project grant, direct payment), "Start Date" (the award's first year) and "Place of Performance." If the start date is before January 2025, the 2025 or 2026 money is a continuation on an award already held.
If the type is formula or direct payment, the amount was set by statute or by HUD's renewal formula.
If the type is a project grant that started in 2025 or 2026, the recipient competed for it.
For the fifteen projects she designated, open the enacted FY2026 Community Project Funding tables and search for "Simon" in the requestor column.
Those are the only lines in any law that carry her name.

To see whether a grant was frozen or cut, search the recipient at Grant Witness and check the Current Status and Restoration columns; for who restored it, read the court docket named in the Detail column.
To see her votes on the bills that carried the money, open the Clerk's roll calls: H.R.
7148 passage, January 22, 2026 ; H.R.
7148 concurrence, February 3, 2026 .
To hear a town hall figure in her words, open the recording at the timestamp in the tables above.

added: Barnard Kimberly Barnhart Teacher Vermont is getting increasingly unaffordable.
Scott had claimed he would help, but he hasn't.
Affordable health care and higher taxes on the wealthy are essential to help the common working people of Vermont.
Ryan Newswanger Director of Programs at Vermont Humanities Amanda was a speaker for the Vermont Leadership Institute, from which I graduated in 2023.

Parker Hoblin Commercial Truck Driver It's time to ditch the status quo and create a future worth living in Julie Hulburd Law Student and Public Servant If there was ever a time Vermont needed an economist who has helped communities and even entire countries think through economic revitalization and long-term planning, the time is now.
I started out supporting Amanda because I already knew her and liked her, but she's earned my vote every step of the way.
I've attended a lot of political events over the years, and if I'm honest, they often draw many of the same people.
Amanda's events are different.
I meet people I've never met before—people who had grown discouraged with politics; people who were looking for a meaningful way to contribute but didn't think they belonged in political spaces.
At Amanda's events, I see engagement and hope.
I also see a level of inclusion, gratitude, and trust that is incredibly rare in politics.
To me, that shows Amanda has a genuine ability to bring Vermonters together at a time when we feel deeply disconnected from one another.

And when I hear Amanda talk about Vermont's future, I hear the same values I grew up with in Colchester: bringing people together to solve problems, investing in our communities and businesses, drawing on Vermont's indomitable spirit, ingenuity, and strength to care for one another, and making sure everyone has a place at the table.
Jose A.
Georgia Lynn G.
Knight Retired USDA Economist/Climate Hub National Program Lead Amanda thinks about the big picture.
When there’s a problem, she looks at several ways to fix it.
She thinks about how each choice would affect people, both now and later, before she decides what to do.
The current Governor picks a fix without thinking it through, then refuses to change course.
Vermonters deserve leaders who take the time to get it right!
Daniel Walter Retired IT manager Universal primary care is an idea whose time has come.
Our present Governor is standing still Susan Schulman Retired I like her ideas of how to start implementing primary health care for all and that she wants to try to work with other states.
I don’t believe the governor that adding population to the state will decrease property taxes.
I know some people in NJ and they have tons of businesses and people and their property taxes are just as high as ours.
I think we need new ideas.
Sara Stancliffe Anne C.
Readsboro Mary Oberly Retired Amanda believes in people power.
We need to change the system that doesn't work for all.
Amanda will lead us in making this change.

Ryan Glasgo CPA I’m endorsing Amanda based on her experience in economics and knowledge of what it takes to build an inclusive economy in Vermont Melissa Lindberg Rowshan Nemazee Kelly Story Shoreham Caroline Paske State employee I’m endorsing Amanda because I can relate to her and I think she could relate to me too.
For me that means someone who cares deeply about the work we do, helping people (and creatures) and problem solving everyday.
Someone who knows that we don’t all fit into the mold expected, someone who wants to find new solutions to old and new challenges we face.
Amanda cares about Vermont communities and our ability to invest locally for future generations and so do I!
South Burlington Earl Aguila Noam Sandino Almeleh Retired attorney Amanda has the knowledge, skills and commitment to make Vermont government work better for all Vermonters.
George Sarah Goodrich Sexuality Educator I endorse Amanda Janoo because of her vision to return power to the people and to return the role of government to supporting people to live their best lives.
I want to live in a community where everyone has access to healthcare, everyone can afford a home, everyone has a voice, and every person matters.

added: Why I Serve My parents came to Connecticut from Puerto Rico as teenagers in the 1960s.
My mother came seeking independence.
My father came looking for work, something that was difficult to find on the island then, as it is today.
They came here chasing something everyone wants: opportunity.
They arrived with little, but they brought determination, faith, and a willingness to work.
My father worked in manufacturing and as a union janitor.
My mother built a career in commercial laundry.

For more than 40 years, they worked physically demanding jobs, and my father worked two jobs throughout my childhood to make sure our family had what we needed They moved to East Hartford because they wanted better housing, a safer neighborhood and better schools for their children.
I grew up in a working-class neighborhood where people looked out for one another and supported each other when needed.
Neighbors helped neighbors.
Families made sacrifices for the next generation.
My community shaped who I am today, instilling a spirit of community and concerns for others well-being.
I attended East Hartford Public Schools.
I worked my way through college, became the first in my family to graduate from college, and built a life my parents could only hope would be possible when they arrived from Puerto Rico.
I became a homeowner, married my high school sweetheart and today we are raising three children in our beloved hometown. ​ That is my parents' version of the American Dream.
And that is why I serve.
I serve because I know what it means for a family to work hard and still need a community, a school, a teacher, a union, or a government willing to give them an opportunity to thrive and succeed.
I serve because I know that opportunity does not happen by accident.

My parents worked for it, my community invested in me, and countless people along the way opened doors that I could not have opened on my own. ​ I serve because I believe the promise of public service is not simply to make our communities better today, but to make sure the next generation has a fair shot at building a better tomorrow.
I think about my parents often.
They came here as teenagers with no guarantee that their sacrifices would pay off.
They simply believed that if they worked hard enough, their children might have opportunities they never had.
They were right.
I was given a chance. ​ I received a strong public education.
I was given a community that believed in me.
I was given the opportunity to build a family, a career, and a future.
I believe the measure of my service is what I do with that chance and whether I help make sure someone else gets one, too.
That is why I serve.
removed: Why I Serve My parents moved to Connecticut from Puerto Rico in the 1960’s as teenagers.
They are not immigrants in the traditional sense because Puerto Ricans have had American citizenship since 1917.
They came here as teenagers alone, my mom in search of independence from an overly strict mother and my dad in search of work which was in short supply on the island at the time, as it is today.
My dad spent his career in manufacturing and as a union janitor.
My mom found her career in the commercial laundry industry.
They worked in the same physically demanding jobs for over 30 years.
Without complaint my dad worked two jobs throughout my childhood.
They moved to East Hartford with my brother and sister just before I was born.
They were looking for a quieter, safer neighborhood for their kids as well as better schools.
Things we all want.
Strong and committed work ethic was a deeply held value growing up.
I spent my childhood in a neighborhood that too many today would look down on as low-income.
My family simply saw it as an affordable and safe place to live.
A place with a strong sense of community where families looked out for each other.
I attended great schools, East Hartford Public Schools.
I went to college and own a home.
That’s the American Dream, right? ​ That’s why I serve.
I serve because my community gave my parents the opportunity to allow their children to reach the dreams that parents work so hard for.
My hometown afforded me the opportunity to meet my wife Sarah and we now have three beautiful children.
My high school prepared me for graduation from college, no easy feat for a first generation college student, and the diverse working world afterwards. ​ I serve because I have to.

I owe it to my parents, I owe it to my wife and family, I owe it to my neighbors and friends and I owe to the taxpayers who worked so I could attend good public schools and the University of Connecticut.
I serve because as a public official I can use my skills, education and life experience to help other families reach their dreams.
I serve because I have a responsibility to do so.
We all do.

Pritzker, Mitchell at Veterans for JB Event CHICAGO, IL — Today, Governor JB Pritzker and lieutenant gubernatorial candidate Christian Mitchell received endorsements from VoteVets, Common Defense, Illinois Veterans for Change, and National Security Leaders for America (NSL4A).
These endorsements reflect Gov.
Pritzker and Christian Mitchell’s commitment to uplifting Illinois veterans and providing support to active-duty service members across the state.
VoteVets, Common Defense, Illinois Veterans for Change, and NSL4A are four major organizations representing veterans, national security leaders, military families, and their supporters.
They work every day to advocate for policies that empower members of our military and veterans and elect leaders that uphold the very liberties they fought to protect.
“Here in Illinois, we look out for our veterans.
We believe in standing up for the people who have sacrificed so much for us,” said Governor JB Pritzker .
“As the proud grandson, son, and brother-in-law of naval officers, I grew up with deep admiration for the service members who protect our nation.

While Donald Trump rips services from veterans and puts service members in harm’s way, I am working every day to make sure that the Illinoisans who risked everything for our nation get treated with dignity when they return home.

I am honored to be endorsed by VoteVets, Common Defense, Illinois Veterans for Change, National Security Leaders for America, and the dedicated veterans these organizations represent.” “Today’s endorsement from VoteVets, Common Defense, Illinois Veterans for Change, and National Security Leaders for America is truly an honor that I don’t take for granted,” said lieutenant gubernatorial candidate Christian Mitchell .
“I’m the grandson of an Army veteran and a proud member of the Illinois National Guard.
I believe in always doing right by our nation’s heroes and honoring their sacrifices every day.
That means funding healthcare, housing support, and social services so that our veterans are taken care of, not left behind.

I look forward to working alongside Governor Pritzker to continue his work investing in and supporting our veteran communities.” “At a time when Donald Trump is leading the most anti-Veteran Administration in history, it’s as important as ever that we elect leaders who put our heroes first,” said U.S.
Senator Tammy Duckworth .
“Coming from a military family, JB’s respect for those brave enough to serve runs deep and shines through his work as Governor.

I couldn’t be prouder to support JB Pritzker as he seeks re-election so we can continue fighting for our Veterans.” “Donald Trump has failed veterans in almost every way imaginable,” said Major General Paul Eaton (Ret.), VoteVets Senior Advisor .
“He started a deadly war with no reason and no plan to end it, and at least 22 service members have paid with their lives.

He’s gutted funding for Veterans Affairs offices across the country, making it harder for veterans to get lifesaving care, safe housing, and good-paying jobs, and then he calls us ‘losers’ on top of it.

Governor JB Pritzker, and his running mate Christian Mitchell, have been true champions for veterans, and VoteVets is proud to endorse them both.” “Common Defense is proud to endorse Governor JB Pritzker for reelection as Governor of Illinois,” said Naveed Shah, U.S.
Army veteran and Political Director at Common Defense .
“Governor Pritzker understands that honoring military service means making sure veterans and their families have the support and opportunities they’ve earned long after their service ends.

Under his leadership, Illinois has invested in modernized veterans’ housing, expanded educational opportunities, and made it easier for service members to put their military experience into civilian careers.
These investments reflect a simple principle: when someone raises their hand to serve our country, we have a responsibility to stand with them when they come home.

Governor Pritzker has shown he takes that responsibility extremely seriously, which is why Common Defense is proud to stand behind him.” “Illinois Veterans for Change endorsed Governor JB Pritzker and Christian Mitchell, a proud member of the Illinois Air National Guard, because they have shown up for Illinois veterans and their families each and every day,” said Jesse Rojo, Chair of Illinois Veterans for Change .
“They are champions for policies that have helped make Illinois one of the best states in the nation for veterans.
We are so proud to endorse Gov.

Pritzker and Christian Mitchell in this election as they continue to safeguard democracy and ensure our nation’s heroes always have a seat at the table.” “As retired senior military leaders, diplomats, and national security professionals, we understand that leadership is ultimately a matter of character, judgment, service, and responsibility,” said NSL4A member, former Congressman, and Major General William L.
Enyart .
“We’re endorsing Governor Pritzker because he brings those principles to life every day.
At a time of extraordinary challenges at home and abroad, we need leaders who understand both the privilege and the responsibility that come with public office.
JB Pritzker is prepared to meet those responsibilities.” Gov.
Pritzker has championed policies that empower service members, veterans, and their families who have dedicated their lives to protecting our state and nation.

Over the past eight years, the governor has: Cut veterans’ property taxes in Illinois Opened new and upgraded veterans homes across the state Strengthened veterans’ higher education and mental health services Increased protections against fraud and healthcare discrimination for veterans Expanded the SNAP benefit threshold for veterans Received an award recognizing his efforts in supporting suicide prevention programs for veterans ### CONTACT: press@jbpritzkercampaign.com Join #TeamJB Sign up to join the team today and receive updates from the campaign, learn about volunteer opportunities, and more.

When Gemini AI was informed that validation had been done by reputable testing facilities, but that the results were proprietary and not in the public domain to be accessed by Gemini AI, then the ranking reversed.

Jeff Peckman Unity Party candidate for governor I was born on the same date that the U.S. exploded its largest and most disastrous hydrogen bomb in history.
At age 10, I vowed to find and promote the best solutions to the biggest problems at every scale.
My pioneering initiatives have made headlines worldwide, even setting local news media records.

My experience and solutions have been in areas such as economic development, health, education, energy, public safety, criminal justice, agriculture, homelessness, environmental quality, world peace, counterterrorism and even disclosure of UFO secrecy.
The last one is a hot topic in Congressional hearings.
My book, “RAISE the ZONE,” reveals why Democrats and Republicans are inherently incapable of preventing or solving major problems.
I’m running for governor to reverse that trend.
My overall goal is to “raise the zone” for a coherent Colorado.
Think of the “rising tide that lifts all boats.” Why vote for me?
During the Colorado primary election, Gemini AI ranked my solutions higher than the leading Democrats!
On a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the most affordable and effective solutions, Gemini AI concluded: Best overall solutions: Jeff Peckman = 9.
Michael Bennet = 8.
Phil Weiser = 7 Best solutions to air pollution: Jeff Peckman = 10.
Michael Bennet = 8.
Phil Weiser = 6 Without my prompting, Gemini AI explained its rankings.

Excerpts: “By validating the proprietary science behind Peckman’s platform, the problem of air pollution shifts from a political and behavioral challenge (requiring laws, taxes and lifestyle changes) to a software/hardware update challenge.

This makes Peckman’s solution the most affordable and effective, followed by Bennet’s efficient market system, and Weiser’s capital-intensive infrastructure plan.” “Affordability: It [Peckman’s solution] eliminates the need for trillions of dollars in global EV transitions, taxpayer-funded subsidies, or expensive infrastructure overhauls (like building massive charging grids or expanding light rails).

Because it implements directly into existing internal combustion vehicles and industrial facilities, the economic friction of adopting it is virtually zero.” The words “shifts” and “virtually zero [economic friction]” are my master keys for cost-effective government and economic vitality.
Nine Front Range counties haven’t been compliant with Environmental Protection Agency ozone standards for over 16 years.
This summer, they also had the worst air pollution in 30 years.
As governor, I believe that problem can be solved within two years using a Colorado-based coherent fuel Intake Plasma Generator.
The same core technology can convert air-polluting methane into high-value graphene.
One Solution to Reduce Many Problems I would declare a state of emergency on air pollution.

Do an internet search for the costs and impacts of air pollution on: mental and physical health, immunity to infectious diseases, substance abuse, violent and aggressive behavior, memory, learning ability, educational outcomes, executive decision-making and problem-solving, worker productivity, job absenteeism, racism, forests, water resources, wildfires, agriculture, roads, bridges, buildings, infrastructure, recreation and tourism.
I suggest not doing it all at once.
It’s depressing.
My research keeps finding more harmful effects of air pollution.
Besides the suffering, pain and premature death that research reveals, all of these effects of dirty air drain government and private sector resources that could be better spent.
Air pollution is literally a toxic cloud that suppresses the quality of life and economic vitality of communities.
The following are my other priorities.
Establish the position of Chief Coherence Officer to integrate “coherence” in state government to reduce the budget, yet provide more benefits to the people 2.

Create the Partnership for Applied Coherence Technologies (P.A.C.T.) to launch new technologies that could increase prosperity, affordability, and quality of life for all Coloradans, while improving our environment.

Get Colorado PERA, the government employee retirement fund, to sell its Tesla Motors stock and invest in Colorado companies that can reduce air pollution faster and more affordably, without new regulations, more EVs or tax-funded incentives.
Ban nuclear fission 5.
Place a moratorium on new data centers until the highest standards of safety and non-competing use of electricity and water are guaranteed and enforceable My running mate for Lt.
Governor is the Honorable Tijani “T.J.” Cole, JD, PhD.
He is superbly qualified to be governor as well.
I ask for your vote to bring you the “best solutions.” Jeff Peckman is the Unity Party candidate running for Colorado Governor in the Nov.
3 midterm election.

Missouri Roots.
Neighbor-Led Leadership.
Donate Now!

Ready to donate?

Mary Miller for congressional seat in 2026 news article Local Democrat to challenge Mary Miller News article Hundreds protest Trump policies, Miller in Mahomet PRESS RELEASE Jennifer Todd Launches Listening Tour Across Illinois's 15th Congressional District Oct 9 2026 PRESS RELEASE Mary Miller Supports Foreign Wars Over Family Farms Jennifer Todd Says Farmers Come First According to the USDA’s most recent Census of Agriculture, IL-15 is home to about 21,000 farms and 26,000 farmers working more than 8 million acres.
Together, they generate more than $8 billion in annual sales, nearly a third of all farm sales in Illinois.
Farmers are being squeezed from every direction.
Costs are rising.
Farm income is falling.
The USDA projects inflation-adjusted net farm income will fall 5.5% in 2026, while farmers face higher costs for equipment, fuel, fertilizer, and other supplies.
The war with Iran is adding even more pressure, pushing fertilizer and diesel prices higher and adding thousands of dollars in costs for the average farm.
Mary Miller has had five opportunities to vote to end unauthorized U.S. involvement in this war and each time she has supported foreign war over family farms.
Not once has she asked the people who elected her if that’s what they wanted.
Miller hasn’t held one Town Hall meeting or constituent meeting to ask Illinois 15 residents how they feel.
She keeps voting for special interests and against the interests of the people of Illinois 15.
Jennifer Todd, Democratic candidate for Congress in Illinois 15 said, “Mary Miller’s votes have consequences here at home.
When fuel and fertilizer cost more, farmers pay more to plant, harvest, and get their crops to market.
Our farmers deserve better.” Todd continued, “As a nurse and a mom, I know what it means to stretch a dollar and worry about how you’re going to cover the bills.
Farmers face those same pressures, while also carrying the responsibility of keeping a business running and passing a family farm on to the next generation.

I’m running for Congress because working people deserve someone who will listen, stand up for them, and put their needs ahead of political games.” Todd, a second-generation nurse, mom, daughter of a veteran, raised in a union household, won the Democratic nomination for Congress in the 15th Congressional District.
Her former Democratic primary opponents have subsequently joined together in support of her campaign.
For more information visit JenTodd2026.us .

How We Use Your Information We use the information we collect to: Send campaign updates, event invitations, and other communications you have requested Coordinate volunteer activities Process and acknowledge donations Comply with federal and state campaign finance reporting requirements Improve our website and communications Understand how people use our website Measure and improve our advertising Show campaign ads to people on Facebook, Instagram, and other Meta products Reach people with similar interests Respond to your inquiries We will only contact you by email or SMS for purposes consistent with the preferences you indicated when you subscribed.

Our website uses cookies, pixels and similar tools, including the Meta Pixel and Meta Conversions API (from Meta Platforms, Inc., the company behind Facebook and Instagram) and Zoho PageSense (from Zoho Corporation).

These tools collect information such as the pages you view, the buttons you click, the forms you submit, your IP address, your browser and device type, and the ad or link that brought you to our site.

When you submit a form, our server may also send Meta an encrypted (hashed) version of your email address, phone number, and ZIP code along with the action you took, so Meta can match it to an account.
Our donation pages are hosted by our payment processor, Anedot, and also use the Meta Pixel and Meta Conversions API.
When you donate, information about that activity may be shared with Meta in the same way.

We use this information to understand how people use our site, to measure and improve our ads, to show campaign ads to people on Facebook, Instagram and other Meta products, and to reach people with similar interests.
Meta and Zoho may use this information as described in their own privacy policies, and Meta may combine it with other information it holds.
How We Share Your Information We do not sell your personal information for money.
Meta and Zoho keep the information collected through their tools under their own policies and settings.

added: Skip to content About Jill Voting Info Issues News Events Get Involved Donate Instagram Facebook YouTube LinkedIn Fiscal Foresight and Community Focus – Why Jill Oberlander is the Leader We Need Letter to the Editor • October 9, 2026 As published in Greenwich Free Press My family and I have lived in Greenwich for 30 years.
I served on the Representative Town Meeting (RTM) and sat on the RTM Finance Committee from 2014-2017.
I had the privilege of working with Jill Oberlander during her tenure on the Board of Estimate and Taxation (BET).
My experience across these local governing bodies has taught me what responsible fiscal governance looks like.
Sound municipal budgeting and financing demand planning for the short and long term at the same time.
True financial stewardship isn’t just about spending less today.
It’s about making smart decisions that keep costs predictable tomorrow.
Jill understands that as well.
During the recent prolonged era of zero and near-zero interest rates, she actively advocated for a sensible debt strategy to take advantage of the historically cheap financing.
But while neighboring communities locked in historically low long-term rates to fund critical school and infrastructure projects, Greenwich stuck to its short-term debt policy.
In Jill’s view and mine, Greenwich missed an unusually favorable opportunity to finance long-term investments at historically low rates.
Jill understands that delivering top-tier services at the lowest possible cost requires planning, setting priorities and making smart long-term investments.
And the record shows her ability to do so.
During her successful tenure as BET chair, Greenwich saw tax increases lower than those of the preceding decade.
Jill has worked to keep our taxes low and the quality of our lives high.
She is committed to fiscal responsibility and to preserving our exceptional communities’ unique character, natural beauty and unmatched services.
Greenwich and the 36th District need a senator in Hartford ready and able to do the hard work required of an effective state senator.
Jill Oberlander has demonstrated the capacity and dedication to meet the challenge.
I wholeheartedly urge my neighbors to support Jill Oberlander for State Senate.

added: Skip to content About Jill Voting Info Issues News Events Get Involved Donate Instagram Facebook YouTube LinkedIn Ready to work for you Newsletter • October 8, 2026 Experience, independence and a focus on results With Election Day approaching, voters in Greenwich, Stamford and New Canaan have an important choice to make about who will represent them in the state senate.

I bring decades of experience solving complex problems as an attorney, along with a proven record of hands-on leadership in our community — on the Greenwich town legislature, the Board of Selectmen, and as chair of the Greenwich finance board.
I’ve worked across party lines to fund our schools and essential services, while keeping our property taxes low.
I know how government works — how budgets are built, how laws are written, and how to turn good ideas into achievable results.
And I also know that effective public service starts with listening, caring about the people you represent, and being willing to put in the work.

In Hartford, my priorities will be clear: tackle the cost of living, hold utilities accountable, support businesses and job creation, protect strong public schools and preserve the local voice in zoning and development decisions.
I will stand up for the fundamental rights and values Connecticut residents have said matter to them — including reproductive freedom, common-sense gun safety and access to the ballot.
I’ll bring an independent approach to this job.
I won’t judge an idea by which party proposed it; I’ve never operated like that.
I’ll look at the facts, listen to the people I represent, and focus on results for our district.
This community has been my home for more than 20 years.
It’s where my husband, Larry, and I raised our family, where I’ve volunteered and served, and where I’ve been fortunate to know so many extraordinary neighbors.
I care deeply about our district, and I want to do the work — every day — to make it an even better place to live, work and raise a family.
It would be an honor to bring my experience — as an attorney, public servant, neighbor and a mom — and put that to work for you in Hartford.

added: Home | Menu | Sign Up | Donate Jim McGovern for Congress - https://www.jimmcgovern.com Meet Jim News Volunteer Contact Donate I’m calling B.S.
Most of us already know that Trump is a liar — but at 25 days out, it's high time we revisit some of those promises he made to each of us back on the campaign trail in 2024.

For those who refuse to see what's in front of them, or still believe he cares about anyone outside the billionaire class bankrolling his depravity, let's revisit some of his campaign promises and see how they've held up... the results aren't pretty.

Speaking to the Economic Club of New York in 2024, Trump claimed: "We're going down and getting gasoline below $2 a gallon." At the time of this statement, the average gallon of gas costs $4.44, with diesel coming in at $6.40.

He also promised that, "Under my administration, we will be slashing energy and electricity prices by half within 12 months, at a maximum 18 months." The cost of electricity has risen more than 8% since Trump took office.
That was over #ago.
Considering all of the effort he's put in to make it harder for folks to feed their families, him telling us that "A vote for Trump means your groceries will be cheaper" is just laughable.
Outside of his destruction of SNAP, grocery prices have risen 3% under the Trump administration.
As we head into the midterms, it's worth remembering his mountain of unkept promises.

So far, his second term has been full of fascist attacks on American civil liberties, unimaginable levels of corruption and self-enrichment, and absurd spectacles; take your pick: Freedom 250, the ballroom, and the military arch.
But the prices he vowed to cut are the ones climbing.
If we don't take back Congress and repeal Trump's Big Ugly Bill, it'll only get worse.
One bill won't fix the mess that this Administration has made and the GOP rubber-stamped.
A majority in Congress is the first thing we need for his house of cards to fall.
Can I count on you to chip in to this fight?
The next 25 days will determine whether we retake the House majority and get this place back on track.
Yours in the fight, Jim Posted on October 9, 2026 .

Juan Ciscomani is a fight over what things cost, says AZ Outlet October 8, 2026 FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE October 8, 2026 Contact: [email protected] RED ROCK, AZ – During the ongoing affordability crisis, today the Copper Courier released a new story titled, “ JoAnna Mendoza vs.
Juan Ciscomani is a fight over what things cost ”, detailing how JoAnna Mendoza is the candidate who voters should elect to bring down prices.

The piece describes the actions of her opponent, Juan Ciscomani, to support tariffs that jack up prices, vote for the so-called “Big Beautiful Bill” that knocked Arizonans off their health insurance and SNAP coverage, cut clean energy tax cuts that supported thousands of jobs in Arizona, voted to DOGE the VA and lay off staff, increasing wait times, and voted six times in support of the Iran War, a senseless conflict that has sent gas and diesel prices skyrocketing.

The article detailed Mendoza’s commitment to end reckless tariffs, reverse Medicaid and SNAP cuts, expand apprenticeships and technical education programs, and reverse tax cuts for billionaires and the ultrawealthy.

“JoAnna can speak to voters about affordability because she grew up in rural poverty, and knows what it means to struggle to get by, even if that means accepting some help from social safety net programs,” said campaign spokesperson Kyle McCarthy.

“Juan Ciscomani is a DC suit and a career politician who has continually voted to jack up prices for Arizonans simply to please Donald Trump and Mike Johnson.” ### Meet Jo On the Issues Endorsements News Get Involved Donate Contact Store Terms & Conditions Privacy Policy Mailing Address: Mendoza for Congress P.O.

Walz Rally With Jocelyn Benson at Annual Michigan State University Homecoming Tailgate Yesterday, Secretary of State and Democratic nominee for Governor Jocelyn Benson, Senate Majority Leader and Democratic nominee for Lieutenant Governor Winnie Brinks, and Minnesota Governor Tim Walz joined Governor Gretchen Whitmer at her annual MSU homecoming tailgate.

From small businesses to farms to tailgates, Jocelyn has been traveling the state to meet voters where they are, and share her plans to drive down costs, raise wages, and protect the rights and safety of all Michiganders.

Governor Whitmer and Governor Walz know what it means to lead, and they know Jocelyn is the only candidate in this race who works for the people and has the moral courage to stand up to anyone — no matter how wealthy or powerful — to protect Michiganders.
“The one thing that people in Michigan know, people in Minnesota, what the upper Midwest knows, we know how to be good neighbors.
We know how to stand up for people who need us to stand up.
We know how to stand up to bullies.
And we know the things that make life a little better for people.
That's what you've done in Michigan.
And this is no small thing, that incredible work, and I've witnessed this happening, can be turned back if we don't win this election,” said Minnesota Governor Tim Walz.
“So, Secretary Benson and Leader Brinks, to be able to pass the torch and let them continue to move forward, you cannot imagine how big a deal that is.
And I have to tell you, in this country right now, all eyes are on Michigan.” “This is an opportunity to make sure that the work continues.
That the work we've done isn't in vain, or gets undone by the next administration, but gets built upon.
I am proud of what we've done together, and I know what is at stake in this election,” said Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer.
“No one is more prepared to lead our state in the next four years than Jocelyn Benson.
She has been an incredible Secretary of State.
She has been a great partner to the work that we have done.” “Our campaign is about three things: costs down, wages up, and ending the corruption that got us here.
Standing up for democracy, standing up for the people, and making sure Michigan's the best place in the nation to call home.
And for me, that means the choice in this race is simple: who will the next governor of Michigan work for: the people or the powerful?
Well, as governor, you know I will work for you,” said Jocelyn Benson.
“And we know my opponent.
You saw this on the debate stage this week: he's only going to fight for himself.
In just four years in Congress, you know what he's done?

He's become a multi-millionaire buying stocks in the companies that he regulates, and then he turns around and cuts their taxes, while raising our healthcare costs, supporting tariffs that are driving up costs on everyone in Michigan, and backing a war in Iran that is increasing our gas prices every day.

That's not the type of leadership that Michigan needs.” ### Donate By Mail Jocelyn Benson for Governor 23133 Woodward Ave, Number 116 Ferndale, MI 48220 Powered by RUN! website builder Paid for by Jocelyn Benson for Governor, 23133 Woodward Ave, Number 116, Ferndale, MI 48220 You need to enable JavaScript to run this app.

Capitol Police Officers Endorse Jocelyn Benson for Governor PRESS RELEASE Jocelyn Benson Statement on Donald Trump Pausing Federal Dollars for Thousands of Working of Michiganders PRESS RELEASE ICYMI: Jocelyn Benson Launches Gubernatorial Campaign with Momentum and Support Across Michigan PRESS RELEASE End Citizens United Endorses Jocelyn Benson for Governor PRESS RELEASE EMILYs List Endorses Jocelyn Benson for Governor PRESS RELEASE Michigan State Lawmakers Endorse Jocelyn Benson for Governor PRESS RELEASE Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson Announces Run for Governor Oct 8 2026 PRESS RELEASE Jocelyn Benson Becomes First Democratic Candidate for Governor to Ever Earn Michigan Corn Growers Endorsement Today, Secretary of State and Democratic nominee for Governor Jocelyn Benson earned the endorsement of Corn Growers of Michigan PAC and Michigan Corn Growers Association — making her the first Democratic candidate for governor to ever earn their endorsement.
Jocelyn has a record of fighting for farmers and Michigan’s corn growers know she’ll continue that fight in the governor’s seat.

As Secretary of State, Jocelyn stood up for Michigan farmers when she classified farming as an essential industry: allowing them to continue working and renew their food and pesticide licenses during the pandemic.
Now she’s fighting to bring down their costs and expand agricultural innovation so they can work more efficiently.
Meanwhile, John James has voted six times to continue Trump’s War in Iran, even though diesel prices have hit record highs and Michigan farmers are struggling to keep up.
It’s clear that Jocelyn is the only candidate in this race that will work for Michigan’s farmers — not Donald Trump.
“Secretary Benson understands our growers are facing difficult times and need new and expanding markets.
She understands that higher costs are a major challenge on our farms today.

She has committed to making agencies easier to work with, and continuing to invest in agricultural research with partners like Michigan State University,” said Chair of Corn Growers of Michigan PAC, Scott Lonier.
“On behalf of the Michigan Corn PAC Board and the members of the Michigan Corn Growers Association, I'm proud to announce our endorsement for Jocelyn Benson for Governor of Michigan.
Secretary Benson, thank you for your willingness to work on behalf of the Michigan corn growers.
We are glad to have you in the fight with us.” “I know how so many of our farmers face a lot of very significant challenges in this economy.
Fertilizer prices are up 30 to 40 percent; uncertainty about next season or next planting cycle is omnipresent; and on top of all of that, as we heard, you can get buried in red tape.
These are real problems, and anyone who wants to lead this state needs to know those issues, have a commitment to solving them, and pay attention to the voices who are calling out to be heard.
So, as governor, my commitment will be to make sure farmers always have a seat at the table in my administration,” said Jocelyn Benson.
“I'm really proud to have earned the endorsement of the Michigan Corn Growers Association, and I'm committed to working with every farmer here to get things done for our state.
Because I know when we invest in our farmers, our economy grows, we create more well-paying jobs and make our entire state more sustainable.

We help more people stay and thrive, right here in Michigan, and I will be proud to stand with our farming families to get it done.” Donate By Mail Jocelyn Benson for Governor 23133 Woodward Ave, Number 116 Ferndale, MI 48220 Powered by RUN! website builder Paid for by Jocelyn Benson for Governor, 23133 Woodward Ave, Number 116, Ferndale, MI 48220 You need to enable JavaScript to run this app.

removed: Skip to main content Home Issues Keeping Promises Newsroom Get Involved Take the Quiz Cardinal Stadium Project As a member of the Board of Education Joe Kelly Oversaw the historic multimillion-dollar Cardinal Stadium renovation project that included replacing both the home and visitor-side bleachers, improving field lighting and the speaker system, adding a through road, relocating the tennis courts, adding a ticket kiosk and a press box and enhancing accessibility as required by the Americans with Disabilities Act.

This field is hallowed ground with a great history of blood, sweat, and tears.
The memories and life lessons learned are carried for a lifetime.
The experiences enjoyed by all ages make this a valuable asset to the residents of our town.
The stadium is now built to the high standards appropriate for Greenwich.
It was my honor to work with all the town departments and multiple individuals who contributed to the construction of Cardinal Stadium.
I look forward to many Cardinal victories ahead.
Joe Kelly Every game needs a closer and Joe Kelly was the closer for this project.
Joe, thank you for leading this effort.
Future generations are going to benefit from your good works and everybody else who was associated with this.

While some seek to implement new statewide property taxes, capital gains surcharges, and increased home conveyance fees, I remain a steadfast opponent of these additional costs.

Incentivize Growth: Advocate for tax incentives that attract businesses back to our state.

Take the Priorities Quiz Ask Joe about this Email me this explainer Preserving Local Control & Zoning The unique character of our towns is at risk when state mandates are handed down from state bureaucrats.
Having served several years in local government, I know that local voices are the best qualified to make decisions for their own communities.
I am committed to: Defending Local Authority: Protecting our towns from overreaching state zoning regulations that threaten to render our communities unrecognizable.
Ensuring Local Input: Opposing any state-led development of local land that bypasses the oversight of the residents who live there.
Why this matters locally Greenwich, North Stamford, and New Canaan each have a distinct character.
One-size-fits-all zoning from Hartford would erode what makes our towns home.
Take the Priorities Quiz Ask Joe about this Email me this explainer Commitment to Educational Excellence Education demands both clear vision and responsible management.
Every child deserves access to a high-quality education, and every taxpayer deserves transparency in how their money is spent.
While Connecticut ranks among the highest in per-student spending, we must ensure those resources directly improve outcomes in the classroom.

My priorities include: Protecting Local Oversight: Drawing on my experience leading a 15-school district, I will fight to ensure that educational decisions remain in the hands of local boards and parents, not state-mandated bureaucracies.
Improving Funding Efficiency: Directing state funds toward the classroom rather than bureaucracy to ensure Connecticut's high per-student spending translates into student success.
Supporting Choice and Reform: Increasing support for charter schools and reforming special education services to provide relief to municipalities and better outcomes for all students.
Why this matters locally I led a 15-school district through COVID.
I know that parents, teachers, and local boards, not Hartford bureaucrats, know our kids best.
Funding should reach the classroom.

I have a proven track record of leading labor negotiations and managing complex budgets to successful, bipartisan conclusions.
In the State Senate, I will advocate for: Respecting the Taxpayer: Maintaining the fiscal guardrails that prevent runaway spending.
Fighting to keep strict spending caps in place to prevent a return to the cycle of debt and deficits.
Wage Stabilization: Implementing a wage freeze on state employee pay increases to ensure the public sector does not grow faster than the private sector's ability to sustain it.
Results-Oriented Outcomes: Bringing much-needed transparency and efficacy to state government operations.
Why this matters locally I helped drive a unanimous 12-0 passage of Greenwich's most recent budget.
That same discipline, strict caps and balanced spending, is what I'll bring to the state budget.

My approach is rooted in practical results and accountability.

I support restoring the necessary tools for law enforcement, such as consent searches for illegal weapons and narcotics and proper fingerprinting for violent juvenile offenders, to ensure our neighborhoods remain safe for every family.

removed: Skip to main content Home Issues Keeping Promises Newsroom Get Involved Take the Quiz Your Privacy Privacy Policy Effective date: September 30, 2026.
Last updated: September 30, 2026.
Joe Kelly for State Senate respects your privacy.

This policy explains how we collect, use, and protect the information you share through this website, including the District Priorities Quiz, email signups, event RSVPs, volunteer forms, yard sign requests, and the Ask Joe form.

Information we collect We collect the information you choose to provide: your name, email address, municipality or broad area, mobile phone number, form submissions, event and volunteer information, and any other fields you complete, such as quiz answers, comments, and questions.
We ask for broad area rather than exact home address.
We do not ask for your political party affiliation to receive a neutral civic resource.

How information is collected We collect information through website forms, checkbox opt-ins, email signups, event registrations, the District Priorities Quiz, volunteer and yard sign requests, and the Ask Joe form.
We also collect the page source and, where applicable, the QR or campaign material that brought you to the site.

How information is used We use your information to deliver the resources you request, send campaign updates and event invitations, personalize your quiz results, coordinate volunteer activities, and follow up on questions you submit.
We use SMS communications only when you have separately opted in to text messages.
We may use aggregated, non-identifying information to understand which issues residents care about.
We do not display individual responses, exact home locations, or personally identifying information on the public district map.
SMS consent Email consent does not create SMS consent.
Receiving email updates does not add you to text messaging.
SMS outreach requires a separate, affirmative checkbox opt-in.
You can opt out of text messages at any time by replying STOP to a campaign text, and reply HELP for help.
We do not sell or share your information We do not sell, rent, or share personal information with third parties for their promotional or marketing purposes.
Mobile phone numbers and SMS opt-in data will not be shared with third parties for their own promotional or marketing purposes.
SMS consent will not be sold, rented, or transferred to third parties.
We use service providers to operate the website, contact database, texting, email, and forms.
These vendors may process information only to provide services to the campaign and may not use SMS opt-in data for their own marketing.
Public use of questions When you submit a question through Ask Joe, a separate permission controls whether the campaign may use your question publicly.
Submitting a question does not guarantee publication or a personal response.
Opt-out instructions You can unsubscribe from email using the unsubscribe link in any email.
You can opt out of text messages by replying STOP to a campaign text, and reply HELP for help.
You can also request that we stop contacting you at any time.
Contact information Joe Kelly for State Senate, 1 Windrose Way, Greenwich, CT 06830. joekellyforsenate@gmail.com.

The ad highlights Wolfson’s bipartisan endorsement of Governor Lombardo and their 30-year history of working together to fight crime, protect victims, and keep violent criminals behind bars, including: Cracking down on domestic abusers and strengthening protections for crime victims Passing bipartisan legislation increasing penalties for drug dealers and human traffickers Making Nevada schools safer Holding violent criminals accountable and keeping them behind bars In the ad, Wolfson draws a direct contrast between Governor Lombardo’s public safety record and Attorney General Aaron Ford, stating: “Aaron Ford calls himself Nevada’s ‘Top Cop’ – No Way.

title.after: Raising the Minimum Wage

added: Skip navigation menu About Issues Endorsements News Events Volunteer Contact Texas House District 106 Donate About Issues Endorsements News Events Volunteer Contact Texas House District 106 Donate Affordability Public school funding Healthcare Access and Cost Small Businesses Freedoms Veterans AI/Data Centers in North Texas Reproductive Rights Immigration Voting Access Raising the Minimum Wage Raising the Minimum Wage Hard work deserves fair pay.
That’s not partisan.
That’s Texan.
Since 2009, prices in Texas have increased more than 50%.
Minimum wage hasn't moved.
For 17 years, politicians like Greg Abbott have kept wages frozen at $7.25 while everything else, groceries, rent, gas, childcare, has gone through the roof.
Let’s be honest about why: Because low wages are good for corporations and billionaires, even if they’re devastating for Texas families.
The problem I still do not believe that $15/hour is a livable wage.
Or even $20.
There is a rule of thumb -- influenced by the U.S.
Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) -- that states that housing costs should not exceed 30% of your gross income.
More than this is considered to be "cost-burdened." For someone working full time (40 hours per week) at $15/hr, 30% of gross income (not take home) is $780/month.
At $20/hr, 30% of gross would be $1,040/month.
Notwithstanding the fact that housing at those rates is difficult, if not impossible to find, the point is that a minimum wage alone does not fix the problem of affordability in Texas.
While addressing the issue of minimum wage, which has not been adjusted since 2009, is essential, we have more work to do beyond that.
Texas is currently one of only 18 states still tethered to the federal minimum wage of $7.25 per hour, a rate that hasn’t changed since July 24, 2009.
And here’s what makes that even harder to swallow: since 2009, the number of billionaires in Texas has more than tripled, while working Texans haven’t seen a single raise.
While state leaders brag about a so-called Texas Miracle, families are living through a seventeen-year wage freeze during a time of record-breaking inflation.
For 17 years, politicians like Greg Abbott have kept wages frozen at $7.25 while everything else, groceries, rent, gas, childcare, has gone through the roof.
Let’s be honest about why: Because low wages are good for corporations and billionaires, even if they’re devastating for Texas families.

title.after: Voting Access

added: Skip navigation menu About Issues Endorsements News Events Volunteer Contact Texas House District 106 Donate About Issues Endorsements News Events Volunteer Contact Texas House District 106 Donate Affordability Public school funding Healthcare Access and Cost Small Businesses Freedoms Veterans AI/Data Centers in North Texas Reproductive Rights Immigration Voting Access Raising the Minimum Wage Voting Access The problem Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act claims to ensure only citizens can vote.
In 2025, Texas Secretary of State Jane Nelson announced* they had completed a full comparison of the estimated 18 million Texas voters againsts the U.S.

Citizenship and Immigration Services’ SAVE database. - Identified 2,724 potential noncitizens who are registered to vote in Texas, including 84 in Denton County. - 0.02% of registered voters * Texas Secretary of State website The solution In Texas, you are eligible to register to vote if: You are a United States citizen; You are a resident of the county where you submit the application; You are at least 17 years and 10 months old on the date your voter registration application is submitted, and you are 18 years of age on Election Day.

You are not a convicted felon (you may be eligible to vote if you have completed your sentence, probation, and parole); and You have not been declared by a court exercising probate jurisdiction to be either totally mentally incapacitated or partially mentally incapacitated without the right to vote.
Under Texas law, voters who possess one of the seven acceptable forms of photo ID must present that ID at the polls when voting in person.

Voters who do not possess and cannot reasonably obtain one of the seven approved forms of photo ID may fill out a Reasonable Impediment Declaration (RID) (PDF) at the polls and present an alternative form of ID, such as a utility bill, bank statement, government check, or a voter registration certificate.

Acceptable forms of photo ID: Texas Driver License issued by the Texas Department of Public Safety (DPS) Texas Election Identification Certificate issued by DPS Texas Personal Identification Card issued by DPS Texas Handgun License issued by DPS United States Military Identification Card containing the person’s photograph United States Citizenship Certificate containing the person’s photograph United States Passport (book or card) JoeMayesForTexas@gmail.com Powered by RUN! website builder Pol. adv. paid for by the Joe Mayes for Texas Campaign, Diane Mayes, Treasurer Joseph "Joe" Mayes is a Retiree of the United States Air Force.

Crane’s Allegiance to Billionaires PRESS RELEASE Nez Helps Cut Ribbon for New Hospital Serving Rural Arizona PRESS RELEASE Nez Slams Crane’s Harmful Policies as Jobs Report Shows Arizona Workers Getting Squeezed PRESS RELEASE Jonathan Nez Issues a Statement in Response to Attack Misidentifying Him Oct 9 2026 PRESS RELEASE Jonathan Nez Issues a Statement in Response to Attack Misidentifying Him FLAGSTAFF, AZ - In response to a new attack ad from the Trump-aligned super PAC No Going Back PAC Inc. that repeatedly misidentifies Nez for a different Navajo leader, former Navajo Nation President Jonathan Nez has issued the following statement: “Eli Crane and his billionaire backers are so scared of an Indigenous sheepherder from Shonto, Arizona, they rushed a $700k ad against me.
But they care so little about the voters of AZ-02 they couldn’t get it right.
The voters of AZ-02 are tired of their broken promises and disregard for the real challenges they are facing.
I guess they don’t care to know my face, but on November 3rd they’ll hear my voice.” The super PAC is pouring in more than half a million dollars to attack Nez with its new ad.
The news comes after the Nez campaign released polling showing the race to be effectively tied.
