added: Home About Values Get Involved Team Linda Before results come in As polls close and before we know any results, I just wanted to say thank you.
While I wish we could've spent more time in person together, I'm thankful we connected through Facebook Lives, phone calls, and those early conversations at your doors.
Over and over again, I was uplifted and reminded why I'm proud to raise my daughter in our community.
This election, we worked our hardest.
I'm proud of how this campaign has shaped the race.
Working class families were the center of the conversation - exactly where we deserve to be.
Thank you for being an active part of our democracy, Linda Michelle Serrato Democrat for HD 45 by Team Linda One more day!
I can't believe we're almost at Election Day!
Team Linda has been working overtime to reach voters and help individuals vote and we have some tips for tomorrow!
If you're still making a decision in HD 45, please take a moment to learn more about Linda Serrato If you are voting in person: If you are going to vote tomorrow, please be kind to our poll workers.
They are adjusting to a different environment than any of us could have predicted.
Be sure to wear a mask and respect social distancing guidelines.
If you live in House District 45 and need a mask, pen, gloves and alcohol wipes, request a Vote Safely Kit from Team Linda!
We can deliver it before voting begins tomorrow.
If you didn't receive your mail in ballot: I know many of us are still waiting for our mail in ballots to arrive.
If you receive it, please take your ballot to an Election Day voting location or the County Clerk's office.
If you don't have it tomorrow, you can vote by signing an affidavit confirming that you do not have a ballot and you can vote provisionally.
All provisional votes are counted.
However you vote, be sure to stay safe.
We can make a difference in our community and our state! by Team Linda This Memorial Day This Memorial Day is a little different than most.
Today, as we recognize our service women and men, we also recognize our frontliners - the countless firefighters, nurses, doctors, and others - who have sacrificed everything to protect us.
Each day, our emergency workers put themselves at risk of coming in contact with COVID-19 without proper protection.
We've lost too many of these selfless workers.
Those bold enough to serve leave a lasting legacy.
Linda’s grandfather served in World War II and earned his citizenship, ensuring her entire family would be Americans.
More than 70 years later, her family remembers how he shaped our futures.

Today, we'll be thinking of all the families - military and frontline - and honoring their loved ones' legacies. by Team Linda Vote Safely This weekend, The Albuquerque Journal endorsed our campaign, citing our campaign's "energy" and "fresh voice"!

We're honored to have the support of BOTH The Albuquerque Journal and The Santa Fe Reporter along with 11 Democratic and progressive organizations like Sierra Club: Rio Grande Chapter, Conservation Voters New Mexico, Animal Protection Voters, Planned Parenthood Votes and many others!
With Election Day is right around the corner, we want to make sure you can vote safely.
Starting this Saturday, if you live in HD 45 and are voting in person or dropping off your mail-in ballot at a voting location, we'll be happy to provide a Vote Safely Kit at your door.
We'll drop off a mask and other items at your home in the early morning.
Click here to sign up!
Stay Safe and Stay Engaged! by Team Linda NEW Endorsements!
Our community deserves bold ideas that help working families thrive.
And now, three more groups agree: Linda Serrato will be the BEST leader for House District 45.

The Santa Fe Reporter , Working Families Party , and Adelante all endorsed Linda Serrato with ProgressNowNM calling Linda a "Progressive Champion!" We need bold solutions to confront this pandemic and put our working families first in recovery.
It's time for a compassionate leader, ready to stand with us and demand corporations pay their fair share.
There's only # days until this election.
She'll stand for us.

Let's stand together for Linda. by Team Linda Working Families Stand with Linda With only # days left to vote, Linda is working harder than ever to earn your support in the race for House District 45!
We just got signs in!
If you're interested in a large or yard sign and you live in HD 45, please email grassroots@lindafornm.com and we'll get you one right away!
Even more exciting, this week, OLÉ endorsed our campaign for House District 45!
I'm proud to have the support of these working New Mexicans fighting for a better future for our families.
Finally, I just wanted to say thanks for all of the support and kindness you've shared during this race.
We're living through tough times.
No one expected to be home schoolers, mask makers, or expert hand washers.
Through it all, Santa Fe has been an example for the nation.
We're social distancing, helping each other and voting by mail.
Thank you for caring about our community and each other.
Now it's time for those values to be the bedrock on which we build our recovery.
We must have compassionate leaders who will protect working class families and demand corporations pay their fair share.
Our communities deserves bold ideas that will protect our future.
If you share these values then I hope Linda can earn your vote. by Team Linda How far we’ve come I can’t believe how far we’ve come.
This campaign started as a long shot with a strong belief that community members in House District 45 deserved a bold voice on behalf of seniors and working families.

Since then, we’ve knocked hundreds of doors, collected more signatures than any of our opponents, received donations from more New Mexicans than all of our opponents combined, and have support from diverse communities including: American Federation of Teachers New Mexico Planned Parenthood Votes New Mexico Sierra Club: Rio Grande Chapter Conservation Voters New Mexico New Mexico Youth Climate Strike Animal Protection Voters Linda is ready to stand for our families in the Roundhouse.
Let’s keep it up and work all the way through Election Day, Tuesday, June 2nd. by Team Linda Recent Posts Today’s Swearing in New Endorsements!
Peaceful Transition If you missed our launch… Join Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham and Linda as we launch for the general election!

MOMENTS TO WATCH: When asked, “You’ve called the Affordable Care Act a disaster.

Would you vote to repeal it?,” Joe Mitchell said, “ Yeah, I would vote to repeal it .” When asked about his response to the rural hospital leaders sounding the alarm about the billions in rural health care cuts Mitchell backs, he had zero answers .

When asked about the War Powers Resolution in the House of Representatives, Joe Mitchell said, “I think the resolutions that have been put up most recently by Democrats have been a knee-jerk and partisan action to defy the president.” Fact check: those were bipartisan resolutions.
He even told Punchbowl News that he would have voted to keep funding the war.

From the gas pump to the grocery store, people can’t make ends meet” said Lindsay James.
“My constituents are making impossible choices because of the reckless decisions coming out of Washington.
They’re tired of the same politicians making empty promises and not delivering - that’s why we see a shift on the ground and why we’re gaining momentum.

When I’m in DC, I’m going to fight corruption, restore the cuts to healthcare, end the war in Iran, and advocate for my neighbors.” ALSO IN THE NEWS: Politico reported , “All three vulnerable GOP-held seats in Iowa looked doomed” and “Senior Republicans believe their internal polling, if it holds, shows likely losses across all three at-risk GOP seats in Iowa.” Punchbowl reported , “If there is a blue wave next month, the Democratic momentum could cost Mitchell in the race for Iowa’s open 2nd District.” ### For press inquiries please contact press@lindsayforiowa.com For other inquiries please contact info@lindsayforiowa.com P.O Box 144, Dubuque, IA 52004 Private Policy Powered by RUN! website builder Paid for by Lindsay for Iowa You need to enable JavaScript to run this app.

Let’s keep it that way—and make it even stronger for the generations to come.

Owen was the CEO of the Western Sugar Cooperative and is the chairperson of 21st Century Equipment.
He also served as the chairman of the Nebraska chapter of The Nature Conservancy.

October 8 - Mark and Solomon Drop in On Folks in 9 Sandhills Towns in One Day On October 8th Solomon and I headed north and dropped in on folks in Arthur, Hyannis, Mullen, Thedford, Seneca, Whitman, Arnold, Stapleton, and Callaway.
Most people were shocked that a congressional candidate would take the time to visit these small towns.
I love driving in the Sandhills, which is why I chose to my home in Lemoyne.
October 7 - Former Valentine City Manager Rick Medema Endorses Mark I am honored that former Valentine City Manager Rick Medema has endorsed me.

White: Why Tennessee’s students need Marsha Blackburn as Governor August 14, 2026 Why Tennessee’s Students Need Marsha Blackburn as Governor Commercial Appeal State Representative Mark White (R-Memphis) August 14, 2026 “The school year has begun for Tennessee students, and Tennesseans will soon cast their votes for who they want to shape the educational opportunities those students will have.

As a teacher and a principal, I saw firsthand the difference a great education can make in a student’s life, and we owe it to the next generation to elect an education-minded governor who will fight to give every Tennessee student a world-class education.

“That is why I’m voting for Marsha Blackburn for Governor… “Marsha will not only allocate plenty of resources to our schools, but she will also work with the state legislature and local school boards to make sure those funds are being used for the benefit of students.
“Our public schools have potential to be the best in the nation, but we aren’t there – yet.
The next governor needs to not only hold our schools fiscally accountable, but also hold them to high standards in their curriculum and policies.
Marsha will champion a strong education strategy that will take Tennessee’s schools to the next level.” Read the full op-ed HERE .
Mark White represents House District 83, which consists of part of Shelby County.
Representative White serves as Chair of the House Education Committee.

added: Skip to main content Skip to footer Home Meet Marsha Issues Bell to Bell: No Cell In The News Join Us Join The Team Team Store Donate In The News: Opinion: The Freest State in the Nation: Marsha Blackburn’s Vision for Tennessee October 9, 2026 Gallatin News State Rep.
William Lamberth, State Rep.
Johnny Garrett, State Rep.

William Slater, Republican Nominee Brian Stewart, Sumner County GOP Chair Baron Lowe October 8, 2026 “When the visionaries of our great nation signed the Constitution, they cemented the American ideals they fought and bled for as the very foundation of the nation we are today.
That sacred document laid the groundwork for something the world had never seen: a government built not to rule over its people, but to protect their inherent rights and God-given freedoms.

“As President Donald Trump works to restore the constitutional balance of power and return authority to the states, we need principled, freedom-fighting governors who respect the Constitution, uphold the rule of law, and ensure their states remain true to the values on which our nation was founded.
“Here in Tennessee, no one is better equipped to answer that call than Marsha Blackburn.
“She has the vision to make Tennessee a national leader when it comes to protecting freedom, limiting government, and elevating individual liberties.
That vision rests on one simple truth: Constitutional rights don’t require a permission slip.
“Our government exists to secure the “blessings of liberty” for ourselves and our families, and that liberty must be broad and enduring.
Our nation thrives when its people are free to live, work, and pursue their dreams, and that is the philosophy that will guide Marsha Blackburn as governor.” Read the full op-ed HERE .

William Lamberth, Johnny Garrett, and William Slater serve in the Tennessee House of Representatives; Brian Stewart is the Republican nominee for TN House District 45, and Baron Lowe is chair of the Sumner County Republican Party.

alt://instagram.fsdv2-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t39.30808-6/825292548_122122395069364925_1605130843068111407_n.jpg|If not me, then who… This is what Travis Manion told his family before his second deployment to Iraq. It wasn't a boast. He was explaining that if he didn't go, a less experienced Marine would be sent in his place. Months later, when his patrol was ambushed in Fallujah, he exposed himself to enemy fire to draw it away from his wounded teammates. Travis was killed, and every other member of his patrol made it home. That is service to one's fellows. It was my honor to serve as guest speaker at the Travis Manion Foundation 9/11 Heroes Run at the Military Aviation Museum here in Virginia Beach. Thank you to the course organizers, race volunteers, and participants for a great event. Find your own "If not me, then who?" moment, no matter how small. Semper Fidelis #IfNotMeThenWho #911HeroesRun #NeverForget

alt://instagram.fsdv2-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t39.30808-6/828534201_122122610781364925_5354465174033929285_n.jpg|independentveteransofamerica got it right endorsing these great veterans running as independents this November! Dan Osborne served in both the Army and the Navy. He has been a union leader and understands if you “don’t have a seat at the table, you are the meal”. He’s running to be a Senator from Nebraska. Sarah Zabel was a Communications and Computer Systems officer in the Air Force. She retired after 31-years service as a Major General. She’s running in Idaho’s First Congressional District. Brian Bengs is a retired as an Air Force Lieutenant Colonel and JAG officer. He started his career in the Navy and is running for Senate in South Dakota. Seth Bodnar is a West Point grad and Rhodes Scholar who served in the 101st Airborne and the Green Berets. And he was the President of the University of Montana! He’s running for Senate in Montana. Steve Woll is a neighbor and friend who served in the Navy as a Meteorology and Oceanography Officer retiring as a Captain. He is running for the VA-03 House of Representatives seat. I’m the Marine Infantry guy on the far right and I’m proud and humbled to say I served alongside all six of these candidates on active duty. I’m running for the House in Virginia District 2. Nobody ever asked our party to serve in the Armed Forces and we are all independents today! See the comments for websites and more information on independent veterans running for office this fall. alt://instagram.fsdv2-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t39.30808-6/836438583_122123651349364925_8169198313266298385_n.jpg|Purple. Independent means no party, not a lean toward one. Today's Virginian-Pilot ran a piece worth your time: "Independent voters deserve more from candidates, campaigns" by John Opdycke. He notes that 48% of Americans now identify as independent. Yet the moment an independent "leans" even slightly one way, they get counted as part of that party. I'd wondered why so many comments on my posts used that word. Now I get it. Call someone a "leaner" and you're right back to two parties. Maybe lighter shades of blue and red, like the maps we all see in the media, right? Wrong. If you want to categorize me, call me purple. I share some ideas with the red side and some with the blue, but I'm best described as a mix of the two. Blue plus red equals purple. In the military, joint is purple: every service working as one team. No one says you lean Marine Corps, but we get it done. If you're purple and independent, share this post and help get the word out. #independent #va02 #virginiabeach #vote #suffolkva #eastville

alt://instagram.fsdv2-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t51.82787-15/805923376_18160623145492496_1302952563746266860_n.jpg|Ran the Yard at the Naval Academy this morning. Visited memorials at Hospital Point. Today, 25 years after 9/11, I remembered LCDR Ron Vauk, lost that day at the Pentagon. Caught up to a group of mids in boots and utes, carrying an American flag. The occasion was obvious — but what exactly were they doing? “Hey — Matt Baker, class of ‘87—“ I started. “Twenty-seven, sir!” the mid in charge cut me off. Still happens every time. “What’s this about?” Turned out to be a 24-hour run, rotating shifts, all day and night. One runner in the group wasn’t a mid at all — an officer on the faculty, already 10 miles in. More groups and individuals carrying flags came into view. Told the lone runner, as he handed off his flag to the next in line, who they were honoring. “You’re running for Ron Vauk, ‘87—“ “Twenty-eight, sir!” “How long?” “An hour twenty.” Caught my breath… “Thanks.” Then kept running. This is what “never forget” should look like. Semper Fi, Ron. — Matt

alt://instagram.fsdv2-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t51.82787-15/836663580_18165572575492496_5591039487783967405_n.jpg|If you watched ABC's "This Week" this weekend, you saw a segment titled "Navy Veterans Vie for Virginia Beach-Area House Seat." You'd be surprised to know he qualified for the ballot by collecting more than 2,500 petition signatures across the district, more than double what Virginia requires. My name is Matt Baker. If you're sick of two parties handing you the same two choices, you're not alone. The news may try to pretend candidates like me don't exist. The ballot isn't going to. On November 3, you decide who represents this district — not Washington, not Sunday morning TV. You. #virginiabeach #hamptonroads #mattbaker #independentforcongress

added: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE January 20, 2026 Session Kicks Off The first week of the 101st Session of the South Dakota Legislature is in the books.
As is typical, it was largely ceremonial, informational, and organizational.
While it didn’t yet have the faster pace or heavier committee agendas that come later, the opening days play an important role in setting the tone and direction for the weeks ahead.

We began the session by hearing the State of the State from Governor Larry Rhoden, the State of the Judiciary from Chief Justice Steven Jensen, and the State of the Tribes from President Kathleen Wooden Knife of the Rosebud Sioux Tribe.
Governor Rhoden emphasized civility and outlined policy goals relating to property tax relief, public safety, and economic development.

Chief Justice Jensen highlighted the ongoing work of South Dakota’s Unified Judicial System, including strategic planning, efforts to strengthen indigent defense, expanded probation and treatment courts, and the importance of judicial security and workforce stability.
President Wooden Knife shared thoughtful remarks on cooperation and respectful relationships between tribal governments and the state.
An especially memorable moment came as part of our preparations to mark the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence.

We were treated to a historical portrayal of the document’s drafter, “Thomas Jefferson,” which provided both a bit of levity and an opportunity to reflect on the principles that form the foundation of our system of government.
It was also a good reminder of the responsibility we have as citizens to ensure the delicate balance of powers crafted by the Founders endures for future generations.
As is also typical during the first week of session, we had the opportunity to absorb all sorts of information.
For example, we received an update on the status of the Rural Health Transformation Funds, of which South Dakota was recently awarded $189 million.

These funds are intended to support innovative approaches to delivering care, strengthening local systems, and ensuring that South Dakotans don’t have to travel unreasonable distances to receive needed services.
Understanding how these dollars will be used, and what outcomes they intend to produce, will be an early-session priority.
We also received a presentation from the South Dakota National Guard.
Their service – both here at home and when called upon nationally – is exceptional, and it was good to receive an update on the status of current operations and future needs.
Beyond formal business, the first week provides the opportunity to reconnect.
It was good to catch up with colleagues, administration officials, and old friends around the Capitol.
With effective lawmaking often depending as much on trust and communication as it does on policy details, these relationships matter.

I also had a chance to connect with folks from the Watertown area who were in Pierre during the week, including leaders from Lake Area Tech, Codington-Clark Electric, and the Senior Health Information and Insurance Education (SHIINE) program.
As we move into the coming weeks, the pace will pick up quickly.
Committees will begin hearing substantive bills, amendments will be debated, and proposals will start moving to the House floor.
This is where the real work of the session takes shape.

Serving in the Legislature is a responsibility I take seriously, and I’m looking forward to digging in and advocating for the priorities of District 5 residents and for the betterment of South Dakota.
Hearing directly from constituents helps guide the decisions I make in Pierre.
If you have questions, concerns, or ideas you’d like to share, I encourage you to reach out.
You can contact me by email at matt.roby@sdlegislature.gov or by phone/text at 605-881-4949.
I’m honored to continue serving District 5 in the State House, and I look forward to keeping you informed as the 101st Legislative Session continues.
CONTACT: Matt Roby mtroby@gmail.com 605-881-4949 Paid for by Friends of Matt Roby

added: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE February 3, 2026 Pace Quickens Weeks two and three of the 101st Session of the South Dakota Legislature brought a noticeable shift in pace.
Committees moved into more substantive work, bills began advancing to the House floor, and the focus turned from orientation to decision-making.
These weeks are where priorities start to take shape and policy discussions become more concrete.
The House has passed several bills I supported that are particularly relevant to District 5 and to communities across our state.
One of those was HB 1044, which approved the use of Rural Health Transformation Funds.
South Dakota was awarded these dollars to support innovative health care delivery models, strengthen local systems, and improve access to care—especially in rural areas.

Ensuring these funds are used responsibly and effectively will be an ongoing discussion as additional awards are made over the next five years We also passed HB 1049, a bill protecting our electric infrastructure from being owned, controlled, or operated by foreign countries of concern.
Reliable and secure energy systems are essential for public safety, economic stability, and national security, and this legislation helps safeguard infrastructure we all depend on.
Addressing workforce needs was another theme.
HB 1035 modified CPA licensure requirements to maintain strong consumer protections while allowing an alternative pathway to licensure in response to ongoing workforce shortages.

Similarly, HB 1029 revised provisions related to the practice of addiction counseling, helping ensure South Dakotans have access to qualified professionals while maintaining appropriate standards of care.
The House also passed HB 1101, which prohibits insurance companies from declining or limiting coverage solely because an individual is a living organ donor.
This commonsense measure ensures that those willing to make an extraordinary, lifesaving sacrifice are not penalized for doing so.
Several bills addressed education, natural resources, and local government needs.
HB 1047 authorized construction to expand the Blue Dog Lake Fish Hatchery, supporting fish stocking efforts and outdoor recreation opportunities that are important to our region.
SB 84 increased income thresholds for the Partners in Education tuition program, expanding access for more families.
HB 1130 allows school districts to pay for property insurance out of capital outlay funds, providing additional flexibility as districts manage rising insurance costs.
Beyond legislation, the past two weeks included several meaningful events and opportunities to learn.
The Legislature took time to memorialize legislators who passed away in the last year, honoring their service and contributions to our state.
I also received a briefing on the work of the Public Utilities Commission, which plays a critical role in overseeing utilities and infrastructure development.

Outside the Capitol, I had the chance to meet with South Dakota Community Support Providers, attend a reception with the South Dakota Catholic Conference and Bishop DeGrood, and participate in the Governor’s Prayer Breakfast featuring Will Graham (Billy Graham’s grandson).

It was also good to celebrate South Dakota Tourism alongside a group from Watertown and to spend time at the Mickelson Criminal Justice Center, where I had the opportunity to test my pistol skills in the annual Attorney General’s Shootout.
It's evident my aim needs a little work.
As the session continues, deadlines will drive even faster movement of legislation, and debates will become more intense.
I am committed to carefully reviewing each proposal and advocating for policies that reflect the needs and values of District 5.
Hearing from constituents continues to be an important part of this process.
If you have questions, concerns, or ideas, please don’t hesitate to reach out.
I can be contacted by email at matt.roby@sdlegislature.gov or by phone/text at 605-881-4949.
It is an honor to serve District 5, and I look forward to keeping you informed as the session progresses.

added: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE February 10, 2026 Getting Busy Week four of the 101st Session marked another busy stretch at the Capitol.
Committee agendas are overflowing, floor sessions are getting longer, and the issues discussed are getting more contentious.
The bill filing deadline has now come and gone.
In total, 570 bills were filed this session, not including resolutions.
That represents an increase of 81 bills compared to last year.
The increase from the first year of a term to the second year of a term is typical, though the overall volume is near a record.

With our time constraints, the large number of bills increases the likelihood that a bill will be defeated (rather than amended) because it isn’t “ready for prime time.” That’s also why you might see a bill defeated despite having an appealing title.
When that occurs, I’d encourage you to seek out the recording of the hearing or floor session to gain the full picture.
You can find them all by navigating to sdlegislature.gov.
I have introduced several bills of my own this session.

These include measures to make an appropriation for Lake Area Technical College; clarify the ability of nonprofits to fundraise through pull-tab machines; allow attorneys to issue subpoenas in administrative actions; require disclosure of third-party litigation funding; request onetime funding for a study on public transportation in South Dakota; and penalize “doxxing” of law enforcement and judges.
Bills of note that had my support and passed the House in Week 4 include: • • SB 4, which provides landlords an additional week to return security deposits.

This change is intended to reduce situations where landlords feel pressured to overpay for repairs or replace items that could instead be fixed, ultimately helping keep costs down for tenants while maintaining fairness for both parties.
HB 1107, which allows greater flexibility when donated land can no longer be used for the purpose it was originally intended.

This bill provides a court additional flexibility to repurpose donated land when conditions change, making the original intended use impossible or impractical. • • • SB 12, which provides a property tax refund from prior years for qualifying veterans and surviving spouses.
This is one of more than 25 bills this year aimed at providing property tax relief, with much more to come on this topic.
SB 46, 47, and 48, which were part of a package of bills that strengthened South Dakota’s open meeting laws.
These measures reinforce the public’s right to know and help ensure governmental decisions are made openly and with accountability.
HB 1056, which requires the state to submit a federal waiver request to exclude soda from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP).
This bill reflects the belief that this important safety net program should be preserved to encourage healthier food choices.
Last week also included valuable conversations with District 5 residents who took time to be in Pierre.

I appreciated the opportunity to talk with municipal government and public power employees from the City of Watertown and Watertown Municipal Utilities, and to discuss healthcare and behavioral health priorities with Watertown healthcare leaders.

I also enjoyed learning about new initiatives from local homebuilders (check out www.beprobeproud.org), chatting with local Realtors about housing (and chili!), visiting with our school superintendents about education priorities, and supporting South Dakota Public Broadcasting alongside advocates from District 5.
And it was a great honor to have dinner with several students from Lake Area Tech’s Student Voice.
It is always encouraging to see familiar faces in Pierre – people who step away from their busy schedules to advocate for their professions and for causes that matter to them.
Those conversations help ensure the policies we debate are informed by realworld experience.
As always, hearing from constituents is invaluable.
If you have questions, concerns, or ideas you’d like to share, please feel free to contact me by email at matt.roby@sdlegislature.gov or by phone/text at 605-881-4949.

added: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE February 24, 2026 Two Intense Weeks in Pierre The best word to describe the last two weeks in Pierre is intense.

With “crossover day” on February 24 (the deadline for bills to pass out of their chamber of origin) and the tendency for controversial bills to be dropped right at the filing deadline, high-emotion issues tend to pile up during this period.
We saw proposals targeting teachers, health care, economic development, and agriculture.
Thankfully, a governing majority of common-sense legislators were able to stop the most harmful proposals and keep our focus on practical solutions that strengthen South Dakota rather than divide it.

While many of the debates have required playing defense, several good bills moved out of the House during this stretch, including: • • • • • • • Expanding the Sturgis Readiness Center to support our National Guard.
Adding coaches to the list of mandatory reporters of child abuse or neglect.
Strengthening protections for seniors and vulnerable adults against financial exploitation.
Providing additional property tax relief for disabled veterans and surviving spouses.
Adjusting assessment methodologies for owner-occupied homes to bring greater stability and fairness.
Protecting patients from retroactive claim denials by health insurers.
Licensing non-medical home care agencies to improve accountability and standards of care.
We also passed bills authorizing counties and municipalities to issue a license for a cigar bar and enabling municipal capital improvement funding tools.
Not every bill will make headlines, but many will make a practical difference in communities across the state.
Two of the largest issues of the session – property taxes and data centers – remain unresolved.
On property taxes, there is broad agreement that some form of relief is warranted.
The debate centers on how significant that relief will be and how to structure it responsibly.
Several proposals remain alive and continue to move through the process.
I expect we will see bills become law that provide relief at the margins and increase transparency.
Achieving substantial structural reform, however, will be a heavy lift.
On data centers, the conversation has focused on balance.
If South Dakota hosts these facilities, we must ensure their negative externalities – such as upward pressure on energy prices – are minimized.
At the same time, we must determine whether we can remain competitive with other states.
The central question is whether to offer a form of sales and use tax exemption on equipment purchases.
That decision will likely determine whether large-scale data center projects move forward here.

Several of my own initiatives are still advancing – including legislation providing a criminal penalty for doxxing law enforcement officers and judges and a bill ensuring subpoena authority for attorneys in administrative proceedings.
A bill providing clarity for nonprofit fundraising through mechanical pull tabs is awaiting the Governor’s signature, along with municipal and building code updates I agreed to carry in the House.
Although there are plenty of policy fights left to be had, the discussions over the remaining few weeks of session tend to be largely budget related.
One of my primary focuses will be HB 1202 – a one-time funding proposal for Lake Area Technical College.
The bill would support construction of a facility to launch three high-demand programs at LATC: industrial refrigeration, HVAC, and water treatment.
Expanding this capacity strengthens our regional economy and addresses real workforce needs.
If you support workforce development and Lake Area Tech, I encourage you to contact legislators – both locally and statewide – and urge support for HB 1202.
Although the last couple weeks have been “intense,” I’m honored to be doing this work on behalf of District 5.

The long hours and emotional debates are balanced by the camaraderie of colleagues and the reminder that the bills we vote on are not academic exercises – they have real-world impact on our families, schools, businesses, and communities.
I’m always happy to receive input or feedback on legislation from constituents.
If you have questions, concerns, or ideas you’d like to share, please feel free to contact me by email at matt.roby@sdlegislature.gov or by phone/text at 605-881-4949.

added: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE March 3, 2026 Crossover Day Drama We reached an important milestone in Pierre last week: Crossover Day – the deadline for bills to pass out of their chamber of origin.
Unlike past sessions where crossover day went late into the evening, the House concluded its work this year relatively early and dramafree.
The Senate, however, experienced a more turbulent day.
A couple of senators were intentionally absent from the floor to avoid contentious votes and potential tie-breaking action by the Lieutenant Governor.
That kind of maneuvering reflects poorly on the Legislature and is a disservice to constituents who expect their elected officials to show up and cast votes on tough issues.
While the turmoil in the Senate received most of the news this week, the House passed several important measures that I was proud to support.
Among them was House Bill 1140, which allows courts to require treatment at certain nonprofit entities as a condition of probation or parole.
House Bill 1300 protects victims of human trafficking and domestic abuse by exempting them from certain clemency notice requirements.
We also passed House Bill 1082, which establishes parameters for reimbursing school districts that provide free or reduced-price meals to students.
Water infrastructure remains a priority across our state.

Senate Concurrent Resolutions 606 and 607 encourage review and approval of Missouri River water rights applications and support congressional authorization and federal participation in major rural water projects identified by the South Dakota Association of Rural Water Systems.
These measures are good steps in the ongoing efforts to ensure long-term water security for our communities.

Other bills passed this week include Senate Bill 111, requiring social media companies to provide users access to their collected personal data and increasing transparency; Senate Bills 81 and 82, which clarify protections for service animals and establish penalties for their misrepresentation; House Bill 1262, appropriating funds for a non-residential, school-based therapeutic services facility in Brown County; Senate Bill 89, creating a task force to study emergency medical services funding; Senate Bill 113, increasing penalties for preventing the practice of religion; and House Bill 88, clarifying procedures related to examining real property in condemnation cases.
I’m especially pleased to report progress on a few of the bills I’ve sponsored.
House Bill 1298, prohibiting the electronic publication of personal information about judges and law enforcement, passed the House by a strong margin and now heads to the Senate.
House Bill 1201, clarifying the ability of certain non-profits to fundraise through mechanical pull-tab machines, was signed into law last week.
House Bill 1234, revising provisions related to serving subpoenas in contested cases, is now headed to the Governor’s desk.
The data center debate continues.
Efforts to position South Dakota competitively from a tax and regulatory standpoint were sidetracked amid the Senate’s above-noted procedural tactics.
However, legislation ensuring sensible guardrails on data center impacts remains active and is likely to become law.
Property tax relief discussions also continue in earnest.
Several proposals have been set aside due to a lack of broad consensus, but a new approach – Senate Bill 245 – appears to be gaining meaningful support in the House.
Additionally, the Governor’s proposal, Senate Bill 96, would allow counties to adopt a half-cent sales tax to directly offset property taxes.
I am more hopeful than I was last week that we have an opportunity this year to deliver meaningful relief.
As always, I value your input.
If you have thoughts on these proposals or other issues still under consideration, please don’t hesitate to reach out at matt.roby@sdlegislature.gov or call/text 605-881-4949.
Serving you in Pierre remains an honor, and I appreciate the opportunity to keep you informed.
CONTACT: Matt Roby mtroby@gmail.com 605-881-4949 Paid for by Friends of Matt Roby

added: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE March 10, 2026 You Can’t Always Get What You Want When I think about the legislative process, a song from the Rolling Stones comes to mind: “You Can’t Always Get What You Want.” That certainly rang true for me and others last week as the House considered a one-time appropriation for Lake Area Technical College to build a new Trades Center.
The project would have allowed the addition of three new programs – HVAC, refrigeration, and water treatment – all areas where South Dakota employers are facing workforce shortages.
Because the proposal involved one-time spending, it required a two-thirds majority to pass.
That meant we needed 47 votes.
In the end, we were only able to secure 43.
A great deal of work went into the effort, especially from LATC President Tiffany Sanderson and others who helped make the case for the project.
While the vote was disappointing, Lake Area Tech will continue pursuing other avenues to move the project forward.
Still, it was frustrating to see some legislators unwilling to make this type of investment in our state’s future.
While the LATC proposal did not pass, the House did approve a number of bills last week that I supported.
Several measures focused on public safety and consumer protection.
These included bills that combat virtual currency kiosk fraud, enhance penalties for drug crimes occurring in our state prisons, and protect the privacy and security of genetic data.
We also passed a bill prohibiting the creation and distribution of non-consensual, pornographic “AI deepfakes” of real people.
The bill was introduced at the request of the Attorney General, and I volunteered to carry it on the House floor.
Learning more about the issue opened my eyes to the very real harm these activities can cause.

The House also approved safeguards against foreign influence in our elections, protections for individuals exercising their constitutional free speech rights, and provisions for wildfire mitigation planning for utilities.
Infrastructure and economic development were also part of last week’s agenda.

The House approved funding for public improvements related to the expansion at Ellsworth Air Force Base, funding to support rural infrastructure in counties across the state, and authorization of loans to support expansion projects at the Rapid City and Sioux Falls airports.

Finally, the House approved requirements for county notifications to townships, expanding community safety zones to include licensed child-care programs, and modifying provisions related to tax increment financing (TIF) districts.
The bill revising TIF district laws was the product of interested parties coming together to agree on reasonable updates.
This was a great example of the type of collaboration that leads to good law.
With only one week remaining, the Legislature is beginning to put a bow on the main run of the 2026 session.

While a few policy issues still need to be resolved, the final days will largely focus on financial matters, including property tax proposals, one-time spending decisions, and final passage of the General Appropriations Act – the only mustpass bill every year.

I intend to run through the finish line advocating for issues important to District 5 and working to ensure South Dakota remains a great place to live, work, and raise a family – both today and for the next generation of South Dakotans.

If you have any final input this week on budget setting or would like to get together for a recap after session, you can reach me by email at matt.roby@sdlegislature.gov or by call/text at 605-881-4949.
CONTACT: Matt Roby mtroby@gmail.com 605-881-4949 Paid for by Friends of Matt Roby

added: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE March 31, 2026 Recap of the 101st South Dakota Legislative Session With the conclusion of Veto Day, the 101st Legislative Session in South Dakota is now officially adjourned.
As with any session, the outcome is a mix of meaningful progress, missed opportunities, and lessons that will be carried forward.
My Bills and Outcomes This year, I was proud to sponsor and support several bills aimed at improving processes, strengthening communities, and updating outdated statutes.
Several measures successfully made it across the finish line and have now been signed into law.

These include allowing attorney-issued subpoenas in administrative proceedings, expanding nonprofit fundraising opportunities through mechanical pull-tabs, updating building codes, modernizing municipal statutes, and adjusting the timeline for landlords to return security deposits.
Each of these represents a practical improvement to how government and everyday systems function.
Legislation prohibiting the doxxing of judges and law enforcement officers has also been signed by the Governor – an important step in protecting those who serve in sensitive public safety roles.
Not every effort was successful.
A proposal to secure one-time funding for a new Trades Center at Lake Area Technical College fell short, despite strong local and regional advocacy.
While disappointing, I remain committed to advocating for technical education and workforce development in future sessions.

Another bill was withdrawn after productive conversations with the Department of Transportation, which agreed to pursue a community transit study using existing resources – an example of how good policy can still move forward, even without formal legislation.
Key Legislation I Supported This session also saw the passage of several significant measures aimed at addressing some of the biggest concerns facing South Dakotans.
Foremost among them was meaningful property tax relief.
Through a combination of one-time funding and capturing additional revenue from the sales tax sunset, homeowners can expect noticeable reductions in their property tax burden in the coming years.

Additional flexibility at the county level – through a county option sales tax – provides another tool to further reduce property taxes in counties that have been impacted most by recent property tax increases.

We also passed consumer protections for virtual currency kiosks, strengthened safeguards for vulnerable individuals against financial exploitation, increased penalties for those who interfere with the free exercise of religion, and authorized local governments to issue licenses for cigar bars.
These measures reflect a continued focus on public safety, individual rights, and local control.
Data Centers: Growth with Guardrails As I’ve discussed in prior columns, large data centers are increasingly considering South Dakota as a location.
These projects can bring significant investment and tangible benefits – but they also have the potential to place real demands on resources.
This year, we took important steps to ensure that growth in this sector happens responsibly.
Legislation passed requiring data centers to pay their own way when it comes to the electric generation they require, rather than shifting those costs onto existing ratepayers.
We also reinforced the authority of local governments to have a meaningful say in where these facilities are sited and put safeguards in place to protect our water resources.
However, one key piece remains unresolved.
We could not reach agreement addressing the tax treatment of data centers.
As a result, South Dakota remains at a competitive disadvantage compared to other states that have adopted more targeted tax policies for this industry.
That is an issue I expect will continue to be part of the conversation going forward.
Investing in South Dakota’s Future In addition to policy changes, the Legislature approved targeted investments across the state.
These included funding for rural healthcare, infrastructure improvements, water and environmental projects, and support for victims of crime.
From riparian buffer initiatives to youth career training and communitybased programs, these investments are designed to strengthen both our economy and quality of life.
And, of course, the Legislature fulfilled its core constitutional responsibility by passing a balanced state budget.

This process involves months of detailed work by appropriators from across the political spectrum, carefully reviewing each request to ensure taxpayer dollars are spent responsibly and in alignment with the state’s priorities.
Conduct and Culture While I am proud of much of the work accomplished this session, I would be remiss if I did not acknowledge some troubling trends in how that work was carried out.
We saw legislators deliberately absent from contentious votes.
We saw disputes over matters as trivial as seating arrangements distract from the business of the people.
We saw unsubstantiated accusations of impropriety or corruption.
And, perhaps most concerning, we saw the questioning of members’ religious convictions and sincerity.
Disagreement is part of the legislative process, and strong opinions are to be expected.
But respect for one another – and a willingness to engage in good faith – are essential to maintaining the integrity of the institution.
South Dakotans deserve a Legislature that debates issues vigorously while still treating one another with basic civility.
Looking Ahead No legislative session is perfect.

Compromise is inherent in the process, and according to the Rolling Stones, “you can’t always get what you want.” But taken as a whole, this year’s work reflects a continued commitment to fiscal responsibility, local control, and common-sense policy.
As always, I appreciate the input, feedback, and engagement from constituents throughout the session.
Your perspective helps shape the decisions made in Pierre, and I look forward to continuing that conversation in the months ahead.
I can continue to be reached by phone/text at 605-881-4949 or by email at matt.roby@sdlegislature.gov.
It remains my honor to represent District 5 in the State House.

added: Meet Matt Volunteer Yard Signs Contact Updates News Contribute PRIVACY POLICY This privacy notice for Friends of Matt Roby (“we,” “us,” or “our”), describes how and why we might collect, store, use, and/or share (“process”) your information when you use our services (“Services”), such as when you: Visit our website at mattrobyforsd.com, or any website of ours that links to this privacy notice; or Engage with us in other related ways, including any sales, marketing, or events Questions or concerns?
Reading this privacy notice will help you understand your privacy rights and choices.
If you do not agree with our policies and practices, please do not use our Services.
If you still have any questions or concerns, please contact us at matt@mattrobyforsd.com.

INFORMATION COLLECTION We collect personal information that you voluntarily provide to us when you express an interest in obtaining information about or from our campaign, when you participate in activities, or otherwise when you contact us.
The personal information that we collect depends on the context of your interactions with us.
The personal information we collect may include phone numbers, email addresses, and names.
We may collect some personal information automatically through cookies.
That personal information may include IP addresses, browser types, email addresses, and names, 2.

INFORMATION PROCESSING We process your information to provide, improve, and administer our Services, communicate with you, for security and fraud prevention, and to comply with law: To respond to user inquiries/offer support to users.
We may process your information to respond to your inquiries and solve any potential issues you might have with the requested service.
To enable user-to-user communications.
We may process your information if you choose to use any of our offerings that allow for communication with another user.
To request feedback.
We may process your information when necessary to request feedback.
To deliver targeted advertising to you.
We may process your information to develop and display personalized content and advertising tailored to your interests, location, and more.
To comply with our legal obligations.
We may process your information to comply with our legal obligations, respond to legal requests, and exercise, establish, or defend our legal rights.
MOBILE MESSAGING / SMS COMMUNICATIONS If you sign up to receive text messages from us, we will use your mobile phone number to send you text message updates from Friends of Matt Roby.
We may also collect, store, and use your mobile phone number to send you other text messages from Friends of Matt Roby.

We will also collect and store other personally identifiable information, such as your name, address, phone number, mobile phone number, email address, username, and/or similar information you may choose to provide to us.
In addition, as noted elsewhere in this policy, we may share this information with our affiliates, partners, and other organizations or entities.

However, text messaging originator opt-in data and consent will not be shared with any non-associated and/or non-related third-party individual, brand, or entity except for with vendors, consultants, and other service providers who need access to such information to carry out work on our behalf (and who will not use such information for their own purposes).
Friends of Matt Roby does not sell your personal information, including your mobile phone number, to third parties.
Mobile opt-in data and consent will not be shared with any third parties.
No mobile information will be shared with third parties or affiliates for marketing or promotional purposes.
All other categories of information sharing described in this Privacy Policy exclude text messaging originator opt-in data and consent.
To stop receiving text messages, reply STOP to any message you receive from us.
For help, reply HELP to any message, or contact us at matt@mattrobyforsd.com 4.

DATA RETENTION We will only keep your personal information for as long as it is necessary for the purposes set out in this privacy notice, unless a longer retention period is required or permitted by law (such as tax, accounting, or other legal requirements).

When we have no ongoing legitimate business need to process your personal information, we will either delete or anonymize such information, or in some cases we may retain it if deletion is not possible (for example, because your personal information has been stored in backup archives).
DATA SECURITY We have implemented appropriate and reasonable technical and organizational security measures designed to protect the security of any personal information we process.

However, despite our safeguards and efforts to secure your information, no electronic transmission over the Internet or information storage technology can be guaranteed to be 100% secure, so we cannot promise or guarantee that hackers, cybercriminals, or other unauthorized third parties will not be able to defeat our security and improperly collect, access, steal, or modify your information.
Although we will do our best to protect your personal information, transmission of personal information to and from our Services is at your own risk.

PRIVACY RIGHTS Withdrawing your consent: If we are relying on your consent to process your personal information, which may be express and/or implied consent depending on the applicable law, you have the right to withdraw your consent at any time.
You can withdraw your consent at any time by contacting us by using the contact details provided in the section “HOW CAN YOU CONTACT US ABOUT THIS NOTICE?” below.

However, please note that this will not affect the lawfulness of the processing before its withdrawal nor, when applicable law allows, will it affect the processing of your personal information conducted in reliance on lawful processing grounds other than consent.

Opting out of marketing and promotional communications: You can unsubscribe from our marketing and promotional communications at any time by clicking on the unsubscribe link in the emails that we send, replying “STOP” or “UNSUBSCRIBE” to the SMS messages that we send, or by contacting us using the details provided in the section “HOW CAN YOU CONTACT US ABOUT THIS NOTICE?” below.
You will then be removed from the marketing lists.

However, we may still communicate with you – for example, to send you service-related messages that are necessary for the administration and use of your account, to respond to service requests, or for other non-marketing purposes.
If you have questions or comments about your privacy rights, you may email us at matt@mattrobyforsd.com.
POLICY UPDATES We will update this notice as necessary to stay compliant with relevant laws.
We encourage you to review this privacy notice frequently to be informed of how we are protecting your information.
If we make an update, we will post a revised version of this policy to our website.
Updates will be documented on this page.
CONTACT US If you have questions or comments about this notice, you may email us at matt@mattrobyforsd.com.
HOW CAN YOU REVIEW, UPDATE, OR DELETE THE DATA WE COLLECT FROM YOU?
Based on the applicable laws of your country, you may have the right to request access to the personal information we collect from you, change that information, or delete it.
To request to review, update, or delete your personal information, you may email us at matt@mattrobyforsd.com.

Survey Overview: The survey finds Brian Jack leading Maura Keller by 5 points on the U.S.
House ballot, a margin within the survey's margin of error.

House results: Jack receives 50% and Keller receives 45%, with 5% undecided.
The 5-point margin falls within the survey's margin of error of ±5.6 percentage points.
Statewide results: Republican Rick Jackson leads Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms 51% to 45% for governor.
In Public Service Commission District 3, Fitz Johnson and Peter Hubbard are tied at 43%, and 14% of respondents are undecided, the largest undecided share of any race tested.
In District 5, Josh Tolbert leads Shelia Edwards 45% to 39%.
Methodology: VoteNexus, Inc. conducted a survey of 301 likely voters in Georgia's 3rd Congressional District from October 2 to 7, 2026.
Respondents were randomly selected and completed the survey online after receiving a unique link by text message.
Results are unweighted.
The reported margin of error is ±5.6 percentage points at the 95% confidence level.
Candidate order was randomized, and ballot results include respondents who lean toward a candidate.
Percentages may not total 100% because of rounding.
This survey was commissioned by Maura Keller for Congress.

added: Home ABOUT PRIORITIES CONTACT DONATE Proven Leadership for Eagle River, Chugiak, & Peter’s Creek Ken McCarty is a proven community leader focused on responsive representation, Alaska values, economic opportunity, and a stronger future for Eagle River, Chugiak, and Peter’s Creek.

DONATE ABOUT KEN MCCARTY Known by Relationships, Not Just Recognition Ken McCarty has spent decades serving the Eagle River, Chugiak, and Peter’s Creek community through leadership, counseling, education, healthcare, and public service.
As the owner of Discovery Cove Counseling and a former Trustee of the Alaska Mental Health Trust, Ken has worked directly with individuals and families facing real-life challenges.
His experience as a State House Representative for District 13 gave him firsthand insight into the importance of responsive, accountable leadership that listens to the people it serves.
Beyond public office, Ken has remained deeply involved in the community through local organizations, youth programs, aviation advocacy, healthcare initiatives, and volunteer service.
Whether helping improve community spaces, supporting local schools, or attending community council meetings, Ken believes leadership starts with being present and involved.

Ken is committed to protecting Alaska values, supporting local families and businesses, and ensuring Eagle River, Chugiak, and Peter’s Creek continue to have a strong voice and dependable representation.  Former State House Representative – District 13  Former Trustee Alaska Mental Health Trust  Community Advocate & Volunteer  Owner of Discovery Cove Counseling  President – Birchwood Airport Association  Marital & Family Therapist WHY I’M RUNNING Eagle River, Chugiak, & Peter’s Creek Deserve More I’m running because our community deserves leadership that listens, responds, and stays connected to the people it represents.
Eagle River, Chugiak, and Peter’s Creek are built on strong families, hard work, independence, and neighbors who take care of one another.
I believe leadership should reflect those same values through honesty, accountability, and real community involvement.
My goal is simple: protect Alaska values, support local businesses and families, strengthen our economy, and help build a stronger future for the next generation.
Leadership is not about politics alone; it’s about relationships, service, and showing up for the community.
OUR PRIORITIES Priorities That Put Alaska First Fair & Transparent Elections Support simple, transparent, and easy-to-understand elections for every Alaskan.
Protect Alaska’s PFD Ensure Alaskans receive their fair share and protect the Permanent Fund Dividend.
Strong Local Communities Empower and support communities across Eagle River, Chugiak, & Peter’s Creek.
Experienced Leadership Bring experience, leadership, and practical solutions to Juneau.
Mental Health Expand access to care, support recovery, and strengthen community resources.
Aviation & Infrastructure Invest in systems that connect communities and support Alaska’s economy.
CONTACT US  ken@mccartyforalaska.com  (907) 406-2300  mccartyforalaska.com Paid for by McCarty for Alaska PO Box 771777, Eagle River, AK 99577

removed: VOTE KATE MCLAUGHLIN ISSUES McLaughlin For Montana Demand that Families Be Put First Every triumph working families ever made, whether it child labor protections, 8 hour workday, minimum wage, or weekends off came because we demanded change.
It is time again to start demanding family security: a liveable wage, lower cost of living, affordable health policies, rights for women, childcare/eldercare, and education.
EDUCATION My sons have all attended Flathead High School.
I believe it is very important to continue education to be a place that builds skills ( kids can learn construction, various art mediums, music, welding and other skills).
Students are encouraged to excel and push themselves towards higher education ( IB Program, partnership with Running Start FVCC).
I attended public school, both my in-laws were teachers and I have friends and family who are currently teaching.
Our education system should support the teachers that work there, ensure buildings that are safe and have adequate space.
Legislation can create a school funding formula to allocate money to provide what our Montana Constitution states: “ Equality of educational opportunity is guaranteed to each person of the state”.
Your zip code should not reflect the value of education your children receive.

ENVIRONMENT The majority of HD9 is public lands (81%) which totals about 54,938 acres of land which is managed by various agencies including: County government, MT Fish, Wildlife and Parks, MT State Trust Lands, US Fish and Wildlife Service and US Forest Service.
This land includes seven recreation sites: Smith Lake, Somers Fishing Access, Lone Pine State Park, Somers Beach State Park, Herron Park and Foys Lake Park.
We are very fortunate to have this land available and belong to all of us.
These areas give us places to swim, fish, hike, hunt, boat, sled and ice skate, among other things.
The Montana Constitution guarantees our right to a clean and healthful environment.
I support a moratorium on data centers in this state until we can study from other states the effects of the water usage, electricity increases to residents, noise and air pollution.
I also support alternative energy sources to reduce our use on a finite source of energy.
I also oppose corporations from other countries coming in to mine our Montana resources.
HEALTHCARE #% of Flathead County is enrolled in Medicaid.
The medicaid expansion program funded through federal dollars continues behavioral health services, and substance use disorder treatment, it also allows seniors to receive long term care.
Continuing Medicaid expansion also keeps Logan Health ( now merged with Billings Clinic) to provide care for our community.
In a Flathead Beacon article they reported " The failure to reauthorize Medicaid expansion would impact 7,500 statewide jobs ... and $775 million in economic activity that it generates.
Montana medicaid has grown to include home births, which helps in keeping costs down, as the average hospital birth is $11,000.
Montana also faces many areas without close access to maternal care and many rural area clinics are in danger of closing.
I support home births and home care for elders in their own homes, but we face a serious lack of healthcare workers in these areas which needs to be addressed.
Unity Montana's strength has always come from its families, it's strong local economies, it's relations with tribal nations and its willingness to come together in times of difficulty.
This campaign is a call to embrace humanity, fairness and responsibility to one another.
The answer is simple: prioritize families, their economy, and unite around shared goals.

I do not know the man, but I am sure he is a good human being.
I am just sharing how he voted and the votes I personally disagree with.
This is more a job performance review than anything else.

It was passed in to law, even though our representative voted against it.
HB 231 Revise Property Tax Rates Our representative voted against lower tax rates on owner qualified homes and for owner occupied residential properties and long term rentals.
It also allowed a rebate to those who own a principal residence.
It was passed in to law, even though our representative voted against it.

It died in the Senate.
