Ways and Means The South Carolina House Ways and Means Committee is made up of twenty-five members and is chaired by Rep.
Bruce Bannister (Dist.
The committee's primary responsibilities are writing the state's annual budget and crafting state tax and fiscal policy.
The committee divides its work in two types of subcommittees: Budget and Legislative Affairs.

On the budget side, the committee is comprised of budget subcommittees that work each year to draft the General Appropriations Bill — the legislation that funds public education, infrastructure, law enforcement, health care, and every state agency — before the full House takes up the spending plan.
On the Legislative Affairs side, the committee is divided into legislative subcommittees that develop tax and fiscal policy for the state.
Rep.
Caskey serves as Chairman of the Constitutional Subcommittee for the budget, and as a member of the General Government Subcommittee for legislative affairs.
Rules The South Carolina House Rules Committee is responsible for the rules that govern how the House of Representatives operates.

It considers amendments to the Rules of the House and handles motions to set legislation for special order — the mechanism that determines the priority and order in which bills are debated on the House floor.
Because of this role, the Committee can have significant influence over the flow of legislation and the House calendar.
Rep.
Caskey serves as Chairman of the Rules Committee.
Joint Bond Review The Joint Bond Review Committee is a joint committee of the House and Senate that oversees the State's capital spending and bonded indebtedness.
Under Title 2, Chapter 47 of the S.C.

Code of Laws , the Committee reviews permanent improvement projects and their funding sources before they are approved, studies the State's existing general obligation and institutional bond obligations and its ability to meet them, recommends priorities for future bond issuance based on the State's needs, and recommends prudent limits on bond obligations relative to projected revenues.
Its work helps ensure that South Carolina invests in needed infrastructure while protecting the State's strong credit and fiscal health.
South Carolina Legislature Rep.
Caskey serves as a member of the Joint Bond Review Committee.

Infrastructure In 2017, the General Assembly passed historic legislation to reverse a decades-long trend of inadequately prioritizing infrastructure.
There’s still more work to do.
The state legislature should continue to fight to fix South Carolina’s roads and bridges.
The SC Department of Transportation must deliver on the investment South Carolinians are making.
Veterans South Carolina is considered to be one of the most military-friendly states in the country.
The state legislature must fight to ensure that South Carolina continues to be a place for the military to call home.
Those who answer the call to serve are willing to pay the ultimate sacrifice and deserve our utmost respect.
South Carolina should remain a magnet for all active military, service members, and veterans.
Public Safety It is imperative to have voices for public safety in the legislature.
Whenever disasters strike, first responders answer the call.
Police officers run towards chaos, firemen perform rescue after rescue, and EMS teams save lives.
They ensure that South Carolina is ready for the unexpected, and they deserve legislators that will champion their cause.
Accountability Situations such as the failed VC Summer Nuclear project prove that the government of South Carolina is not immune to corruption and misconduct.
The fight for reform begins in the House, and that requires lawmakers who are willing to take steps to create real ethics reforms.
The rule of law should apply to everyone equally.
South Carolinians must be able to hold their government officials accountable, and the legislature needs to take an active role in ensuring the pathways to do so are created.
Transparency Government is not meant to take place behind closed doors.
South Carolinians should never be left out of the loop, especially when it comes to legislation that could affect their livelihood.
The state legislature must take action to ensure that the government maintains an open and honest relationship with the citizens of South Carolina.
Opportunity South Carolinians deserve a government that works for them.
That means cutting out unnecessary red tape, lowering taxes, and creating an environment where individuals and private businesses are able to thrive.
The government should not act as a barrier to the pursuit of life, liberty, and happiness.

added: Menu Meet Micah Record Issues State House District 89 Resources Vote Contact Donate LEGISLATIVE RECORD District 89 & the State House A record of delivering results for the people of District 89 and South Carolina.

Tax Relief Lower Costs for Families I co-sponsored the largest income tax cut in state history, supported an increased Homestead Exemption for seniors and led an extension of Lexington County school property tax relief. $1B+ Roads & Quality of Life I supported more than $1 billion for South Carolina roads and bridges, secured $2.44 million for Cayce floodwater improvements and secured funding for a community center in Springdale. $400K Safe Streets, Safe Kids I supported $400,000 for Lexington County Sheriff’s Office body cameras and tougher penalties for child exploitation. $50,500 Education I helped increase starting teacher pay to $50,500, up from $30,000 in 2017, while keeping the focus on preparing students to be college, career or military ready.

District 157 Community Town Hall (October 17) • Verified Election & Community Resources – Official Government Election Resources – Campaign & Community Resources In-person advance voting for the 2026 General Election begins on Tuesday, October 13, 2026 , and runs through Friday, October 30, 2026 , across Appling, Evans, Jeff Davis, and Tattnall Counties.
This guide provides practical election information for voters across House District 157: verified voting locations, weekend schedules, absentee ballot rules, and identification requirements.

Start Here: Quick Election Reference Advance Voting Window: Tuesday, October 13 - Friday, October 30, 2026 Mandatory Saturday Voting Days: Saturday, October 17 & Saturday, October 24, 2026 Absentee Application Deadline: Friday, October 23, 2026 (must be received by county) General Election Day: Tuesday, November 3, 2026 (7:00 AM - 7:00 PM) Official Voter Status & Sample Ballots: Georgia My Voter Page (mvp.sos.ga.gov) Quick Links to Sections Early Voting vs.

Election Day Weekend Advance Voting Dates and Hours Where to Vote Early in District 157 Absentee Ballots and Drop Boxes Accessibility and Curbside Voting Acceptable Forms of Photo ID What’s on Your Ballot Glennville Community Town Hall (October 17) 1.
Early Voting vs.
Election Day The primary operational difference between early voting and Election Day is where you are permitted to cast your ballot.
During the advance voting window (October 13 - October 30), registered voters may cast a ballot at any designated advance voting location within their home county .
For example, a Tattnall County resident living in Collins or Glennville may vote at the central elections office in Reidsville while in town during the day.

Feature Advance Voting (Oct 13 - Oct 30) Election Day (Tuesday, Nov 3) Location Any designated early voting site in your county Strictly your assigned home precinct Hours Regular weekday and scheduled Saturday hours 7:00 AM - 7:00 PM statewide Out-of-Precinct Rules Flexible across the county Must vote at your assigned precinct On Election Day (November 3) , countywide flexibility ends.
Under Georgia law ( O.C.G.A. § 21-2-385 ), you must vote at your specific assigned neighborhood precinct.
Voters who arrive at an incorrect precinct on Election Day before 5:00 PM are directed to their correct home precinct.
Early voting provides voters greater scheduling convenience across the three-week period.

Weekend Advance Voting Dates and Hours Georgia election law establishes two mandatory Saturday voting days across every county in the state: Saturday, October 17, 2026 Saturday, October 24, 2026 These weekend dates accommodate commuters, agricultural workers, and shift workers whose daily routines make weekday voting difficult.
While state law requires counties to open on both Saturdays, exact operating hours are established by each individual county Board of Elections (typically 8:30 AM or 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM).
Check your county listing below or visit the Georgia My Voter Page to confirm local weekend hours.
Where to Vote Early in District 157 Each of the four counties in District 157 designates a central elections facility for advance in-person voting.

Below are the official physical locations and contact details for each county: County Designated Early Voting Facility Physical Address Regular Weekday Hours Office Phone Appling County Board of Elections Office 83 South Oak Street Baxley, GA 31513 8:30 AM - 5:00 PM (912) 367-8113 Evans County Courthouse Annex (Suite 8) 201 Freeman Street Claxton, GA 30417 8:30 AM - 5:00 PM (912) 739-0708 Jeff Davis County Public Safety Facility 15 Public Safety Drive Hazlehurst, GA 31539 8:30 AM - 5:00 PM (912) 375-6635 Tattnall County Central Elections Office 114 W Brazell Street Reidsville, GA 30453 8:30 AM - 5:00 PM (912) 557-6417 Note for Tattnall County voters: Advance early voting is conducted at the Board of Elections central office in Reidsville.

Glennville voters should plan to travel to Reidsville during the advance window or utilize the Saturday voting dates. [!NOTE] Operating schedules and entrance details are subject to official county determination.
Official county election notices and the Georgia My Voter Page take precedence over third-party summaries.
Absentee Ballots and Drop Boxes Georgia voters who choose to vote by mail or drop box operate under statutory rules established by O.C.G.A. § 21-2-381 and Senate Bill 202.
Absentee Application Deadline Your county elections office must receive your completed absentee ballot application by Friday, October 23, 2026 .
Postmark dates do not satisfy this deadline; the application must be physically received by your county board of elections by the close of business.
Drop Box Regulations Absentee ballot drop boxes are located indoors within county election offices.
Under state law, drop boxes are accessible exclusively during active advance in-person voting hours.
When polling closes for the day, drop boxes are locked and secured by election officials.

Switching from Absentee to In-Person Voting Under O.C.G.A. § 21-2-388 , if you requested a mail-in absentee ballot but decide to vote in person, bring your unused paper ballot with you to the early voting location.
Surrender the paper ballot to the poll clerk, who will mark it as canceled in the state database and issue you a standard in-person ballot.
If you do not have the paper ballot with you, poll officials will require you to sign an affidavit affirming that the absentee ballot was not used before issuing an in-person ballot.
Accessibility and Curbside Voting Georgia election law contains specific accommodations to ensure every eligible citizen can cast a ballot safely and privately.
Curbside Voting Under O.C.G.A. § 21-2-409.1 and O.C.G.A. § 21-2-385(b) , curbside voting is available to: Voters who are 75 years of age or older.
Voters with a physical disability that prevents entering the polling facility.
When arriving at the voting facility, a driver or companion may enter the lobby to notify election workers that a qualified voter requires curbside service.
Two election workers will bring the voting materials to the vehicle.
In-Booth Voter Assistance Under O.C.G.A. § 21-2-409 , any voter who requires assistance due to physical disability or difficulty reading English may receive help from a person of their choice.
The law specifies that an assistant may not be the voter’s employer, an agent of the employer, or an officer or agent of the voter’s labor union.
Acceptable Forms of Photo ID Georgia law ( O.C.G.A. § 21-2-417 ) requires in-person voters to present government-issued photo identification at check-in.
The six acceptable forms of photo identification are: Any valid state or federal government-issued photo ID, including a free Georgia Voter ID card.
A Georgia driver’s license (even if expired within statutory grace limits).
A valid U.S. passport or passport card.
A valid employee photo ID issued by any branch, department, or agency of the federal government, Georgia, or any Georgia county or municipality.
A valid U.S. military photo ID.
A valid tribal photo ID card.
Provisional Ballots If you arrive at the polling site without an acceptable form of photo identification, election workers are legally required to issue a provisional ballot.
To have the ballot counted, you must present valid photo identification to your county board of registrars within three business days following Election Day.
What’s on Your Ballot District 157 voters will see federal, state, and local candidate races on their ballot, along with three proposed state constitutional amendments.

Georgia House District 157 Voters across Appling, Evans, Jeff Davis, and Tattnall Counties will choose their representative in the Georgia General Assembly between Democratic nominee Micah King and Republican nominee Bradley B.
Anderson .

Statewide Constitutional Amendments Your ballot includes three proposed constitutional amendments: Amendment 1 (HR 1081): Increasing the Conservation Use Value Assessment (CUVA) farm and timber property tax cap from 2,000 to 4,000 acres.
Amendment 2 (HR 1110): Requiring nonpartisan elections for all probate court judges statewide.
Amendment 3 (HR 1243): Creating a constitutionally dedicated trust fund for emergency 9-1-1 dispatch operations.
For a plain-English explanation of what a YES or NO vote means on each proposal, read our Georgia 2026 Ballot Measures Guide .
You can view your complete personalized sample ballot at the official Georgia My Voter Page (mvp.sos.ga.gov) .

District 157 Community Town Hall (October 17) On the evening of the first mandatory Saturday advance voting date, our campaign is hosting an open community forum in Glennville: Event: District 157 Community Town Hall & Open Floor Q&A Date & Time: Saturday, October 17, 2026 | Starting at 6:00 PM Location: South Tattnall Middle School Gym (721 E Barnard St, Glennville, GA 30427) Admission: Free and open to all residents of Appling, Evans, Jeff Davis, and Tattnall Counties.
Format: Open-floor microphone for direct constituent questions on healthcare, farming, cost of living, and rural infrastructure.
Voters who cast an advance ballot during Saturday voting hours are invited to join their neighbors that evening for direct discussion.

added: DONATE Endorsed by president Trump Home About Issues News Volunteer Shop Home About Issues News Volunteer Shop Home About Issues News Volunteer Donate Home About Issues News Volunteer Donate DONATE Michael Whatley Hosts Make More, Keep More Press Conference in Shelby October 9, 2026 SHELBY – Today, Michael Whatley hosted a Make More, Keep More press conference in Shelby alongside Congressman Tim Moore, NC Senator Ted Alexander, and NC Rep Paul Scott where they highlighted how Cooper’s far-left policies made life more expensive for North Carolina families.
Under Cooper’s watch energy costs skyrocketed 30%, housing costs went up by 85%, and healthcare costs rose to the highest in the country.
Congressman Moore, Senator Alexander, and Representative Scott joined Whatley to address how Roy Cooper raised costs on families and businesses across North Carolina.
Click HERE to see photos of the event “Roy Cooper made life more expensive for families across North Carolina.
From energy, to housing, to healthcare Cooper made prices skyrocket thanks to his far left policies.
And on day one of his campaign, Cooper said he wanted families and seniors to pay $5,700 more in taxes every single year.
While Roy Cooper wants you to pay more, I will always fight for our families to make more and keep more of their hard earned money,” said Michael Whatley.

“Western Marylanders send a lot of money to Annapolis,” said Senator McKay.
“This week, $2.8 million of it came back home to our fire companies, our kids, our parks, and an airport that keeps Washington County in business.
That’s not new spending.
That’s our money, back where it belongs.” Two volunteer fire companies are getting equipment they’ve been waiting on.
Goodwill Volunteer Fire Company No.
1 in Allegany County will receive $100,000 toward a new tanker, replacing a 1990 Ford that has been on the road for 36 years.
In Garrett County, the Kitzmiller Volunteer Fire Department will receive $50,000 for its Rescue 78 unit.
Neither company has to put up a matching dollar.
“Our volunteers drop everything, day or night, to answer the call,” said McKay, who chairs the Maryland Fire and EMS Coalition.

“Nobody should be asking them to do it in a truck that’s older than some of the firefighters riding in it.” In Washington County, $1.5 million will go toward the air traffic control tower at Hagerstown Regional Airport, and $#,# will build a paved walking and biking loop at Marty Snook Park, giving families a safe path away from the main park road.

In Garrett County, the Town of Grantsville will receive $320,000 for new playground equipment, and an additional $111,375 will complete the state’s purchase of the Wilt property after a survey found the tract was 81.37 acres larger than first thought, keeping that land open for hunting, hiking, and the outdoors.
In Allegany County, $61,000 will add accessible seating and entry at Allegany College of Maryland’s Bazarnic Field, so every fan can get into the game.
“A tanker, a rescue unit, a playground, a trail, and a control tower.
None of that was dreamed up in Annapolis,” McKay added.
“Our communities asked for it, and I’m going to keep making sure Western Maryland gets its fair share.” The Board of Public Works approved all seven items on September 16, 2026.
### Stay up to date on Senator McKay’s fight for Western Maryland.

The political bosses in Annapolis and Baltimore want to take away the guns of law-abiding Marylanders, and Senator McKay is leading the charge to stop them.
In Western Maryland, the Second Amendment is not an abstract debate.

It is the rifle handed down from a grandfather, the opening day that empties classrooms and job sites across Allegany, Garrett, and Washington Counties, and the right to protect your family in places where help can be a long way off.
“I am grateful to the NRA for this endorsement, and to every gun owner in Western Maryland who has stood with me,” McKay said.
“The folks in Annapolis and Baltimore who want to take your guns are not going to quit, and neither am I.

I will keep fighting for your Second Amendment rights for the next four years.” ### Stay up to date on Senator McKay’s fight for Western Maryland — sign up for his District Newsletter at MikeMcKayMD.com/#newsletter .

added: Voting information for Cascade County Election Day is Tuesday, November 3 Mail Ballot Voters For those registered to receive a mail ballot at your home, the ballots are being mailed on Friday, October 9 .
If you have not received your ballot by Friday, October 16, you should visit the Election Office immediately to fix the situation.

Ballot Drop Box Locations The ballot drop boxes located in the foyer of the County Annex Building at 325 2nd Avenue North and in the Election Office (at that same address) will be available starting Monday, October 12th .
Mailing a Voted Ballot to Ensure Timely Delivery Remember, your ballot must be in the hands of the election officials ON NOVEMBER 3rd A postmark date is not considered receipt.
To ensure your ballot arrives in time, mail your voted ballot via USPS by Wednesday, October 28 .
After October 28, voted ballots should be hand-delivered and deposited in one of the drop box locations.
You can mail a completed voter registration form to the Election Office ( not recommended after October 2 ) or visit the Election Office to register to vote.
If you register to vote in person at the Election Office after October 9 , you can request a ballot be issued on the spot, vote it while in the election office and deposit it in the drop box.
While Montana allows same-day voter registration, it’s not wise to wait until November 3rd .
Make a plan to register earlier than November 3rd.
On Monday, November 2nd , you can register and request a ballot on the spot until NOON .
Thereafter, plan on standing in line at Exhibition Hall on November 3rd.

The Election Office will be closed on November 3rd , but the ballot drop box in the foyer at 325 2nd Avenue North (next to the library) will be available for ballot deposits until 8:00 pm on election day.
Polls on November erd All election operations will be moved to Exhibition Hall at Expo Park on November 3rd from 7:00am until 8:00pm .

View Event → Oct 3 One Colorado Prism Awards Saturday, October 3, 2026 6:00 PM 10:00 PM Denver Art Museum (map) Google Calendar ICS Every year, Monica looks forward to joining One Colorado’s Prism Awards.
The Prism Awards is One Colorado’s annual gala to honor individuals and organizations who have made a substantive difference in the lives of LGBTQIA+ Coloradans and their families.

Join hundreds of LGBTQIA+ Coloradans, allies, community leaders, and supporters for an unforgettable evening celebrating the people and organizations making a difference across our state. ‍The evening begins with a cocktail reception and silent auction, followed by the Prism Awards ceremony with inspiring honorees and special guests, dessert, and an opportunity to invest in a future where every LGBTQIA+ Coloradan can thrive.

Tickets for purchase at https://www.one-colorado.org/events/prism-awards View Event → Oct 3 Taco Bell 50k (yes, 50k) Saturday, October 3, 2026 7:30 AM 4:00 PM Taco Bell (2 locations in District 9) (map) Google Calendar ICS Did you know Denver hosts a Taco Bell 50k?!
It has been described as Urban Legend.
More mysterious and barking spiders than the Barkley Marathons.
The International Taco Bell 50k boasts a higher DNF rate than the famed Leadville 100 Trail Race.
The race has been held annually in Denver, Colorado in early October, which coincidentally coincides with International Taco Day.
The event is volunteer run and all donations go to the Achilles Heel Foundation which supports runners who are injured.
To be clear: Monica is NOT running the Taco Bell 50k.
She enjoys being an yearly fan from the safety of her front yard.
You have several options to celebrate International Taco Day and the Taco Bell 50k in District 9: 1.
You, yes you, can register to run.
Gastric training advised. https://tacobell50k.com/ 2.
Support the runners at our two Taco Bell locations along the route in District 9.
One is at 7150 Leetsdale Drive, and the other is in Holly Hills at 6460 E Yale Ave.
If you live along the route, go outside and cheer for these wacky runners.
If you do not live on the route, you are welcome to message Monica and join the crew in her front yard.
Enjoy the tradition!

View Event → Sep 30 CCHI Community Health Voices Conference Wednesday, September 30, 2026 11:00 AM 4:00 PM Colorado Health Capitol (map) Google Calendar ICS Monica will join the Colorado Consumer Health Initiative (CCHI) Community Voice Conference to listen and learn.
The event is hosted by one of Monica’s favorite advocacy groups: CCHI.
Join CCHI for our annual Community Voices Conference (CVC), a space for community members to learn about and practice storytelling as a means for personal, social and political change.
This year’s theme: Courage to Speak, Power to Stay .

In a moment when the ground feels like it’s shifting beneath us, CVC is about finding the courage to tell your story anyway, and using that story to stay rooted, connected, and ready to act in your community.
The conference will feature a keynote speaker, small‑group workshops on advocacy and storytelling, a panel discussion, and dedicated time for lunch and networking.

While we appreciate the continued support from our partner advocacy organizations, we ask that no more than two members from other advocacy organizations attend to preserve the intention of this conference as a space primarily for community members.
Registration required: https://cohealthinitiative.org/events/community-voices-conference-2026/ stipends available for community members to attend.

View Event → Sep 20 Athletes Protecting Youth Sports (No on 134 and 135) Sunday, September 20, 2026 10:00 AM 2:00 PM Infinity Park Turf Field (map) Google Calendar ICS Calling all athletes and sports fans!
Join us to knock doors and have real conversations with House District 9 voters about Propositions 134 and 135.
No experience needed, we'll pair you with a trained canvasser and walk you through everything.
These measures sound reasonable on the surface, but they go much further than most voters realize.
We're here to help voters see the real consequences for all kids, not just some.
Wear comfortable shoes and bring a water bottle.
We'll have scripts, walk packets, and support on-site.

Sign up here: https://www.mobilize.us/familiesnotpolitics/event/1030843/ View Event → Sep 19 CANCELLED - South by Southeast Summer Series at Eisenhower Park Saturday, September 19, 2026 4:00 PM 7:00 PM Mamie D.
Eisenhower Park (map) Google Calendar ICS Due to the weather forecast, the Jazz Band performance at Mamie D.
Eisenhower park within the South by Southeast Summer Series is CANCELLED.
South by Southeast was developed after an extensive visioning series to find out what southeast Denver residents wanted to see in the district.
Community members expressed a strong desire for improved restaurants and retail, walkability and bikeability, and a community gathering place.
While the city continues to work to create this grand vision for the area, planning and development can take a very long time.
So, these festivals showcase the possibilities and opportunities available in southeast Denver.

More information here: https://www.denvergov.org/Government/Agencies-Departments-Offices/Agencies-Departments-Offices-Directory/Denver-City-Council/Council-Members-Websites-Info/Diana-Romero-Campbell-District-4/South-by-Southeast-Summer-Series View Event → Sep 19 Denver Democrats Central Committee Meeting Saturday, September 19, 2026 11:00 AM 3:30 PM Denver South High School (map) Google Calendar ICS The Democratic Party of Denver Central Committee meets multiple times throughout the year.
This meeting is in-person only.
All members of the Central Committee are required to attend or delegate their vote to a proxy.
Members of the public are welcome to attend, but cannot participate in any of the proceedings.
At this meeting, the Denver Democrats will vote on a number of items including whether to adopt an oppose or support stance on Denver ballot initiatives.
Schedule 10:00 AM = Doors Open / Check-In Begins 11:00 AM = Gavel in Your Districts Upon registration, you'll be asked to indicate your State Senate District, State House District, and Precinct.
If you do not know these details, you can look them up here .

View Event → Sep 17 Frontline Farm Volunteer Day at Celebration Garden Thursday, September 17, 2026 8:00 AM 12:00 PM Celebration Garden (map) Google Calendar ICS Every Thursday is volunteer day at Frontline Farm’s Celebration Garden in southeast Denver.
Monica will be volunteering this day, but you are welcome to sign up for any and all Thursdays.
Get some sunshine and support the farmers get the good work done!
Bring sunblock, a full water bottle, and closed toe shoes.

Please register in advance at https://www.frontlinefarming.org/events/celebration-farm-volunteer-day-2026-09-17-08-00 View Event → Sep 16 Virginia Village and Ellis Community Association Happy Hour Wednesday, September 16, 2026 5:00 PM 7:00 PM Junction Food and Drink (map) Google Calendar ICS Drop by any time between 5-7pm at this neighborhood event.

Meet your neighbors, learn what’s happening in Virginia Village, and help shape the future of the community.
Appetizers provided.
Drinks and additional food available for purchase at the locally-owned businesses inside Junction Food and Drink.

Your input and participation is very important and makes a positive difference in our community.

For more information, visit: https://www.uhna.com/most-recent-minutes View Event → Sep 7 Living with Harmony event at Native Foods Monday, September 7, 2026 5:00 PM 7:00 PM Native Foods (map) Google Calendar ICS Come party with the Living With Harmony peeps as we celebrate our community at our PLANET-Based Party in Denver with the co-founders, Andrea Rose and JP.
This event will be at Native Foods restaurant in Glendale, CO. with employee-owner, Michael Olivas, with innovative, tasty and nutritious plant-based cuisine.
Free to attend.
There is plenty of party space, but come early to find a good seat, to order food and to socialize before the presentation.
Monica will speak briefly and there will be a separate keynote.
Living With Harmony supports Native Foods and their efforts to use reusable dinnerware, flatware and cups for diners.
Come hungry and bring your own containers to bring home extra food or leftovers and to help the planet.
Visit our sponsored non-profit, Bleating Hearts, a local animal sanctuary that provides lifelong refuge for rescued animals.

Presentation procedure to be announced.
Monthly reports and other monthly business.

AI notetakers will not be enabled. *The makeup and respective roles of the County Central and Executive Committees are explained in the County Party Rules here .

One Big Walk. step-by-step to a brighter future.
Matthew Montavon is hitting the pavement and walking across District 17 to meet directly with YOU!

Whether you are a Democrat, Republican, or Independent, Matthew believes that true representation means showing up, listening, and finding common-sense solutions to our community's non-partisan challenges.

From his 27 years of public service with the United Nations fighting hunger to his volunteer work right here in Southwest Florida with Habitat for Humanity and AARP Tax-Aide, Matthew has dedicated his life to community development, fiscal accountability, and public service.
Now, he's bringing that global experience and common ground perspective straight to your neighborhood.

Come out to share your thoughts, discuss Matthew's fight for campaign finance transparency and expanded veterans' services, or simply walk a few blocks along the trail with him! track #teammonty live day 1 - sept 27 Day 1 kicks off in Fort Myers!
We are starting the morning at 8:00 AM at Panera Bread (5037 S.
Cleveland Ave) and making our way through the heart of the community.
Along the route, Matthew will be making pit stops at local landmarks, historic community pillars, and public forums to listen to your concerns, share his vision, and earn your vote.
Learn more day 2 - sept 28 Today, we cross county lines!
We are kicking things off at 8:00 AM at Dunkin’ on N Cleveland Ave and heading north along the Tamiami Trail.

We will be exploring our beautiful local environment, discussing conservation and community issues, and hosting public gatherings along the way. learn more day 3 - sept 29 Today, we are continuing our trek deeper into Charlotte County.
We are starting the morning at 8:00 AM at Charlotte Flatwoods Environmental Park and making our way up the Tamiami Trail corridor through Punta Gorda and into Port Charlotte.

We will be making stops at beloved local business landmarks to talk with residents, support local business owners, and hear about the issues impacting your daily lives. learn more day 4 - sept 30 We are lacing up our sneakers at 8:00 AM sharp, starting from Pioneers Pizza in Port Charlotte.
From there, we are heading toward local parks and neighborhood favorites, making our way up to the edge of Sarasota County.

It is going to be a fantastic day of community conversation, outdoor recreation, and local food. learn more day 5 - oct 1 Our morning begins at 8:00 AM sharp at Bocca Lupo Coal Fired Pizza in North Port.
From there, we are hitting the pavement and heading northwest along the Tamiami Trail corridor into Venice.

Today’s route features beautiful waterfront public spaces and essential community hubs where we will be discussing local conservation, infrastructure, and community services. learn more day 6 - oct 2 Our morning begins at 8:00 AM sharp at the Jacaranda Library in Venice.
F rom there, we are walking through the historic heart of Venice, stopping at beautiful neighborhood parks, and making our way up toward Nokomis.
Today's route is a perfect mix of community hubs, green spaces, and local waterfront business staples.
Click Here day 7 - oct 3 We’re starting a little later today, and we’ll see you at 2:00 PM at the Nokomis Sunset Hut.
From there, we are heading north up the Tamiami Trail corridor, trekking through the beautiful trails of Osprey, and heading into South Sarasota.
Today's route features world-class natural parklands and neighborhood staple venues perfect for lively community discussion.
Click Here day 8 - oct 4 We are launching our morning at 8:00 AM sharp from Mellow Mushroom.
Day 8 takes us right through the heart of Sarasota, focusing on supporting our fantastic local culinary staples, neighborhood markets, and coastal business corridors.
It is the perfect opportunity to discuss the local economy, small business growth, and community infrastructure. learn more day 9 - oct 5 Our morning begins at 8:00 AM sharp at Stokes Seafood.
From there, we are heading north up the Sarasota coast, focusing our walk on higher education, the future of our workforce, and our local students.

Our final destination for the day is the historic campus of Ringling Museum of Art, a cornerstone of our community's cultural landscape. learn more visit the facebook event page take the next step with us Whether you want to walk a mile with Matthew, have questions about his platform, or want to help us power this campaign across FL-17, we want to hear from you.
Building a brighter future takes a team, and every step counts.
Have a Question?
Reach out to our campaign team directly to learn more about Matthew’s vision for Southwest Florida.
Ready to RSVP?

Let us know you're coming so we can share exact daily meetup locations, times, and parking details. walk with matthew, or volunteer download our volunteer agreement PRIVACY POLICY Political Advertisement Approved and Paid for by Matthew Montavon, Democrat for Congress

added: Skip to content Mosteller for WV AEP District 21 Issues Donation Education Endorsements Home Infrastructure Opioid Pandemic Privacy Policy volunteer WomensRights Women’s Reproductive Freedoms I’m proud to be endorsed by Planned Parenthood.
We all watched as one Supreme Court justice nominee after another lied to our faces, claimed that Roe was settled precedent and that they respected precedent.
The first chance they had to overturn Roe v.
Wade, they jumped on it.
They gaslit us and told us it would actually help women by sending it back to the states.
Our state legislature decided to impose an effective ban on abortions with very narrow exceptions.

We’ve seen in Texas, women who meet the criteria for a “life of the mother” exemption had to take their case all the way to the Texas Supreme Court, telling women who were dying after their fetus died inside of them.
I’ve always said every right wing accusation is a confession.
We’re seeing those death panels they were talking about.
They didn’t show up from the Affordable Care Act like they claimed, but on a case by case basis by state supreme courts.

When you send me to the legislature, I will do everything I possibly can to make your voice heard loud and clear on this issue, and will push for a state constitutional amendment, enshrining reproductive rights for all women in this state.

added: Skip to content Facebook X-twitter Instagram Menu Contribute Texas Tribune Democrat Nathan Johnson pitches back-to-basics attorney general’s office after 12 years under Paxton October 9, 2026 In 2018, a little-known Dallas lawyer named Nathan Johnson took on a well-funded, far-right state senator and won, flipping a district that had been in GOP hands for 30 years.
Eight years later, Johnson is trying again, this time on a statewide stage, as he vies to be Texas’ next attorney general.
It’s an uphill battle: The last time a Democrat was elected as Texas’ top lawyer, Forrest Gump was in movie theaters.
In the years since, national conservatives have come to rely on the state agency as a launchpad for partisan legal battles, and Johnson’s opponent, fellow state Sen.
Mayes Middleton , has a vast oil and gas fortune he could call on to keep the seat red.
Read more here .

added: HB 94 September 17, 2019 admin Criminal Law and Courts Comments are Closed 0 This Act will increase payments of child support arrears or retroactive support from payments for settlements and awards from negligence, personal injury, and workers compensation cases by requiring that all insurers share information with an insurance claim data collection organization.

The Division of Child Support Services (“Division”) uses an insurance claim data collection organization to match individuals who are in arrears on child support or who owe retroactive child support with individuals with insurance claims based upon negligence, personal injury, or workers’ compensation cases.
The data collection organization performs a data match of the claimants provided by insurers and child support obligors provided by the Division.

The data collection organization provides reports of matches to the Division so that the Division can issue a lien against the insurance claim to collect the child support arrears or retroactive support.
Currently, some insurers voluntarily submit claim information to the insurance claim data collection organization and in 2018, $424,977 in unpaid child support was collected through this process.
This Act requires that all insurers submit claim information to the insurance claim data collection organization and is expected to collect an additional $150,000 – $200,000 in unpaid child support.
This Act also allows written notice of a lien or action to perfect the lien to be sent by electronically or by first class mail to conform to industry practices.
This Act also makes technical corrections to conform existing law to the standards of the Delaware Legislative Drafting Manual.

Co-Prime Sponsor: Poore; Status: Signed HB 102 September 17, 2019 admin Criminal Law and Courts Comments are Closed 0 This bill allows a person who is arrested or convicted of any crime, except a violent felony, which was a direct result of being a victim of human trafficking may file an application or for a pardon or expungement or make a motion to vacate judgment.
This bill also makes changes to the Human Trafficking Interagency coordinating by adding another member of the judicial branch and a representative of the Department of Education.
This bill also adds locations where a public awareness sign must be placed.

Co-Prime Sponsor: Poore; Status: Signed SB 57 September 17, 2019 admin Consumer Protection Comments are Closed 0 This Act makes clear that a retail licensee may only purchase authorized product from an importer, also known as wholesaler, except that a retail licensee may purchase up to 20 gallons a day from a premises licensed to sell for off-premises consumption.
This Act also clarifies that off-premises licensees may sell untapped kegs for off-premises consumption.
Co-Prime Sponsor: Poore; Status: Signed Prev.
removed: HS 1 for HB 105 September 17, 2019 admin Health and Social Services Comments are Closed 0 Step therapy protocols are a mechanism by which health insurance companies require patients to try one or more prescriptions drugs before coverage is provided for the actual drug prescribed by the patient’s health care provider.

This Act creates a Step Therapy Exception Process whereby patients who are required by their insurance company to go through step therapy protocols can, under certain circumstances, bypass step therapy to obtain the initially-prescribed medication.
This Act does not apply to state or federal governmental plans.

Co-Prime Sponsor: Poore; Status: Signed HB 40 September 17, 2019 admin Open Government/Government Operations Comments are Closed 0 This bill: (1) increases the number of directors on the Board and allows the Board to appoint four additional directors; (2) implements clarifying language; (3) sunsets the former Advisory Council to replace it with a subcommittee structure to allow greater participation from members of the public and to allow the Corporation to appoint and receive assistance and expertise from a greater variety of experts; and (4) allows the Board of Directors to amend the Certificate of Incorporation with approval from the General Assembly.
Co-Prime Sponsor: Poore; Status: Signed HCR 34 September 17, 2019 admin Social Policy Comments are Closed 0 This resolution recognizes April 29, 2019 as World Wish Day in Delaware.
Co-Prime Sponsor: Poore; Status: Passed Prev.

DE Delaware roots Community-backed leadership Nisha Lodhavia for State Senate People Before Politics.
Common-Sense Solutions.
Lower Costs · Stronger Schools Better Healthcare Farms & Small Business District 15 · Vote November 3 Meet Nisha → Where She Stands → Donate today Get involved Showing up.
Listening.
Getting Things Done.
Showing up.
Listening.
Getting Things Done.
I'm Nisha Lodhavia , I’m running for the 15th District Senate seat to be your voice.
For me, it’s not about politics or pushing an ideology.
It’s about people.

It’s about focusing on common sense solutions that will lower costs, strengthen public schools, improve access to affordable health care, protect women’s health care, and grow an economy that works for all families.
For too long, partisan politics has distracted us from real progress.
My service in the community has convinced me of something simple and powerful: together, we can do better.
I am committed to working across differences to improve everyday life by creating opportunities for everyone.
So, let’s roll up our sleeves and show what we can achieve by uniting with purpose.
Your vote is your voice.
I would be honored to have your trust and your support.

RSVP WTVP LWV Illinois 16th Congressional District Candidate Forum Broadcast on WTVP and streaming on-line WTVP PBS and the League of Women Voters of Greater Peoria present a candidate forum for Illinois’ 16th Congressional District seat in the U.S.
House of Representatives.

The forum will last approximately one hour and air on WTVP PBS (television channel 47.1) on October 8 from 8 - 9 p.m. and will be available to stream on demand at https://video.wtvp.org/ and on the PBS app.
The program will be available to public media stations throughout Illinois for broadcast.
Republican candidate Darin LaHood and Democratic candidate Paul Nolley have confirmed their participation.
The forum will be pre-recorded on-site at the WTVP Studio.
Mark Welp, host of WTVP’s At Issue, will moderate along with LWVGP president, Chris Kaergard.
The public is encouraged to submit their questions for the candidates through the following form: https://form.wtvp.org/forum/ .

added: Home Issues 2026 Ballot Questions Positions Meet Ed Yard Signs Fundraiser Events Contribute Volunteer Professional Endorsement Voter Endorsements News Photos Contact Endorsements Events The Dartmouth Democratic Town Committee will host a Candidates Night for the Massachusetts House 9th Bristol District race on Tuesday, August 11, at 6:00 p.m. in the Select Board Room (Room 304) at Dartmouth Town Hall.
Doors will open at 5:00 p.m.
The event will feature Democratic candidates seeking to represent the 9th Bristol District in the Massachusetts House of Representatives.
This seat will be a vacant seat for the first time in over 14 years!

Ed will participate in the forum and welcomes the opportunity to continue to speak directly with residents about the future of the district, the priorities facing local communities, and the issues affecting families throughout Dartmouth and New Bedford.

The forum is designed to give voters the opportunity to hear directly from the candidates, learn about their positions on key issues, and gain a better understanding of their vision for the 9th Bristol District and the Commonwealth of Massachusetts.

The evening's program will include: Candidate introductions and opening statements Questions focused on priorities for the communities of the 9th Bristol District Discussion of statewide issues affecting Massachusetts residents Audience questions Candidate-to-candidate questions The event will also be recorded and broadcast by Dartmouth Community Television, giving residents across the district the opportunity to watch and stay informed.
Community members are encouraged to attend, engage in the discussion, and learn more about the candidates seeking to represent the 9th Bristol District .

added: Skip to content Time For A Change Home September 30, 2026 energy policy , politics , public health Green Energy is Energy Sovereignty If there is one thing the Iran war has taught us, it is that having lots of oil in your country does not shield you from the consequences of a global shortage.
We are a major oil- EXPORTING nation.
We have scads of crude.
But for one reason or another, we don’t have the refined products we need.
We export one grade of crude and import a different one.
Our refineries have been allowed to age and close instead of being upgraded, because that takes capital ($$$) and companies are averse to spending it.
But you know what?
Nobody can tariff the wind.
The sun doesn’t have to go through a strait on the other side of the world.
And we all live on a gigantic ball of superhot rock that won’t run out of heat for billions of years.
There are also locally available resources like hydropower, tidal energy, and more.
Energy generated in our own locale is the safest, cheapest way to power our future.
We should be promoting the renewable energy industries in every way possible.
While we in Idaho cannot do a lot about federal policies, we can: Restore a fair export credit to promote solar and wind installation.
Allow “balcony solar” as several other states already have, so that renters and people with less capital to spend can also generate some power.
Promote agrovoltaics, where solar panels and row crops or pasture share the same land, to the benefit of the crops.
Panels also pair very well with pollinator meadows and bee keeping.
Streamline permitting for smaller-scale wind projects.
We also have the local ability to promote energy efficient buildings and public transportation to save fuel.
Electric school busses not only cost less to run, but save the children riding on them from diesel fumes that cause respiratory problems.
Induction stoves in place of gas stoves cut the rate of asthma attacks by a lot.
Heat pumps are the most efficient way to heat and cool a building, and buildings can be far better insulated than is currently common.
Clean energy is a win-win situation.
Except for the fossil fuel barons currently gouging us for every penny.
They can go jump in a lake.

title.before: Albany Times Union Commentary: Readers deserve to know when AI generates the news

removed: top of page Home Meet Pat Record of Results Endorsements Events News Chat With Pat Pat Fahy for State Senate DONATE Request a Lawn Sign!
All Posts Search Albany Times Union Commentary: Readers deserve to know when AI generates the news Senator Patricia Fahy Sep 29 3 min read Let’s fast-forward two months, and it’s election night 2026.
Polls have closed in New York, and you join millions of people glued to their phones, eagerly awaiting results.
Then, a headline appears on your phone: “BREAKING NEWS: CANDIDATE X WINS SEAT IN CONGRESS.” You recognize the candidate and hundreds of people begin commenting and sharing, so you share it as well.

There’s just one problem: The race hasn’t been officially called yet, and the headline was posted by an AI-generated website — the same kind that now make up a stunning one-third of all new websites created — but not before thousands of people saw it and accepted it as fact.
For many, the damage could already be done — to their trust in our news, accurate reporting and even our institutions — at a time when that trust is already dangerously low.
And New Yorkers’ trust in AI?
Virtually nonexistent, with only 29% holding a positive view.
New Yorkers need to know what was written by a human being with editorial control and what was generated or “written” by a machine, bot or algorithm.
My FAIR NEWS Act, with Assemblymember Nily Rozic, would require a disclaimer on articles or media substantially generated or written by AI.
The bill awaits Gov.
Kathy Hochul’s signature.
I have firsthand experience with generative AI reporting false information.

When I introduced this legislation, a headline flashed across my phone screen: “New York Passes Law Regulating AI in News and Entertainment — National Today.” Anyone with a basic knowledge of the legislative process could tell you that introducing a bill is a long way off from getting it passed through both houses of the Legislature.
This outlet’s generative AI misread the press release or other information it received, generated a false article, then made it available to countless readers almost instantly.
It’s not the first time it’s happened, either.
In Wyoming in 2024, a reporter at the Cody Enterprise used AI to generate at least seven articles that fabricated quotes from six different people, including the governor.
Or how about a breaking news alert that announces a mass shooting that never happened, like the app NewsBreak sent out in 2024?

In a more innocuous example, but one that shows how AI-generated material can pass through layers of editorial control, the Chicago Sun-Times published an AI-generated list of book titles for summer reading; almost half were fabricated titles and made-up authors.

As recently as this year, a New York City Council candidate is accused of using generative AI to fabricate news stories and endorsements, without any disclaimer that AI had been used, in an attempt to mislead voters.
Generative AI is particularly dangerous because it regurgitates information without analyzing whether it is accurate or true.

For example, in the lead-up to the 2024 election, AI chatbots were disseminating information circulating online from quasi-news accounts that claimed Donald Trump won the 2020 presidential election, substantiating now-debunked electoral fraud theories and misinformation — misinformation that had the power to sway voters.
According to researchers at the University of Maryland, one out of every 10 news articles published each day in the U.S. now contains some form of generative AI.
Journalists and news guilds across the country have raised concerns in an attempt to maintain the rigorous standards that govern their critical work.
Journalists holding government at all levels accountable and asking the hard questions is one of the hallmarks of our democracy.
It is no small part of why our American experiment continues.
My FAIR NEWS Act is simple: When journalists, published media or news companies substantially use generative AI, they must disclose it to the reader and the public.
This legislation isn’t about telling the news media what they can or can't write about, what their angle should be, or even how they write it.
It’s about telling the public whether they’re reading a human-generated piece or an AI machine-generated one.
For 250 years, America has been unique among nations of the world because we are a country founded on an idea rather than a shared culture or ethnicity.
And how our story is told matters.
We must ensure that story continues to be told accurately, by human beings, and in a way that builds public trust rather than eroding it.

The inaugural class exemplifies a passion and commitment to public safety with recipients hailing from both Sullivan and Orange counties.
Read More Karen Fisher 10/22/25 Karen Fisher 10/22/25 Delay All-electric Mandate Several Assembly Democrats plan to petition Gov.
Kathy Hochul to roll back the statewide mandate to build all-electric buildings starting next year.
The All-Electric Buildings Act was tucked in the state budget in 2023, and bans new gas hookups in new buildings under seven stories starting Jan.
The mandate would apply to all other buildings constructed after Jan.

Kay says affordable housing has been a priority of hers since she was elected.

Through advocacy and direct support, Kay has made food accessibility one of her top legislative priorities.

“This funding will allow Middletown to renovate and revitalize the Kleiner Center and make it a destination for families here in Orange County.” Read More Karen Fisher 8/1/25 Karen Fisher 8/1/25 Kay Secures $100,000 Grant for Town of Fallsburg Police FALLSBURG, NY — Assembly Member Paula Elaine Kay (D-Rock Hill) announced today that the Town of Fallsburg Police Department has been awarded a $100,000 grant for upgrades to make officers safer and their work more efficient.
The funding will modernize the department’s facilities and help meet the demands of a growing community by funding new personnel lockers, filing shelves, and pass-through evidence lockers.

Read More Karen Fisher 7/18/25 Karen Fisher 7/18/25 Kay Secures $2.5K Evergreen Meadows ROCK HILL, NY — Assembly Member Paula Elaine Kay (D-Rock Hill) has secured a $250,000 line-item continuation in the New York State FY 2026 budget to support EverGreen Meadow Services, Inc., a Rock Hill-based nonprofit that serves girls across New York State who are at risk of self-harm or suicide.
The funding helps address multiple acute needs by bringing mental health programs and services into the 100th Assembly District and catering to an underserved, vulnerable population.

Read More Karen Fisher 7/10/25 Karen Fisher 7/10/25 Paula Opposes NYSEG Rate Increase MONTICELLO, NY — Assembly Member Paula Elaine Kay (D-Rock Hill) has announced that she has joined the New York State Public Service Commission's NYSEG rate case as an intervenor.
Kay stands in opposition to NYSEG’s proposed 23% rate increase, which is slated to take effect in May 2026 and would add roughly $33 to the average monthly bill in Sullivan County.

The grant, administered by the New York State Council on the Arts, marks a significant investment in the cultural and economic life of the region.

title.after: Rebuilding the American Cattle Herd

added: Senator Ricketts’ Rebuild the American Herd Plan 01 Stand Up for Nebraska Beef Against Foreign Imports Nebraska produces the best beef in the world.
Senator Ricketts will continue to stand up to cheap foreign beef that undercuts Nebraska farm families.

DELIVERED ■​ Fought the October 2025 plan to import more Argentine beef. ■​ Led Nebraska's delegation in demanding that Argentine beef pass full USDA safety inspections. ■​ Introduced bill to increase oversight of fake foreign organic products like beef trimming from being imported.

GOING FORWARD ▶​ Keep opposing imports that cut into Nebraska ranchers' bottom line. ▶​ Steady trade policy, so ranchers can afford to grow their herds. ▶​ Hold every pound of imported beef to the same standards Nebraska ranchers already meet.
02 Real Competition in Meatpacking When ranchers have more choices, Nebraska ranches grow stronger.
Senator Ricketts has fought for new places to process Nebraska beef like he did in North Platte with Sustainable Beef.
DELIVERED ■​ Helped make Sustainable Beef a reality through a rancher-owned plant in North Platte.

It can process up to 1,500 head a day and brings 875 jobs and over $1 billion a year in projected economic impact. ■​ After hearing from ranchers about the lack of competition in the packing industry, Senator Ricketts worked with them to create new options that benefit them. ■​ As governor, he secured $20 million for North Platte's wastewater system, which the plant needed to open. ■​ As governor, he put $10 million in federal relief toward hometown lockers.

The grants helped small processors with fewer than 25 employees and under $2.5 million in sales. ■​ As governor, joined fellow governors in pressing President Biden's Justice Department in 2021 for answers on its investigation into the Big 4 meatpackers.
GOING FORWARD ▶​ Make Sustainable Beef the model.
Back more independent and rancher-owned packers so producers have more buyers. ▶​ Stand with President Trump's call for a DOJ investigation into the Big 4 packers.
They control about 80% of the market.
Hold them accountable for any collusion or price fixing. ▶​ Find ways to make USDA certification more accessible for small local lockers.
03 Open Markets for Nebraska Beef Around the World Strong export markets mean stronger prices back home.
Senator Ricketts is working every day to grow them for Nebraska ranchers.

DELIVERED ■​ As governor, led trade missions to Japan, Vietnam, the UK, the EU, Mexico and Canada to sell Nebraska beef. ■​ As governor, oversaw record Nebraska ag exports three years in a row, peaking at nearly $10 billion in 2022.

Nebraska beef exports hit a record that year too. ■​ Secured a $3 billion commitment from Vietnam to buy Nebraska beef, grain and soybeans. ■​ Voted for the Working Families Tax Cuts Act, which doubled federal funding to open new markets for American farm products. ■​ Wrote the MARKET Act to expand market access for Nebraska farmers and ranchers.

It would also reduce dependence on Communist China. ■​ Led Nebraska delegation letter on the importance of the Mexican and Canadian markets to Nebraska agriculture. ■​ Worked to relist Nebraska packing plants as approved exporters to Chinese markets.

GOING FORWARD ▶​ Secure new markets around the world, so Nebraska ranchers aren't at the mercy of Communist China. ▶​ Protect trade promotion funding so American beef stays competitive overseas. ▶​ Hold Communist China to its trade promises. ▶​ Grow premium markets, like the UK's new tariff-free quota, that pay more per calf.
04 Honest Labels for American Beef Nebraska families and consumers deserve to know their beef was born, raised and processed in the USA.
Senator Ricketts is fighting for labels that tell the truth so American ranchers get the credit they deserve.
DELIVERED ■​ Cosponsored the American Beef Labeling Act to bring back mandatory country-of-origin labels and protect American ranchers. ■​ Wrote the bipartisan FAIR Labels Act with Sen.
Fetterman, requiring clear labels on lab-grown and plant-based products. ■​ Led the Senate resolution naming May as National Beef Month.

GOING FORWARD ▶​ Require country-of-origin labels to identify foreign products so shoppers know what's American and what's not. ▶​ Pass the FAIR Labels Act, so families can tell real beef from imitations.
05 Keep the Ranch in the Family Nebraska families have worked this land for generations, and they know how to care for it better than any bureaucrat in Washington.
Senator Ricketts has spent his career keeping the federal government's hands off Nebraska farms and ranches.

DELIVERED ■​ Was the first governor to take on President Biden's 30x30 plan, which threatened to put Nebraska farm and ranch land under federal control. ■​ Held town halls across rural Nebraska and signed an executive order to push back on 30x30.

Rallied more than 60 Nebraska counties to pass resolutions opposing the plan. ■​ Voted as senator to block President Biden's WOTUS rule, and took the EPA to task for ignoring farmers and ranchers. ■​ Voted for the Working Families Tax Cuts Act, which made the death tax exemption permanent at $15 million per person.

That protects more than 44,000 Nebraska family farms. ■​ Cosponsored the Death Tax Repeal Act to end the death tax for good. ■​ Introduced bipartisan bills to keep Nebraska farmland in Nebraska hands and expose foreign buyers like Communist China.

GOING FORWARD ▶​ Pass the Death Tax Repeal Act, so no Nebraska family ever has to sell the ranch to pay the IRS. ▶​ Stop any future federal land grab, so no administration can bring back 30x30. ▶​ Keep Washington's hands off farm ponds, ditches and private water. ▶​ Keep Communist China and other foreign adversaries from buying up Nebraska farmland.
06 More Grass, Less Red Tape, Faster Disaster Recovery When drought or fire hits a Nebraska ranch, families need help fast, not a stack of federal paperwork.
Senator Ricketts is cutting red tape so ranchers can rebuild their herds.

DELIVERED ■​ Introduced the bipartisan FENCE Act, so ranchers can use virtual fencing to rebuild after disasters. ■​ Worked with the Trump administration to open Valentine National Wildlife Refuge to grazing after past administrations kept it closed. ■​ Voted for the Working Families Tax Cuts Act, which boosted disaster aid for ranchers. ■​ Made drought aid available sooner.

Ranchers now qualify after four weeks of drought instead of eight. ■​ As governor during the 2019 floods, cleared the way for hay trucks and gave ranchers more time to handle livestock losses. ■​ Surveyed wildfire-burned pastures with Secretary Rollins and Gov.

Pillen then pushed USDA to loosen its fence rules to better assist ranchers. ■​ Joined a September 2026 Senate letter to USDA and Interior, urging them to finish the BLM grazing rule and review CRP and the Endangered Species Act.

GOING FORWARD ▶​ Give ranchers every tool to rebuild after disaster, including virtual fencing through the FENCE Act. ▶​ Open CRP land to grazing and haying when drought or fire hits, without waiting on Washington. ▶​ Cut the permitting delays that leave Nebraska towns and farms exposed to the next flood. ▶​ Make sure disaster aid reaches ranchers in weeks, not months, so they can restock and keep their herds.
07 Protect the Herd from New World Screwworm New World screwworm is a flesh-eating parasite that can kill cattle and shut down markets overnight.
Senator Ricketts is fighting to keep it out of Nebraska and protect the herds our ranchers spent generations building.
DELIVERED ■​ Backed the suspension of Mexican cattle imports. ■​ Backed the new sterile fly facility at Moore Air Base in Texas.
It will produce about 300 million sterile flies a week. ■​ Pressed USDA in June 2026, with Sen.
Grassley, to speed its response.
That followed the first U.S. cases in Texas and New Mexico.

GOING FORWARD ▶​ Get the Texas fly plant running at full speed. ▶​ Fund the surveillance and veterinarians needed to stop the screwworm before it reaches Nebraska. ▶​ Back strict border checks that stop screwworm before it spreads north.
08 Reshore Materials Needed to Feed the Herd Nebraska cattle depend on vitamins in their feed, and right now Communist China makes most of them.
Senator Ricketts is fighting to bring that production home, so our ranchers are never at Communist China's mercy.
DELIVERED ■​ Introduced the bipartisan Securing American Agriculture Act with Sen.

Elissa Slotkin to end America's farm dependence on Communist China. ■​ Wrote the bill to force USDA to track every key farm input Communist China controls, including the feed vitamins our cattle rely on. ■​ Wrote the bill to demand a plan to pull that production out of Communist China and bring it home.

GOING FORWARD ▶​ Pass the Securing American Agriculture Act. ▶​ Bring vitamin and feed supplement manufacturing plants back to American soil, out of Communist China's hands. ▶​ Treat the feed our cattle depend on as a national security fight against Communist China.
09 Train the Next Generation Here in Nebraska Nebraska's ranching future depends on young people who know the work and want to stay home to do it.
Senator Ricketts is investing in Nebraska students, so the skills our ranches need are taught right here.

DELIVERED ■​ As governor, created the Nebraska Career Scholarships program, which helps students at Nebraska universities, state colleges and community colleges train for in-demand careers. ■​ Voted for the Working Families Tax Cuts Act, which opened Pell Grants to short-term job training programs at community colleges and technical schools. ■​ Required scholarship recipients to complete a Nebraska internship or apprenticeship, keeping young talent working in our state. ■​ Funded grants for hometown lockers that included money to hire and train new staff. ■​ Voted for the Working Families Tax Cuts Act, which doubled the time young farmers and ranchers qualify for beginner help on crop insurance, from five years to ten.

GOING FORWARD ▶​ Partner with Nebraska colleges to train the next generation of ranchers, vets, meat cutters and food safety inspectors. ▶​ Expand hands-on training and apprenticeships that keep young Nebraskans working close to home.

item_pages.value: ENDORSED BY John Carlson New Haven RTC Chairman "I endorse Peter Lumaj as Secretary of the State for several reasons.
To begin with, he has the qualifications required to do the job.
His familiarity with law and running a business will no doubt be a huge boon in running SOTS.
Secondly, he has the character to ensure the job gets done without bias, and with honesty and integrity.
As we’ve seen from recent events, not only in BPT, but elsewhere, we need someone who will take the appointment seriously and without fear of political backlash from any party or backers.
“Fear not”, Peter is the candidate who is not afraid to let everyone know what he stands for and what he won’t stand for.
Lastly, he is an experienced candidate which will aid him in this run." View all endorsements →

added.text: The Back Office Behind the Movement
What Kansas's SAVE Law Can Teach Nebraska
Who Has Access to Nebraska's Election Systems?

added: Radio Ads Take Action Volunteer Join $10 Army Request Yard Sign Register to Vote Like on Facebook Follow on X Connect Donate JOIN $10 ARMY VOTERTREE DONATE CISA’s 2026 Election Infrastructure Security Plan Is a Warning, Not a Reassurance Sep 25 4 min read The federal government’s own election-security plan identifies vulnerabilities in voter-registration systems, election software, vendor access, and election infrastructure.
Nebraska should respond with greater verification, transparency, and state control.
CISA’s newly released 2026 Election Infrastructure Security Plan should get the attention of every election official in Nebraska.
The plan reports that hackers have attempted to breach statewide voter-registration systems in all 50 states, with confirmed success in at least 20.
CISA specifically identifies statewide voter-registration databases as attractive targets for foreign adversaries.
That is not a theoretical risk.
Voter-registration databases are critical election infrastructure.
CISA identifies additional vulnerabilities as well.
Election-related software can contain vulnerabilities requiring remediation.
Certification requirements can complicate timely security updates.
Vendor transparency concerning vulnerabilities and patch status can be inconsistent.
And election infrastructure can sometimes be reachable through broader government networks, creating opportunities for an attacker who compromises one system to move laterally toward another.
CISA also identifies another risk that deserves more attention: insiders.
Its definition extends beyond election employees.

CISA specifically identifies contractors and vendors as potential “third party insiders” because their authorized access to systems or sensitive information can extend the trust boundary beyond the election office.
It also discusses the possibility of foreign adversaries attempting to exploit insider access.
That should lead Nebraska to ask some straightforward questions: Who has access to our election infrastructure?
What hardware is inside it?
What software is running?
What communications capabilities exist?
Who can access those capabilities?
And can Nebraska independently prove that the computerized result matches the ballots cast by Nebraska voters?
Nebraska Already Has the Most Important Safeguard: Paper Nebraska is already a paper-ballot state.
The Secretary of State says ballots cast by mail or at polling places are paper ballots and that those ballots are secured and fed into tabulation machines for counting.

The state uses ES&S optical scanners; according to the Secretary of State, DS200s provide precinct-level tabulation in roughly one-fifth of Nebraska counties, while larger counties centrally count ballots using DS450 or DS850 equipment.
That means Nebraska does not need to reinvent its election system to create an independently verifiable record.
We already have one.
The question is whether we are taking full advantage of it.
CISA recommends paper ballots precisely because they provide transparency, auditability, and resilience against software failures or manipulation.
CISA then recommends manual post-election audits of those paper ballots before final results are certified.
Nebraska already conducts post-election audits, but the current process samples selected precincts and races rather than manually verifying every contest statewide.

The Secretary of State says general-election audits currently select 10% of precincts, with at least one in every county, and hand-count one federal, one state, and one local race in the selected precincts.
I believe we can build on that foundation.

Trust, But Independently Verify Nebraska’s Secretary of State currently states that its tabulation machines are stand-alone equipment that are not connected to the internet or any other network, including for transmitting election results.
As Secretary of State, I would not simply assume that is true because a vendor or government document says so.
I would verify it.
Evidence submitted in litigation involving Michigan election equipment documented an ES&S DS200 configuration containing cellular communications hardware.
That does not establish that Nebraska’s DS200s contain or use the same hardware or configuration.
It establishes why we should know.
Nebraska should maintain a verified inventory of the hardware, firmware, software, communications components, network capabilities and configurations actually deployed in our election equipment.
Any communications hardware that is unnecessary to conduct Nebraska elections should be physically absent or disabled in a manner that can be independently verified.
If our machines are truly isolated, we should be able to demonstrate that.
If our paper ballots match the computerized count, we should be able to demonstrate that too.
Trust should never substitute for verification.
Three Principles for Nebraska If I am elected Secretary of State, three principles will guide my approach.
First, the paper ballot marked by the voter should remain the authoritative evidence of voter intent.
Electronic tabulators can provide speed and convenience.
But Nebraska’s ability to establish the result of an election should never depend exclusively upon software.

I will pursue stronger manual verification of Nebraska’s paper ballots before certification so that the computerized count can be independently checked against the physical record created by Nebraska voters.
Second, Nebraska must know and control who has privileged access to its election infrastructure.

CISA recommends role-based, least-privilege access, comprehensive audit logs documenting who changed what and when, and separation between public-facing systems and master voter-registration databases.

I will pursue strict controls over vendor and contractor access and a policy prohibiting foreign nationals or foreign-controlled entities from privileged access to Nebraska’s voter-registration, election-management, ballot-processing or tabulation systems.
That is my proposed policy standard.
It is not a claim that CISA found foreign-controlled vendors operating Nebraska’s tabulators today.
Third, Nebraska election officials, not private consultants, should administer Nebraska elections.

Vendors may manufacture equipment, print ballots, provide maintenance, or perform narrowly defined technical services under strict contracts, documented access controls, chain-of-custody requirements, and public accountability.
Government cannot outsource its ultimate responsibility for an election.
CISA itself says state and local election officials have the primary responsibility for protecting election infrastructure.
That responsibility should come with meaningful control.
Nebraska Elections Must Remain Nebraska’s Responsibility CISA can provide threat intelligence and technical expertise.
Vendors can provide equipment and specialized services.
Nebraska must control its voter records, its ballots, its election systems, and its ability to independently verify the count.
That is what genuine decentralization should mean.
Technology can assist Nebraska elections.
It should never become indispensable to establishing the truth of an election.
We already have paper ballots.
We already have local election officials.
We already have the physical evidence necessary to verify our results.
Let's use it.
Nebraska elections must remain Nebraska’s responsibility.
That is the responsibility of the Secretary of State, and it is one I intend to take seriously.

added: About Randy Issues Donate Privacy Policy Effective Date: March 9, 2026 Georgians for Randy Peters (the "Campaign," "we," "us") respects your privacy.
This Privacy Policy explains how we collect, use, and share information when you visit our website, sign up for updates, volunteer, or otherwise interact with us online.
Information We Collect a.

Information You Provide We may collect personal information you choose to provide, including your name, email address, mailing address, phone number, and zip code, when you submit forms such as contact, volunteer, event RSVP, sign-up, or donation-related forms. b.
Donation-Related Information If you donate, a third-party payment processor typically processes the transaction.
We may receive donation-related information such as name, contact information, amount, date, and confirmation.
We generally do not receive your full payment card number. c.
Text Message Opt-In Information If you opt in to SMS or MMS communications, we collect your phone number, consent records, and messaging activity. d.
Information Collected Automatically We may automatically collect IP address, device identifiers, browser type, pages viewed, links clicked, and approximate location derived from IP address.
We may use cookies and similar technologies.
How We Use Information We use information to: Communicate with you and respond to requests.
Send updates, newsletters, and messages you request.
Manage volunteering, events, and outreach.
Improve our website and communications.
Protect against fraud and security incidents.
Comply with campaign-finance and election laws and enforce our rights.
How We Share Information We do not sell your personal information.
We may share information with: Service providers and vendors supporting operations (hosting, email, analytics, CRM, texting providers, payment processors).
Legal and safety disclosures as required by law or to protect rights and safety.
Campaign-finance disclosures when donor information must be reported or disclosed as required by law.
Text Message Policy Opt-in texts are used for campaign-related communications, including fundraising, informational, and volunteer messages.
Text messaging opt-in data, consent, and related collected personal information will not be shared with or sold to any third parties, unless required by law.
We may share text messaging information with service providers who deliver messages on our behalf, and when required by law.
Message and data rates may apply.
Message frequency varies.
Reply STOP to opt out.
Reply HELP for help.
Your Choices You may: Unsubscribe from emails via the unsubscribe link in any email.
Opt out of text messages by replying STOP .
Contact us to request access, correction, or deletion of your personal information, subject to legal and operational limits.
Data Security We use reasonable safeguards to protect your personal information and employ industry-standard security technologies.
However, no method of transmission over the internet or electronic storage is 100% secure, and we cannot guarantee absolute security.
Third-Party Links Our website may contain links to third-party websites or services.
We are not responsible for the privacy practices or content of such third parties.
We encourage you to review the privacy policies of those third parties when accessing their websites or services.
Children's Privacy Our website is not intended for use by individuals under the age of 13.
We do not knowingly collect personal information from children under 13.
If we become aware that we have collected personal information from a child under 13 without parental consent, we will take steps to remove such information from our records.
Changes to This Policy We may update this Privacy Policy from time to time to reflect changes in our practices or for other operational, legal, or regulatory reasons.
Updates are effective upon posting of the revised policy on our website.
We encourage you to review this page periodically.

Contact Us If you have any questions or concerns regarding this Privacy Policy or our privacy practices, please contact us at: Georgians for Randy Peters PO Box 763 Milledgeville, Georgia 31061 Phone: 770-241-6286 Georgians for Randy Peters PO Box 763 Milledgeville, Georgia 31061 770-241-6286 Quick Links About Randy Issues Privacy Policy Get Involved Join the movement to bring conservative leadership to the Georgia State House.
