They're Waiting Until You've Voted Republicans already admitted they'll redraw our maps.
The only question is when.
Saira Draper October 09, 2026 Republicans have a plan for our maps after Election Day.
Here's what it is, and how your vote can stop it.

Click to view my Instagram reel on the most important reason to vote for Keisha Lance Bottoms Georgia Republicans plan to redraw our political maps right after the November election, in a lame-duck session while Governor Kemp is still in office to sign them.
They backed off in June because redrawing was politically risky right before an election, not for the reasons they gave.
The best way to fight back is to elect Keisha Lance Bottoms governor –her veto would give us the leverage to force fair maps, and to flip seats in the legislature.
In this Edition of the Draper Paper Their plan: a lame-duck map grab Why the governor's veto is our best leverage Watch and share: my new video You're invited!

Support Tanya Miller for Attorney General Their plan: a lame-duck map grab It's an open secret that Republicans plan to call a special session after the midterms to draw new electoral maps for Congress, and the Georgia State House and Senate.
They laughed about it during the special session in June, after their plans to redraw the maps then were put on hold by Republican party leaders.
Let's back up.
On April 29 , the Supreme Court issued its decision in Louisiana v.
Callais , gutting what was left of the Voting Rights Act.
That law was the guardrail stopping Georgia Republicans from drawing rigged maps that silence minority voters.
Overnight, the Voting Rights Act was gone.
Within weeks of the Callais decision, Governor Kemp called a special session and put redistricting on the agenda.
He asked lawmakers to redraw Georgia's congressional maps and their own legislative districts and to pass those maps right away.( AP via PBS ).

Then, on June 17 , hours before the special session began, House Speaker Jon Burns stood before a packed Capitol atrium and announced that the House would not take up redistricting during that special session.
Check out our Guide to Georgia Legislative Procedure and Redistricting Terms here.

Speaker Jon Burns’ broken promise Although Republican leaders claimed they delayed redrawing political boundaries to allow for public input and court reviews, that excuse was just a political trick to avoid voter backlash before the midterm election.
Instead of holding hearings, they are running out the clock to push through partisan maps in a “surprise” post-election session.
Speaker of the House Jon Burns, R-Newington, speaks during a special legislative session at the state capitol, Wednesday, June 17, 2026, in Atlanta.
(AP Photo/Mike Stewart) Standing before a large crowd of angry Georgians, Speaker Burns laid out his reasons for not redrawing the maps in June ( watch the press conference ).

He said when the House learned redistricting was one of the governor’s priorities for the June special session, "we knew it was not the right path forward for our state at this time ." Notice those last three words.
Not never.
Just not now.

He said redistricting should be done "the Georgia way — responsibly, transparently, and with ample opportunity for public input." He promised "joint reapportionment meetings to hear from voters in every corner of the state," in "a fair and bipartisan environment." He also stated that the state’s decision to drop redistricting plans was driven by a commitment to a "thoughtful, fact-driven process" rather than "partisan gain.” And he pointed to the courts.

With several cases pending over Georgia's maps, he said Republicans "look forward to receiving additional judicial opinions to assist in our future map drawing efforts." He made this point in his letter to Governor Kemp that morning.
Senate President Pro Tem Larry Walker III, standing beside him, was even more candid.
He said the Callais decision "left no doubt that we would need to draw new maps.

The question was when." He said the Senate wanted "to allow the judicial process to further develop in other states" while "receiving additional public input before considering any changes to our maps." But those weren't the Republicans' real reasons for delaying redistricting.
Before the special session, Republicans polled redistricting, and it polled poorly.

Behind closed doors, Republican lawmakers worried that a redraw diminishing Georgians' ability to elect the politicians of their choosing would spark a backlash, leading to even bigger Democratic wins in the midterms.
With their own members on the ballot in November, House and Senate Republican leaders rejected their own governor's call.
It wasn't a moral decision.
It was a political one.
How do we know these reasons were a pretext?
Compare each one to what has happened since.
"Ample opportunity for public input." Not one of the promised joint reapportionment meetings has been held.
Not in a single corner of the state.
In September, the Speaker's office told the AJC that none were even scheduled.
And Walker, who promised "additional public input" in June, told the AJC he had not committed to the joint hearings at all.
"Additional judicial opinions." The federal district court is now in the process of reviewing Georgia's maps , but no decision has been issued yet.
If Republicans redraw the maps in a lame-duck session before those opinions come down, the pending litigation excuse was never real.
"Not to rush through it." A lame-duck session called weeks after Election Day, with no hearings held and the courts still deciding, is the very definition of rushing it.
"Not the right path forward … at this time." Republicans never said they wouldn't redraw.
Walker said it himself: "The question was when." The answer: after the voters are done voting in the midterms.
If Republicans truly cared about transparency and public input, they had all summer and fall to hold hearings.
Instead, they are running out the clock until a lame-duck session, when voters will have no chance to weigh in and no election left to hold them accountable.

So much for "not partisan gain." As I told the AJC last month : "If Keisha Lance Bottoms wins, they're going to push this through, and I think any promises of halting for pending litigation or transparency will be out the window." What Happens Next Instead of facing voters before the midterms, Republicans plan to rush a partisan redistricting map through a lame-duck session later this year while Governor Kemp is still in office to sign it, locking in legislative republican majorities for a generation before a new governor can take office.
When I wrote to you in April , I laid out two paths Republicans could take.

One of those paths was to redraw the maps in a special session this year, too late to affect the midterms, but early enough to avoid a veto from a Democratic governor or a fight with a Democratic House or Senate.
That is exactly the path they've chosen.
Here's how it will work.
Wait until the votes are counted in November.

If Democrats make significant gains in the State Legislature or win the Governor and other statewide races, call legislators back to the Capitol in a lame-duck session, in November or December, and draw the rigged maps they refused to draw in June while Governor Kemp is still in office to sign them.
Politically, Georgia is a 50/50 state.
We've proven that in election after election.
But with rigged maps, Georgia Republicans could lock in their majorities for a generation, no matter how Georgians vote.

And make no mistake about what that would mean: The same one-party rule that has controlled our state for more than two decades, without real checks and balances, that has given us sky-high costs and unchecked data centers popping up in our backyards while our power bills keep going up will remain in power.
Rigged maps would make that the permanent state of affairs, no matter how you vote.
Why the governor's veto is our best leverage If you elect Keisha Lance Bottoms as governor, every single thing Republicans want for the next four years has to get past her veto.
Their budget priorities.
Their tax bills.
Their pet projects.
All of it.
So if Kemp signs the maps before she takes office, why does it matter who wins the governor's race?
Because a map isn't permanent.
The legislature can redraw maps any year it chooses, and a Democratic governor can make sure it chooses to.
Democratic candidate for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms speaks at a joint campaign rally with U.S.
Sen.
Jon Ossoff at the Tabernacle in Atlanta on May 31, 2026.
(Source: Arvin Temkar/AJC) And Georgia's governor holds more cards than most.
The governor sets the revenue estimate that caps the entire state budget and can strike individual spending items with a line-item veto.
Republicans do not have the two-thirds majorities in both chambers they would need to override her.
That's leverage.
And Governor Bottoms can use it to force Republicans back to the table on fair maps.
Without a Democratic governor, those rigged maps stand for a generation.
With her as governor, we have a fighting chance.
The same goes for the legislature.
Flipping the Georgia House or Senate would give us a second check on one-party rule and a seat at the table when maps are drawn.
That's why it matters that you vote all the way down your ballot.
Watch and share: my new video I made a short video explaining all of this in about a minute.
Almost nobody is talking about this issue, and that's exactly what Republicans are counting on.
Please watch it, share it with every Georgian you know, and follow me on Instagram for more.

added: Skip to main content Saira Draper for State Senate District 44 for SD44 About Meet Saira Endorsements District 44 Get Involved Get Involved Work with Saira Canvass News + Events Get Help Join the Campaign Donate Accessibility Text size EN English Español Tiếng Việt ← All News Posted: October 9, 2026 at 11:07 AM EDT A Guide to Georgia Legislative Procedure and Redistricting Terms Articles Breaking down the essential terms governing district mapmaking, voting rights, and statehouse procedures in Georgia.
Georgia's General Assembly, also known as the "Gold Dome," has its own vocabulary to describe legislative processes.
Here's a guide tos ome of the common terms, along with some additional helpful information.
Mapmaking and Voting Rights Redistricting: The process of redrawing the boundaries of congressional and state legislative districts in Georgia.
This process determines which voters are grouped together to elect each representative.

Gerrymandering: The practice of drawing district lines specifically to give one political party an unfair advantage, enabling it to win more legislative seats relative to its overall share of the vote.
Voting Rights Act: The 1965 federal civil rights law enacted to protect minority voters from discrimination, including prohibiting electoral maps that dilute their voting power.
Louisiana v.
Callais : An April 2026 Supreme Court decision that gutted the remaining protections under the Voting Rights Act against discriminatory redistricting maps.
Legislative Sessions and Authority Special Session: A meeting of the Georgia legislature called by the governor outside the standard January-to-April regular session.

A special session is strictly limited to the topics specified by the governor on the agenda, known as "the call." Lame-Duck Session: A legislative session held after an election but before newly elected officials take office.
During this period, outgoing officials can act on legislation without facing immediate accountability from voters.
Veto Override: The constitutional mechanism by which the Georgia General Assembly passes a bill into law over a governor's veto.
To successfully override a veto, a two-thirds vote is required in both the Georgia House of Representatives and the State Senate.

Terms of Service · Privacy Notice · Accessibility · Do Not Contact We aim to meet WCAG 2.2 Level AA. ✕ Voting information for people with disabilities Information about the upcoming Elections The November 3, 2026 elections will be critical for Georgia’s future.
Review the Democrats running for statewide office , and remember to vote all the way down your ballot.
Supporting the statewide candidates AND your local representatives is crucial.
Flipping a chamber would allow us to pass meaningful legislation that helps hardworking Georgians.
It would also allow us to push back against likely efforts to redraw maps this December.
What you can do now Confirm your voter registration and make any necessary updates by October 5.
Make a plan to vote—and encourage your friends and family to do the same.
I strongly recommend voting early in person if possible.

Early voting offers flexibility (you may vote at any early voting site in your county), helps avoid long lines, provides time to resolve issues, and reduces the risk of encountering disruptions at your polling place.
There is good additional voting guidance at the Democratic Party of Georgia website .
Voters with disabilities can find excellent information on voting rights, accessibility tools, and available resources at REV UP Georgia .
If you can do more Volunteers are urgently needed.
You can serve as a poll worker, poll watcher, or support the Voter Protection Hotline.
Learn more about voter protection volunteering .
If you have concerns or questions, call the Voter Protection Hotline at 888-730-5816 .

added: Skip to content The Latest Issues Scott’s Anti-Corruption Plan Making AI Work for Mississippi Endorsements Store Volunteer Voting Info The Latest Issues Scott’s Anti-Corruption Plan Making AI Work for Mississippi Endorsements Store Volunteer Voting Info Facebook X-twitter Instagram Tiktok Donate Making AI Work for Mississippi District Attorney Scott Colom's AI & Data Center Plan Across the country, people are being asked to adapt to new technology that is changing their work, their children’s schools and their household budget faster than anyone has written rules for it.

A record 27 percent of American workers now say they worry technology will make their job obsolete , more than double the share in 2017, and the worry runs highest among workers without a college degree.
But so far, the people writing the rules for artificial intelligence are the people who own it .
District Attorney Scott Colom’s position is that Mississippi deserves investment, but the rules should be written for the people who have to live with them.
In Mississippi that is not a theory, and it is not a question for ten years from now.
AI is showing up here as a line on a power bill and a building going up on the other side of a treeline.
That is where he is starting.
Mississippi already has a senator in position to do something about this, but she has refused to act.
Cindy Hyde-Smith sits on the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee .
A bill to stop data center power costs from being pushed onto ordinary customers was introduced on July 16 and referred to that committee , where it still sits.
Its House companion passed 417 to 3 on September 16 .
Five senators have since signed onto the Senate bill, every one of them a Republican , four of them the day after that House vote.
John Kennedy, right next door in Louisiana, is one of them; Cindy Hyde-Smith is not.
That is not an oversight.
It is a choice about who she answers to.
Cindy Hyde-Smith would not put her name on a bill to keep these costs off our power bills.
The industry noticed, and its super PAC is spending on her behalf in Mississippi right now .
We are paying a senator who works for somebody else.
“I prosecute cases for a living, so my instinct is to follow the money and make people show their work.
Mississippi has been overlooked for too long to turn our backs on anybody willing to create jobs here.
But everybody in this state pays their own way, and rich tech companies should not be the exception,” said District Attorney Colom.

“That is why I am calling for an immediate pause on data center construction until tech companies sign commitments that they will pay their fair share, including ensuring jobs are not temporary and paying for the energy that these data centers require without jacking up our utility bills.
Mississippi can do well in this economy, but only if somebody from here is in the room when the terms get written.
We already have a seat in that room.

Cindy Hyde-Smith just has not been using it.” Scott's Plan: District Attorney Scott Colom is calling for a temporary pause on data center construction until these five rules are met: The companies pay their own way.
Mississippians do not.
A company that builds in our state pays for the electricity and the water it uses.
Right now the opposite is happening.
An independent analysis found the average Entergy Mississippi household is now paying about $10.60 more every month because of data center investments.
That is roughly $127 a year, and about $38 million taken from Mississippi households statewide through March, on track for $74 million by the end of this year .
That is money out of Mississippi families’ pockets for somebody else’s power, and nobody asked us.
Show us the deal before the concrete is poured.
Make public what a project will draw from our grid and our water system, and what it will pay — in plain language and public forums — while local communities can still do something about it.
Today we are not allowed to see it — state law lets these agreements stay confidential , and in 2024 the Legislature waived parts of Public Service Commission oversight for the Amazon projects .

The same fight is playing out over taxes: Madison County’s assessor valued five Amazon buildings at about $292 million each, Amazon said $69 million and would not open its construction costs, and when the county backed its assessor and denied Amazon’s appeal, millions of dollars stayed with local schools.
One assessor doing the job was all it took.
Mississippi should not have to get lucky to keep our dollars where they belong: in our communities.
Hire Mississippi workers, and put it in writing.
The good jobs are the whole reason to want these projects here.
The construction jobs and the permanent jobs must go to people who already live here, at a wage you can raise a family on.
And not simply a promise at a ribbon cutting — in the contract, with a penalty for breaking it.
If AI touches our lives, a real person must answer for it.
What crosses a prosecutor’s desk today is AI used to steal — scam calls that empty a retirement account, fake images made of real people, including children.
That is already a crime, but most local prosecutors do not have the tools or the training to make the case.
District Attorney Colom will fight to get it to them.
And when an automated system is handling our money, our health care or our benefits, we should be told, and a real person should have to answer for the decision.
Mississippi decides what gets built in Mississippi.
Clarksdale rezoned land for a data center and set its own terms ; Jackson put a six-month hold on data centers while it works out its own rules.
Both decisions are right, because both are theirs to make.
There is a push in Washington to take that authority away from states and communities, and District Attorney Colom will oppose it.

added: Skip to content Donate to Support Sean M C Cann for Congress Donate to Join Team M c Cann If you've saved your information with ActBlue Express, your donation will go through immediately. $# $# $# $# $# $# $# $# $# $# Other Amount Other Amount About Issues Endorsements Latest News Vote About Issues Endorsements Latest News Vote Take Action Take Action Donate Donate Donate Donate Oct 9, 2026 Cook Political Report Moves MI-04 to Toss-Up as Sean McCann Builds Historic Momentum to Unseat Bill Huizenga Press Release Major Ratings Shift Comes on Heels of McCann’s Record-Breaking $1.8 Million Fundraising Quarter KALAMAZOO, MI – Today, the nonpartisan rate rater Cook Political Report officially moved Michigan’s 4th Congressional District to a Toss-Up , marking major momentum in the race between Sean McCann and longtime Republican Congressman Bill Huizenga.

The new rating from one of the nation’s leading nonpartisan election forecasters underscores the increasingly competitive landscape in Southwest Michigan and comes on the heels of McCann’s historic $1.8 million fundraising quarter, shattering records for a Democratic challenger in MI-04.
The shift comes as national Republican and MAGA-aligned groups continue pouring millions of dollars into the district to defend Huizenga.
“This rating change has confirmed what we have been seeing on the ground for months,” said Simone Archer Krauss, campaign manager for Sean McCann .
“Voters are frustrated with rising costs while Bill Huizenga looks out for himself and the special interests that have bankrolled his campaign.
Sean has shattered fundraising records and assembled a growing coalition of voters in Southwest Michigan ready for change.

The national GOP is pouring millions into a district they once considered safe because they see the same thing we do: Sean is on track to win this race and bring change to Southern Michigan.” The ratings change comes amid growing scrutiny of Huizenga’s support for Trump’s tariff policies , rising energy costs , and his ties to special interests .
With less than a month until Election Day, the Cook Political Report’s new rating places MI-04 among the nation’s most closely watched congressional battlegrounds.
From Cook Political Report Analysis : GOP Rep.
Bill Huizenga has spent weeks hammering Democratic state Sen.
Sean McCann…But polls continue to show the two candidates effectively tied.
Trump, who won this seat by 5.5 points in 2024, has a favorability of 39% in one of the Democrats’ most recent polls.

Huizenga, who’s served in Congress since 2011 and previously served in the Michigan legislature, has done little to separate himself from the national Republican party over the course of career and may not be able to survive this difficult political environment.
This race moves from Lean Republican to Toss Up.
### About Sean McCann: Sean McCann has spent his career standing up to the powerful and on behalf of people in Southwest Michigan.
From cracking down on slumlords to serving as a State Senator, Sean has fought to change broken systems.
In the State Legislature, he stood up to polluters to protect Lake Michigan, and he cut taxes for working families.

Sean knows Washington is broken and he’ll fight for the change we need – banning members of Congress from trading stocks, negotiating for lower drug prices, and stopping massive tax breaks for billionaires and big corporations, so we put hard-working people first.
Born and raised in Michigan, Sean attended Western Michigan University before serving as a Kalamazoo Commissioner, State Representative, and now State Senator for Southwest Michigan.
Along the way, he’s earned a reputation among Democrats and Republicans alike as a serious problem-solver who works across the aisle and stands up for families trying to make ends meet.
As a husband and father raising his family in Michigan, Sean understands what’s at stake for working families.

In Congress, he’ll bring the same work ethic, common sense, and determination he’s brought to public service throughout his career, and fight every day to make Washington work for people it’s supposed to serve.
About the race for Michigan’s 4th Congressional District: MI-04 is one of the country’s key 2026 battlegrounds.
The R+3 district has been named a top “Red to Blue” race by the DCCC and rated a toss-up by Sabato’s Crystal Ball.

Cook Political Report has consistently moved this race in Democrats’ direction, calling the district “ a bright spot for Democrats .” Poll after poll has shown Sean McCann leading Bill Huizenga, and McCann continues to post strong fundraising numbers.

According to Cook, Sean McCann’s State Senate seat (MI-19) “makes up about a third of the 4th District and includes 45% of the 4th’s primary electorate.” Governor Gretchen Whitmer and Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson each carried MI-04 with more than fifty percent of the vote in 2022.
MI-04 covers Southwest Michigan and includes the cities of Kalamazoo, Battle Creek, Holland, St.
Joseph, Benton Harbor and the outer suburbs of Grand Rapids including Ottawa County.

Sean has also received endorsements from Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer, Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, Senator Elissa Slotkin, Congresswoman Hillary Scholten, former Congressman Mark Schauer, over 15 labor groups, and over 70 local elected officials and community leaders.

added: Skip to content Donate to Support Sean M C Cann for Congress Donate to Join Team M c Cann If you've saved your information with ActBlue Express, your donation will go through immediately. $# $# $# $# $# $# $# $# $# $# Other Amount Other Amount About Issues Endorsements Latest News Vote About Issues Endorsements Latest News Vote Take Action Take Action Donate Donate Donate Donate Oct 8, 2026 ICYMI FROM THE ‘GANDER: “Rep.
Bill Huizenga’s votes show he put data centers and coal plants over constituents” Press Release The ‘Gander “Rep.

Bill Huizenga (R-Holland) has voted to support Trump’s AI race—and data shows it could cost Michiganders a lot of money.” KALAMAZOO, MI – In case you missed it, The ‘Gander reported on Congressman Bill Huizenga’s support of policies that favor AI data center expansion and keeping aging coal plants running, that leave Michigan families footing the bill.
Huizenga backed legislation scaling back clean energy investments and supported keeping the J.H.
Campbell coal plant open, an effort reportedly costing more than $260 million, while experts warn that his energy policies could drive household utility bills up by $300 a year.
Read more about what Southwest Michigan families are reading about Huizenga’s record of putting the interests of AI data centers ahead of the constituents he was elected to represent.

In 2025, alongside other Michigan Republicans, Huizenga supported the Trump administration’s reconciliation bill, which cut Medicaid coverage for 15,000 residents in Michigan’s 4th Congressional District—the one Huizenga represents—which includes Allegan, Van Buren, northern Berrien and Kalamazoo counties, and portions of Ottawa and Calhoun counties.

T he “One Big Beautiful Bill,” or OBBBA, also scaled back clean energy investments established during the Biden administration and paved the way for new data center construction nationwide—including in Michigan —as part of the Trump administration’s ongoing plan to have the US lead the “golden age” of artificial intelligence.
Experts say this data center construction, along with powering the data centers once they’re built, won’t just strain the area’s electrical supply.
It’ll also strain Michiganders’ wallets, with expected yearly utility bills rising by $300.

This is expected to further impact low-income Michiganders, who are already reeling after Huizenga and other Republicans supported a 2025 appropriations bill that eliminated federal funding for a Department of Energy program that helped their households increase energy efficiency and reduce energy bills.
The push for data center construction has also narrowed jobs and investment into the state’s clean energy infrastructure.
New data shows that, since Trump was re-elected in 2024, over 8,000 jobs and over $1.7 billion in investment in Michigan’s clean energy sector have been cancelled or delayed .
Huizenga has also publicly supported the Trump administration’s executive order to keep the J.H.
Campbell coal plant in West Olive open despite a state-approved plan to close the facility to expand renewable energy and pushback from his constituents and other Michiganders.
Reminder: Sean has a long record of fighting to lower energy costs: Sean is calling for a three-year freeze on utility rate increases to give Michigan families relief from repeated rate hikes.
Sean is a cosponsor of SB 768, legislation that would freeze utility rates for three years and prevent utility companies from raising rates during that period.
Sean helped pass SB 353 , 880 , and 881 , measures that expanded eligibility for the Michigan Energy Assistance Program (MEAP) and addressed utility participation in the program.
Sean helped pass HB 5028 , which limited homeowners associations’ ability to prohibit certain energy-saving home improvements.

The contrast in their records is clear: Huizenga has consistently backed federal energy policies that could increase costs for Michigan households, while Sean McCann has supported legislation aimed at limiting utility rate hikes, expanding energy assistance, and helping families lower their energy bills.
About Sean McCann: Sean McCann has spent his career standing up to the powerful and on behalf of people in Southwest Michigan.
From cracking down on slumlords to serving as a State Senator, Sean has fought to change broken systems.
In the State Legislature, he stood up to polluters to protect Lake Michigan, and he cut taxes for working families.

Sean knows Washington is broken and he’ll fight for the change we need – banning members of Congress from trading stocks, negotiating for lower drug prices, and stopping massive tax breaks for billionaires and big corporations, so we put hard-working people first.
Born and raised in Michigan, Sean attended Western Michigan University before serving as a Kalamazoo Commissioner, State Representative, and now State Senator for Southwest Michigan.
Along the way, he’s earned a reputation among Democrats and Republicans alike as a serious problem-solver who works across the aisle and stands up for families trying to make ends meet.
As a husband and father raising his family in Michigan, Sean understands what’s at stake for working families.

In Congress, he’ll bring the same work ethic, common sense, and determination he’s brought to public service throughout his career, and fight every day to make Washington work for people it’s supposed to serve.
About the race for Michigan’s 4th Congressional District: MI-04 is one of the country’s key 2026 battlegrounds.
The R+3 district has been named a top “Red to Blue” race by the DCCC and rated a toss-up by Sabato’s Crystal Ball.

Cook Political Report has consistently moved this race in Democrats’ direction, calling the district “ a bright spot for Democrats .” Poll after poll has shown Sean McCann leading Bill Huizenga, and McCann continues to post strong fundraising numbers.

According to Cook, Sean McCann’s State Senate seat (MI-19) “makes up about a third of the 4th District and includes 45% of the 4th’s primary electorate.” Governor Gretchen Whitmer and Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson each carried MI-04 with more than fifty percent of the vote in 2022.
MI-04 covers Southwest Michigan and includes the cities of Kalamazoo, Battle Creek, Holland, St.
Joseph, Benton Harbor and the outer suburbs of Grand Rapids including Ottawa County.

Sean has also received endorsements from Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer, Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, Senator Elissa Slotkin, Congresswoman Hillary Scholten, former Congressman Mark Schauer, over 15 labor groups, and over 70 local elected officials and community leaders.

Senate ICYMI Montana Voices: Bodnar “Will bring positive change,” Bankhead is “A Democrat in name only, ”Alme was “Forced down our throats by the Republican Party” ICYMI Kurt Alme Says “We can't vote to limit the use of force in the Gulf,” Doubles Down on His Support of the Costly and Unauthorized War in Iran ICYMI Former NARAL Head Calls Out Alani Bankhead for Lying About Reproductive Freedom Record PRESS RELEASE After Months Hidden Away by His Party Bosses, Kurt Alme Will Finally Face Seth Bodnar and Montanans PRESS RELEASE 10 Questions Kurt Alme Has Spent Months Dodging Oct 9 2026 PRESS RELEASE 10 Questions Kurt Alme Has Spent Months Dodging After spending months skipping forums forcing the cancellation of the MTFP/Nonstop Local debate, Alme finally faces Montana voters on Sunday.
Here’s what they deserve to hear him answer: MISSOULA, MT — On Sunday, at the Montana Broadcasters Association debate, Kurt Alme will share a stage with his opponents for the first time.
Ahead of the debate, the Bodnar campaign is releasing 10 questions Alme has spent this campaign avoiding.
Why did you drop out of the MTFP/Nonstop Local Debate, and will you commit to any more debates across the state so voters can hear directly from you?
You engineered a rigged primary, have never run for office before, and are unknown to Montana voters.
Still, you skipped forum after forum, and a statewide debate was cancelled because you wouldn’t show up.
If you’re this dismissive of Montana voters, why should anyone believe you’ll answer to them in Washington?

You said Congress “can’t vote to limit the use of force” in the Gulf, while promising you’d never support “another forever war.” Do you believe Congress has any constitutional role at all in the use of military force in Iran?

Eighteen American service members have been killed in a war Congress never authorized, diesel prices in Montana are above $6, and when asked whether it should end, you said only that it’s important to “continue to support our president.” Specifically name the circumstances under which you would vote to end the war in Iran.
Your office let a man who admitted to sexually abusing a six-year-old child walk away with less than a year behind bars, and without ever registering as a sex offender.
What is your explanation for that?
Why did your office decline to prosecute up to 79 percent of the sexual abuse cases assigned to it?
You called Medicaid a “permanent handout,” even though it is how tens of thousands of Montanans get their health care and it is a lifeline for rural hospitals.
Do you support Medicaid expansion?
Why, when you worked in the governor’s office, did you lobby against three bills to lower the cost of insulin, and let a company who sold fake cancer drugs off the hook with a slap on the wrist?
Yes or no, has the debt grown by $3.6 trillion since January 2025, passing $40 trillion?
Is the Party that controlled all three branches of government during that time responsible?
Montana ranchers are watching foreign beef flood our markets while cattle herds sit at a 75-year low.
You’ve said nothing.
Do you support the Administration’s decision to flood the market with 660 million pounds of foreign beef?
“Party bosses can hand Kurt Alme a nomination, but they can’t answer Montanans’ questions for him.
On Sunday, Montanans will hear what Alme sounds like without a script,” said Bodnar campaign spokesperson Kelly Webster.
Seth Bodnar is a Green Beret, business leader, and former president of the University of Montana running for the U.S.
Senate to be an independent voice for Montana.
Seth is guided by a lifelong commitment to duty, honor, and country.

He graduated first in his class at West Point and served multiple overseas deployments, leading soldiers in the 101st Airborne Division and the 1st Special Forces Group, and serving as a special advisor to the commanding general in Iraq.
After his military service and a successful career in business, Seth spent the last eight years leading the University of Montana.

Under his leadership, the university achieved record high graduation rates, doubled research funding, launched the largest infrastructure renewal in campus history, restored financial stability, and was named the #1 military-friendly university in the country.
Raised by two public school teachers, he believes leadership is about service, not party loyalty.
Seth and his wife, a fifth-generation Montanan, are raising their three children in Montana.

title.after: Best Available Technology for Data Center Cooling: What Montana Should Demand | Shane Klakken

added: top of page News Principles Calendar About Menu Close Donate Best Available Technology for Data Center Cooling: What Montana Should Demand By Shane Klakken, Montana House District 37 July 8, 2026 Best Available Technology (BAT) for Data Centers That Bring Their Own Power (Behind-the-Meter / On-Site Generation) Here in central Montana, water is life.
Our farms, ranches, and communities depend on every drop, especially during dry summers.
When big AI data centers come calling, one of the biggest questions is how they plan to keep their thousands of servers from overheating.
The good news is that technology has improved.
There is now a clear “Best Available Technology” (BAT) that can sharply reduce both electricity use and water consumption.
Old Way vs.
New Way Traditional air cooling — basically giant fans and cooling towers that evaporate huge amounts of water — is outdated for today’s power-hungry AI servers.
These systems can suck down 1 to 5 million gallons of water per day per large facility and waste a lot of electricity.
The best available technology today is advanced liquid cooling , especially direct-to-chip cooling .
This method runs a special liquid coolant through metal plates placed directly on the hottest parts of the computer chips (the CPUs and GPUs).
It’s often combined with rear-door heat exchangers or some air cooling for the rest of the equipment.
Even better for water-conscious areas like Montana is pairing this with closed-loop dry coolers .
Instead of evaporating water into the air like old cooling towers, the heat is transferred to the liquid and then released into the outside air through large radiator-style coolers.
Once the system is filled, ongoing water use can drop to nearly zero.
Another strong option for the most advanced facilities is immersion cooling , where servers are actually submerged in a special non-conductive fluid.
This can cut cooling energy use dramatically.

Why This Matters to Rural Montana • Water Savings : Modern liquid cooling systems can reduce or eliminate the massive evaporative water loss that worried so many neighbors in Broadview, Great Falls, and Bonner. • Lower Power Bills : These systems are far more efficient.
Good facilities now aim for a PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness) of 1.10 to 1.20.

That means much less wasted electricity, which helps keep rates stable for farms and homes instead of driving them up. • Less Strain : Lower energy use means less pressure on NorthWestern Energy’s grid and fewer calls for new power plants.

The Bottom Line for Montana When any company proposes a hyperscale AI data center in our state — whether near Billings, Great Falls, or elsewhere — local leaders and residents should insist on Best Available Technology as a condition of approval.
No outdated evaporative cooling towers.
Require closed-loop liquid cooling, clear performance numbers on water use and PUE, and independent verification.
We don’t have to choose between progress and protecting our water and way of life.
The technology exists today to do both.
Montana should demand the best — not settle for yesterday’s methods that waste our most precious resources.
Rural communities have every right to ask: “Show us you’re using the best available technology to protect our water and keep our power costs reasonable.” That’s just good stewardship.

title.after: From Grass Range to the Rocky Mountains: Carrying Central Montana's Voice to the Article V Summit | Shane Klakken

added: top of page News Principles Calendar About Menu Close Donate From Grass Range to the Rocky Mountains: Carrying Central Montana's Voice to the Article V Summit By Shane Klakken, Montana House District 37 September 2, 2026 Most weeks, my job doesn't take me any farther than the Capitol in Helena, or a kitchen table in House District 37 talking crop insurance and county roads with a neighbor.

This month it took me to a resort ballroom outside Denver, sitting alongside a former U.S. senator and a room full of state lawmakers from across the country, all wrestling with the same question: what happens when Washington won't fix itself, and it falls to the states to do it instead.

I represent a roughly 12,000-person district covering Petroleum County and most of Fergus County, and I was in Aurora, Colorado, for the Convention of States Article V Summit — a gathering built around a part of the U.S.
Constitution most Montanans have never had reason to think much about.
Article V is the section that lays out how the Constitution gets amended, and it offers two paths to get there.
One runs through Congress.

The other runs through the states themselves, two-thirds of which submit an application to convene a convention to propose amendments, which then still need 38 states to ratify before anything changes.
It's never been used.
I believe it's time central Montana — and the rest of the country — took a hard look at why.
We came down for the summit to learn more about the Article V process and how states put together the requirements to come together and propose amendments to the U.S.
Constitution.
It's not the first time I've carried that fight home.
In my very first session in Helena, I introduced House Joint Resolution 5, an effort to add Montana to the growing list of states formally applying for a convention.

The resolution made it further than any similar measure had in Montana before — clearing the House Business and Labor Committee and reaching the floor for a full debate — though it ultimately fell short of passage.
It didn't pass the House, but Montana got a resolution like this onto the floor for the first time ever, and we got members on record with their votes.
That's real progress, and now we're working to bring more of them around.
I don't think it takes much imagination to see the federal government now does a lot more than its eighteen enumerated powers.
A Constitution Studied in a Living Room, Then a Small Church in Grass Range I didn't come to this issue through party politics.
I came to it through COVID — and through a small country church.
I got involved with this as a freshman legislator because of COVID, honestly.
We had rules imposed without going through the legislative process — bars were deemed essential but churches weren't, big box stores stayed open while mom-and-pop shops were shut down.
That got me looking hard at what was going on, and it got me looking into our Constitution.
That search led me to Patriot Academy, an organization that teaches the founding documents.
I brought the material home to my living room, then felt compelled to bring it to my congregation at the small church I attend in Grass Range.
We ran through the Biblical Citizenship course twice, and on the third pass, worked through Constitution Alive as well.
When you teach something, you learn it a lot better.
Founding Father John Jay charged citizens to study, and teach, the Constitution to the rising generation so they know how to be free and how to defend their rights.
I believe that's true of any subject, and that's what I did.
It was in that study that I first ran across Article V — the way the Constitution provides for its own repair, as I like to put it.
That curiosity led me to ConventionOfStates.com, and from there, to a role as a district captain gathering petition signatures alongside one of the organization's Montana co-directors.
The two of us got to talking, and a few weeks later, that conversation reached a state senator in Billings.
Sen.
Tom McGillvray had heard there was no candidate lined up for House District 37 and asked if anyone locally might be interested.
My co-director didn't hesitate — he told the senator he'd call me.
I'm a 32-year veteran of military, wildland firefighting and law enforcement service, and I'd describe myself as having been largely disengaged from local civic life before that call.
It caught me off guard.
I'd been thinking, if anything, about a seat on a rural electric or telephone cooperative board, not the Montana Legislature.
I told him it wasn't something I'd expected.
I'd been pretty unengaged locally on any civic body — not on any boards or commissions, nothing with real decision-making power in my community.
I figured I needed to do something.
A day or two after that first call from Sen.
McGillvray, I'd agreed to run.
I'm now in my first term, seeking a second, and I raised my hand to carry the Article V resolution myself when no one else stepped forward.
Sharp Company in Aurora The Colorado summit put me in a room with some of the movement's best-known figures — former U.S.
Sen.

Rick Santorum; Rob Natelson, a former University of Montana law professor now retired from the Article V Information Center in Colorado; and Convention of States co-founders Mark Meckler and Michael Ferris.
Ferris is an attorney who has argued before the U.S.
Supreme Court on Constitutional issues and prevailed.
These folks are incredibly accessible.
I have personal cell phone numbers for people who've told me to call or text anytime I have a question.
Part of the summit's purpose, as I see it, is simply taking the fear out of a process most people have never seen in action — and reminding skeptics that conventions aren't some untested experiment.

The Constitution doesn't spell out exactly how a convention would be run, how delegates get there, or how it's controlled — but the same is true of juries, and nobody's scared of those, because we have history and experience with how they work.
There were roughly twenty conventions held in this country before the Constitutional Convention of 1787 and eleven afterwards — Conventions aren't new to America.
We just haven't seen one in a while, and people mistake that for not knowing how it's done.

A Rancher's-Eye View of Federal Overreach For a district built on cattle, grain and wide-open country, my argument leans hard on ground central Montanans already know well: who's really in charge, and who's paying for it.
I point to Article I, Section 8 of the Constitution, which lists eighteen specific powers granted to the federal government — and nothing more.
It doesn't take much imagination to see the federal government now does a lot more than those eighteen powers.
The way they do it is through money.
About half of Montana's budget is federal money, and when they send it, they attach strings — do this, or you don't get it.

I think about Montana's old fight over the state speed limit, once effectively dictated by Washington through highway funding, as a familiar example of federal leverage — and I'd point to education as a modern one.
Education is not one of those eighteen powers.
I'm not against education, or even consistency in education, but it's a state responsibility, not a federal one.
Education is not for the federal government to dictate how it's done.
The urgency, to me, comes down to arithmetic most ranchers understand better than most economists: you can't keep spending money you don't have.
Forty trillion dollars is unimaginable.
Roughly 25% of GDP now goes just to servicing the interest on that debt.
That can't go on forever — eventually the money runs out.
Neither party, Republican or Democrat, has shown any real appetite for reducing spending or fiscal discipline.

Convention of States organizes its goals around three pillars: limiting the scope and jurisdiction of the federal government, fiscal restraint, and term limits for Congress and federal bureaucrats — an idea that polls at 80 to 85% public support, though I'd caution it needs to be designed carefully so power doesn't simply shift to unelected agencies instead.

My own 32-year run through federal service — nine years in the Army National Guard, nine more flying lead planes as a wildland firefighter for the Forest Service, and 11 years in law enforcement with U.S.
Customs and Border Protection — gave me a front-row seat to how that growth actually happens on the ground.
The federal government grows — that's just what it does.
It doesn't know fiscal discipline.
In the Forest Service, it happens through grade creep: the same job gets upgraded again and again until it's a much higher pay grade for identical work.
In Customs & Border Protection, we built what I'd call fiefdoms — five air branches along the northern border with no real operational need for that many, just expansion for its own sake.
"It's a Tremendous Duty" I frame this fight less as ideology than obligation — a duty I believe the founders handed to state legislators on purpose.
It's our duty as legislators to check the federal government.

That authority to call a convention of states to propose amendments wasn't given to us thoughtlessly — the founders knew that at some point, the states would need to check federal overreach, what people often call tyranny, and rein in its growth and lack of discipline.
I'm candid about the odds and the stakes alike.
If we keep doing what we're doing now, which is essentially nothing, and expect a different result — that is insanity.
If we do our duty and use the Article V process, the worst outcome is nothing changes.
But at minimum, we raise national awareness about how this country is supposed to work.
At best, we get real amendments proposed and ratified by 38 states, and that changes how this country actually operates.
So yes — it's a tremendous duty, and a real opportunity, both to educate the country on how the process works and to make immediate, meaningful change.

I plan to bring the resolution back to Helena and keep building support among my colleagues, one conversation at a time — the same way I built support for it back home, starting with a living room, a small church in Grass Range, and a district that, cows included, isn't quite as outnumbered on this issue as it might look.

title.after: Growing Wealth Shouldn't Require Already Having It | Shane Klakken

added: top of page News Principles Calendar About Menu Close Donate Growing Wealth Shouldn't Require Already Having It By Shane Klakken, Montana House District 37 September 16, 2026 If you've spent any time around a cattle sale barn or with your CPA, you know the frustration of watching good opportunities pass you by simply because you don't have the paperwork to prove you're "wealthy enough" to be let in the door.

That's essentially how federal securities law has treated private investment opportunities for decades, and Montana's own Congressman Troy Downing (MT-02) has introduced a bill in Washington to fix it.
The bill is called the “Informed Investor Access Act”, and it deals with something called "accredited investor" status.

Under current federal rules, if you want access to certain private investment opportunities — the kind of deals that used to be available to a broader range of Americans before Wall Street pulled up the ladder — you generally have to prove a net worth over $1 million or an income over $200,000 a year.
It doesn't matter how much you know about markets, how carefully you've studied a deal, or whether a licensed professional has looked at your finances and told you it's a sound move.
If you don't hit the wealth number, you're locked out.
Congressman Downing's bill takes a different approach.

Instead of gatekeeping access by your bank balance, it would let you qualify as an accredited investor if you're receiving personalized advice from a registered investment adviser or a broker-dealer — professionals who are already legally bound to act in your best interest.
Advisers operate under a fiduciary duty.
Broker-dealers operate under something called Regulation Best Interest.

The SEC's own staff has said these two standards, while not identical, generally land in the same place: the professional has to put your interests ahead of their own and have a reasonable basis for believing the recommendation actually fits your situation.
That matters here in central Montana.
We're a state built on people who know how to judge risk — whether it's reading the sky before starting the swather to cut hay or figuring out if a piece of equipment is worth the note on it.

Plenty of ranchers, farmers, small business owners, and working families around Fergus and Petroleum counties have the financial sophistication to make a sound investment decision, guided by a professional who's already accountable to regulators.
What they don't have, in a lot of cases, is a seven-figure net worth.
This bill says that shouldn't be the only thing keeping you from participating in a good investment.
There's a bigger picture here too.

The number of publicly listed companies in America has been cut roughly in half since the mid-1990s, down to around 4,000 today, and a lot of that growth is happening in private markets before a company ever goes public — if it goes public at all.
Meanwhile, public stock indexes have become more concentrated than they've been in decades, with a handful of mega-cap tech companies making up a third of the S&P 500.
If regular investors are locked out of the private side of the economy, they're increasingly left holding a public market that's less diversified than it used to be.
Opening a responsible, advice-based path to private investment is one way to correct that imbalance without throwing out investor protections.
The idea has drawn support beyond just Montana.
The Institute for Portfolio Alternatives, the Financial Technology Association, the Investment Advisers Association, the U.S.
Chamber of Commerce, and several other trade groups representing both advisers and everyday investors have all backed the bill since Downing introduced it this summer.
Trade press covering securities law has noted it as a straightforward, bipartisan-friendly fix to a rule that hasn't kept pace with how Americans actually get financial advice today.
Congressman Downing has made a habit of bringing forward legislation that reflects how Montanans actually live and work, rather than how Washington assumes we do.

This bill is no exception — it trusts working people who've done their homework and have a licensed professional standing behind them, instead of assuming that only the already-wealthy are capable of managing risk.

Downing is seeking a second term representing Montana's Eastern District this cycle, and bills like this one — practical, plainly explained, and aimed at leveling a field that's been tilted too long — are worth keeping an eye on as that race unfolds.
As always, we need to watch this one as it moves through the process in DC.

title.after: I-194: Read the Fine Print Before You Vote | Shane Klakken

added: top of page News Principles Calendar About Menu Close Donate I-194: Read the Fine Print Before You Vote By Shane Klakken, Montana House District 37 October 1, 2026 This week, Russ Cleveland of Montana PLAN brought an I-194 town hall to the Yogo Inn in Lewistown.
The measure will be on our November ballot, and most of us will decide on a few lines of ballot language that even Cleveland admits is hard to follow.
So here’s a plain look at what was said, what each side has going for it, and what nobody can promise yet.
What it would do Cleveland’s pitch rests on an old idea: the state grants corporations their powers, so the state can change them.
I-194 would strip “artificial persons” (corporations, LLCs, nonprofits, unions, trusts and partnerships) of the power to make political contributions or expenditures.
Any money or thing of value going to a campaign would have to come from a named individual instead.
Businesses could still lobby the legislature, endorse candidates and host candidate forums.
What they couldn’t do is put a company name on a campaign check or give away goods and services they normally sell.
Cleveland’s example was a business owner who could still support a candidate publicly and could still write a personal check, just not one from the company account.
Why supporters back it Montana has fought this fight before.
A century ago, copper money out of Butte and Anaconda was buying Senate seats, and Montanans answered with the 1912 Corrupt Practices Act.
It held for 98 years, until Citizens United.
Cleveland says a single Montana Senate race hit $162 million in 2024.
Supporters point out that in a state with so few voters, every outside dollar counts for more.
They also say money can hop between trusts, nonprofits and PACs until nobody can say where it started.
Cleveland noted the campaign gathered about 50,000 signatures using only volunteers.
He also argued that once a donor’s name is attached to a check, voters can weigh who is behind a message, and that transparency has to come first before anyone can talk seriously about limits.
Where the questions are Start with what it doesn’t do.
Cleveland calls it a “base hit,” not a home run.
There are no spending caps and no contribution limits.
It only aims to show who’s paying.
He says backers plan to pursue a constitutional amendment in 2028, which tells you they see this as a first step, not the last word.
Next, the courts.
Cleveland expects a legal challenge and pointed to an injunction against a similar Hawaii law.
Because it’s a citizen initiative, a court can’t trim it.
It stands or falls as a whole.
And because it’s a statute and not a constitutional amendment, a future legislature can amend or weaken it.
That happens to citizen initiatives more than folks think.
Then there’s the reach.
“Artificial persons” covers a lot of ground out here, including nonprofits, trade groups and unions.
Cleveland says everyday operations are untouched and that most small businesses never write political checks.
But the line between educating and advocating will get tested.
Enforcement can come from any group of citizens, and violators could see shareholders held personally liable.
Supporters call that a strong deterrent.
Skeptics may call it a lawsuit waiting to happen.
Cleveland also admitted the ballot language is poorly drafted.
A longer version with fuller definitions would become law, but most voters will only see the short summary.
The Montana Chamber of Commerce opposes the measure.
Cleveland says it speaks mainly for its biggest donors.
I didn’t hear the Chamber’s side that night, and you should.
A fair warning Nearly everything above about what I-194 would do comes from the people promoting it.
That’s one side of the table, and it deserves the same scrutiny as any other.
What I’d suggest Read the full text, not just the ballot summary.
Look up who’s funding both the yes and no campaigns on the Commissioner of Political Practices website.
Ask hard questions of anyone who says this measure fixes everything, or ruins everything.
Central Montanans have never needed anybody to read the fine print for us.
Let’s not start now.

title.after: Keep the Land Moving: Montana’s Quiet Guard Against Forever Ownership | Shane Klakken

added: top of page News Principles Calendar About Menu Close Donate Keep the Land Moving: Montana’s Quiet Guard Against Forever Ownership By Shane Klakken, Montana House District 37 September 10, 2026 Out here in central Montana, land isn’t just dirt and grass.
It’s the place where a family sinks roots, raises kids, and hopes the next generation can keep the place going if they choose to.
That’s why a short line in our state constitution deserves more attention than it usually gets.

Article XIII, Section 6 says simply: “No perpetuities shall be allowed except for charitable purposes.” The language is almost word-for-word the same as the 1889 constitution that came with statehood.
The 1972 convention left it alone.
No long debate.
No fancy rewriting.
They kept it because the idea still made sense.
A “perpetuity” is any arrangement that tries to lock property up forever—or for so long that future owners can’t really control it.
Think of a ranch that can never be sold, never divided, never mortgaged, no matter what happens fifty or a hundred years down the road.
Or a trust that keeps land in one bloodline until the end of time.
The constitution says those deals are not allowed.
The only permanent arrangements it blesses are charitable ones—land given forever to a church, a hospital, a school, or a public park.
Why does this matter to people who work the land?
First, it keeps property alive in the marketplace.
If a family hits hard times—drought, low cattle prices, medical bills—the land has to be able to move.
Banks won’t lend against property that can’t be sold.
Young people who want to start ranching need a chance to buy in.
The rule against perpetuities stops one generation from tying the hands of every generation that follows.
Second, it pushes back against the old idea of permanent family empires.
Our grandparents knew what concentrated land ownership could do.
The constitution’s framers, both in 1889 and 1972, wanted freeholders, not a permanent landlord class.
They believed ordinary people should be able to own land, use it, improve it, and pass it on—or sell it—without some long-dead relative still calling the shots from the grave.
Third, it leaves room for real charity.
A family that wants to give a section of ground forever to the county for a park or to a church for a cemetery can do it.
The law makes a clear distinction between private control that never ends and public-spirited gifts that serve the whole community.
Montana has put the constitutional rule into everyday law.
Under the Uniform Statutory Rule Against Perpetuities, most future interests have to vest within roughly 90 years or within 21 years after the death of people alive when the interest was created.
That is long enough for careful estate planning.
It is not long enough to lock a place up until the Second Coming.
For ranch families, this is practical freedom.
You can still leave the home place to your kids.
You can still set up a trust that lasts for a good long while.
You just cannot invent a scheme that pretends the land will never again be free to change hands.
That limit protects the next generation from being trapped by yesterday’s decisions, and it protects the community from having productive ground frozen in place while the world moves on.
Some people hear “rule against perpetuities” and think of dusty law books and lawyers arguing over technicalities.
That misses the point.
At its heart, the rule is a vote of confidence in living people.
It says the folks who walk the ground today should have the power to decide what happens to it, not some ironclad plan written in 1925 or 2025 that no one can touch.
Central Montana has always valued that kind of practical independence.
We respect the past, but we do not let it own the future.
Article XIII, Section 6 is one of the quiet ways our constitution keeps that balance.
It is not flashy.
It does not get debated on the coffee-shop radio every morning.
Yet it helps make sure that land remains something a working family can still buy, sell, mortgage, and pass along—rather than a permanent monument to someone else’s will.
That is worth protecting.
In a place where the horizon is wide and the next generation still matters, keeping the land free to move is not a technicality.
It is common sense written into the highest law of the state.

title.after: Logged In – Week In Review: June 21–27, 2026 | Shane Klakken

added: top of page News Principles Calendar About Menu Close Donate Logged In – Week In Review: June 21–27, 2026 By Shane Klakken, Montana House District 37 July 1, 2026 It’s time to get logged in to the week in review.
Next weekend is the Fourth of July, and I want to make sure you’ve got it on your calendar.

Come on out to Lewistown for the festivities, and head to the fairgrounds beginning at two o’clock, where the American Legion will conduct an opening ceremony and the Judith Mountain Players will put on a “Reenactment of the Signing of the Declaration of Independence”.
This is the 250th anniversary of this great nation, and that’s worth celebrating right here at home.
Now, to the week.

It started out Monday morning when I headed over to the Yogo Inn for a 2-day small business seminar — except I had the wrong start day on my calendar and showed up a day late thinking I was ten minutes early.
I did get to visit with a few folks, including a woman who runs a business called Wide Oak Pastures out of Georgia.
By all accounts, she gave a good presentation to those who actually had the right day written down.
From there, the week picked up considerably.
I sat in on an AI zoom meeting covering the pros and cons of artificial intelligence data centers in communities like ours.
Locally, the sentiment is pretty clear — people are concerned about the electricity draw and the water usage that come with large hyperscale AI data centers.
I hear that.
Those are legitimate concerns.
But here’s what I want folks to understand: those are technically solvable problems.
My position is that if a hyperscale AI data center is going to come to Montana, it comes on our terms — not on the industry’s terms.
Montana has a history of getting the short end of the stick when outside industry moves in fast and we’re not prepared.
We’re not going to let that happen here.
That said, let’s be clear about something.
Artificial intelligence is already here.
You’re using it right now.
Online banking?
Data center.
Your iPhone?
AI.
We already have somewhere between twelve and thirty data centers operating in the state of Montana.
The conversation we need to be having is specifically about hyperscale facilities — and we need to define that problem precisely before we start writing law around it.
My deeper concern with AI isn’t the buildings.
It’s the intelligence itself.
There are things AI may already be doing that we don’t fully understand, and we need to find out.
If it’s doing something it shouldn’t be, we rein it in.
If it’s doing something it should be doing, we set the guardrails and move forward responsibly.
That’s not anti-technology — that’s just good governance.
Legislative days ran Thursday and Friday in Helena.

I showed up a day early to attend an event sponsored by the Leadership Institute, which was a meeting that focused on pulling our caucus together after a tough primary season and getting our legislative agenda squared away heading into the general.
Thursday brought a plenary session at the Capitol with solid ethics training — what money legislators can accept, how can it be accepted, and what the law says clearly on all of it.
Good, thorough work.
We also covered wildfire funding, which is a complicated conversation involving taxing jurisdictions and who bears the cost when fires burn across different land categories.
That one will keep developing.
There was also a breakout session on Montana’s judicial system.
As I shared last week, I was at the Fergus County Courthouse with Chief Justice Cory Swanson and District Judge Heather Perry.
Cases are backlogged.
Citizens aren’t being served as efficiently as they deserve to be.
That’s a problem worth fixing, and I’m glad it’s getting attention at the legislative level.
On Saturday, we said goodbye to Bob Gacke — a friend to Lewistown and a friend to me personally.
I first heard his voice when I was out on the ridge at the ranch, cutting trees for a fuels mitigation project, and my cell phone rang.
Bob was instrumental in helping me bring a US Constitution class to Lewistown, which ultimately put me on the path to serving in House District 37.
Teaching the Constitution to adults and homeschoolers taught me something I carry with me every day: a constitutional republic only works when the people who live in it stay engaged.
Bob understood that.
Thank you, Bob.
Honored to have known you.
Finally — vote Dan Wilson for Montana Supreme Court Associate Justice this November.
He’s a constitutionally grounded judge who lets the law drive outcomes.
We need that on our Supreme Court.
Until next week, stay engaged.

title.after: Logged In – Week(s) In Review | Shane Klakken

added: top of page News Principles Calendar About Menu Close Donate Logged In – Week(s) In Review By Shane Klakken, Montana House District 37 September 23, 2026 Well, it's been a while since I've caught you up, and I've had my notes out this week just to keep it all straight, because it's been a busy stretch since September 3rd.
Back in Winifred, District 37 sat down with landowners and Fish, Wildlife and Parks to talk about our elk overpopulation problem.

If you missed it, I put a couple videos up on Facebook, TikTok, YouTube and Instagram — one on the meeting itself, and a follow-up with an idea on how to help make ranchers whole when elk tear up their crops during that unprotected stretch from June to August 15th, when there's no hunting season to thin them out.
That second video alone pulled over 9,000 social media video views, so I know this one's on a lot of your minds too.

On the 8th I made a run to Helena to pick up U.S. and Montana Constitutions for our eighth graders — a tradition I take seriously — and happened to be there the day Governor Gianforte rolled out his Fair Flat Montana Tax plan.
The next day I sat in on a Winnett City Commission meeting, working through what to charge folks with a second, unused water meter on their property.
September 10th was heavy — the commemoration of Charlie Kirk's assassination, marked here in our own way — and that evening the Fergus County Farm Bureau put on a good meeting up in Denton.

The 11th brought the 25th anniversary of September 11th, and I shared where I was that day at our memorial at Veterans Park, sandwiched between the tail end of the Montana Early Childhood Leadership Summit, where childcare struggles came up again — not just a Lewistown problem, but a statewide one.
Then came the Chokecherry Festival on the 12th — six a.m. setup, a full day of good crowds thanks to cool weather keeping folks around longer than usual.
I left my mug at a booth and didn't get it back until I swung through on my way home from Great Falls.
Small towns take care of each other that way.
The 15th was a full one: a sit-down with the CEO of American Prairie where I passed along, again, the ag community's ongoing concerns about their activity here — that hasn't changed.

Same day, the Central Montana Association of School Superintendents met at Central Feed, and that evening the Yogo hosted a presentation on I-194, the Anti-Citizens United initiative, put on by its supporters.
It was well done, but I'll say plainly: we still need a session from the folks opposed to it before anybody here makes up their mind.
Hear both sides.
On the 16th I met with the DEQ director about the old sewage lagoon situation in Winifred, and I'm getting that information back to folks there.
The 17th closed out the interim Local Government Committee meeting in Helena — watch it on legmt.gov under streaming.

We approved continued funding for the statewide public-safety radio system before it runs out in mid-2027, and we're working to bolster 911 call-center funding, too — that dollar per phone line brings in $14 to $16 million a year, and it's not enough.
We're waiting on an accurate dollar number from the 911 Advisory Council before we push for more.

We also heard testimony on short-term rentals, a plea to carve a new County 57 out of Missoula County for the Swan Valley, Seeley Lake, Greenough and Potomac areas — folks who feel a big county isn't built for rural needs, which I understand well — plus resort-area infrastructure financing for Big Sky, a pilot Grants Assistance Office with $500,000 to help Montanans navigate grant applications, and final language on a homeowners association act that, I made sure to confirm, won't touch anybody who isn't already in an HOA.

I got home on the 18th just in time to feel that little earthquake up in Great Falls — over in about a second — and I'm headed back that way today for a retirement party for an old colleague from my US Customs & Border Protection days.
Last thing: we've got an election coming.
The November election quickly approaches and I'm asking you to vote for Troy Downing to keep representing Montana’s eastern district in DC, Kurt Alme to join Senator Sheehy as our second U.S.
Senator, and Dan Wilson for associate justice on our state Supreme Court.
Don't take my word for any of it — come hear from them yourself at the harvest dinner in Lewistown on October 4th.

added: top of page News Principles Calendar About Menu Close Donate Logged In – Week In Review By Shane Klakken, Montana House District 37 March 20, 2026 This week brought a full slate of civic life, ballot news, and community events worth your attention.
Here's where things stand.
Thursday evening, the Council on Aging hosted a public meeting on data centers — their potential in Montana, and what that might mean for communities like ours.
With 180 seats capacity and word that the room could fill fast, the message was simple: show up early.
I was glad this conversation is happening.
Montanans deserve a full, honest look at what data center development offers and what it costs.
I hope we got that 360-degree view.
On the community calendar: Saturday, March 21, the Lewistown Bowhunters Banquet takes place at the Trade Center starting at 5:00 p.m.
I'll be there — first time attending — and I'm looking forward to it.
I'm a bowhunter myself, so this is very much my kind of room.
Mark Sunday, March 29 on your calendar as well.
The Lincoln–Reagan Dinner at the Yogo Inn runs from 5:00pm to completion.
Tickets are $40 at the door, and you can sponsor a table of eight for $320.
Call me at 406-217-6107 if you'd like to arrange a table.
This year's dinner matters more than usual.
Local races are contested — sheriff, county attorney, and a county commissioner seat — and at the national level, U.S.
Attorney Kurt Alme will attend as the Republican Party's pick for U.S.
Senate following Senator Daines' late departure from the race.
I don't love that the party made that call rather than voters, but that's the situation we're in.
Come learn who he is.
Come talk to him.
Talk to the local candidates too.
That's what this dinner is for.
On ballot initiatives: two are circulating right now, and both deserve your careful attention.
I-194, backed by a group called the Transparency in Elections Initiative, aims to get big dark money out of Montana politics.
Think of it as the anti–Citizens United measure for our state.
It would require that corporate political money be traceable — not banned outright, but no longer hidden.
The original version was deemed legally insufficient by Attorney General Austin Knudsen, and the Supreme Court agreed.
The language is being rewritten.
In the meantime, signatures are being gathered on the revised initiative.

Pay attention to who's asking for your signature, and know your rights: under a law Governor Gianforte signed last session, the person collecting your signature must identify themselves by name, disclose who they work for, and tell you whether they're being paid.
You also have the right to see the actual petition language.
We learned hard lessons from CI-28, the abortion initiative that passed despite some questionable signature-gathering practices.
That's why we passed these protections.
CI-132 would enshrine in the Montana Constitution that judges must be nonpartisan.
On the surface that sounds reasonable — judges should be impartial.
And once elected, yes, they absolutely should be.
But let's be honest: everybody has a bias.
Everybody leans somewhere.
Right now, judicial races are technically nonpartisan, but the money flowing into them tells a different story.
The last Supreme Court race saw the bulk of campaign dollars come from out of state.
Corey Swanson won as Chief Supreme Court Justice despite huge money campaigning against him, but it was outside money that drove that conversation, not Montanans.
I supported giving judges the option to affiliate with a party if they choose — that's freedom of association, which both our U.S. and Montana Constitutions protect.
CI-132 would take that option off the table permanently.
I think the initiative should match the reality of how these races actually work, not paper over it.
Finally, Governor Gianforte is pushing the Montana Supreme Court to expedite its review of the lawsuit against Senate Bill 542 — part of last session's “property tax reform" package.
I did not vote for that bill, and I'll tell you why: it violated Montana's single-issue requirement.
For a bill to become law it is limited to a single topic as spelled out in our 1972 Montana Constitution.
SB 542 had three, including a $92 million appropriation buried inside a tax bill.
That's not how we're supposed to do things.
The governor wants the court to move quickly on this.
We'll see how the Supreme Court responds.
My job is to keep you informed.
You can find more at ShaneKlakken.com, on Facebook and X at "Shane Klakken for Montana," on Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube.
If you want to be on the newsletter list, sign up on my website.
And if I haven't called you yet about the Lincoln–Reagan Dinner — I'm working through the list.
