title.after: Montana's Flat Tax Debate: Fair Question, Honest Answer | Shane Klakken

added: top of page News Principles Calendar About Menu Close Donate Montana's Flat Tax Debate: Fair Question, Honest Answer By Shane Klakken, Montana House District 37 August 12, 2026 If you've been following the runway into the 2027 legislative session, you've heard the term "flat tax" a lot lately.
Governor Gianforte has made it his top priority for his final session in office, and Senate leadership just requested draft bill language this week to get it moving.

Before we're all trading soundbites at the coffee shop, I want to walk through what's actually being proposed — and give it to you straight, because both the supporters and the critics have real points worth hearing.
Here's the plan in plain terms: Montana currently taxes income in two brackets — 4.7% up to $65,000 for a single filer, and 5.4% above that.
The governor wants to collapse those into one flat rate of 4.7% for everybody, regardless of income.
That's it.
It's a rate change, not a rewrite of what counts as taxable income.
"It's a tax break for the wealthy." Is that fair?
I'm not going to dodge this one, because there's a real number behind it.
Under the flat tax as proposed, income below $65,000 is already taxed at 4.7% today — that doesn't change.
The only income that gets a rate cut is income currently taxed at 5.4%, which means the dollar savings flow to people earning above that threshold.
Nobody's rate goes up.
But it's fair to say the marginal benefit concentrates at the top.
The honest defense of a flat tax isn't "everybody saves the same amount." It's a philosophical case: equal income taxed equally, regardless of how much of it there is.
A graduated system intentionally taxes success at a higher rate the more you earn.
A flat tax says a dollar is a dollar.

That's a legitimate value to hold — but it's a fairness argument, not an equal-outcome argument, and we ought to be honest about the difference when we're selling it to folks in Fergus County and Petroleum County who aren't anywhere near that $65,000 line.
"It'll kill my business." Where's that coming from?
I've had a couple of ranchers and small business owners tell me flat-out this reform worries them.
Here's what I've learned digging into it: a flat tax rate, by itself, does not touch business deductions.
Depreciation, Section 179 equipment expensing, ordinary and necessary business expenses — all of that gets subtracted before you ever calculate taxable income.
Whether the state applies one rate or two to what's left over doesn't change what you're allowed to deduct.
Where the fear comes from, I suspect, is that some flat tax proposals — nationally, and in other states — have paired a lower rate with eliminating deductions to make the math work.
That's not what's on the table in Montana right now, but it's a fair thing to watch for as the bill takes shape this session.
If you're worried, ask specifically: which deduction or credit do you think disappears?
If nobody can point to one, we're dealing with an assumption borrowed from somewhere else, not this bill.

A flat tax has real advantages — simplicity, less incentive to game the system, and it makes future tax hikes harder because lawmakers would have to raise everyone's rate at once instead of quietly targeting a bracket.
Montana still has one of the highest income tax rates in the region; Wyoming and South Dakota have none, and Idaho's flat rate sits at 5.3%.
We're competing for people and capital whether we like it or not.

But the strongest version of this reform protects ranch and small business income through depreciation and Section 179, keeps a meaningful standard deduction for lower earners, and ties any further rate cuts to revenue triggers rather than promises.
That's the version worth backing.
As this bill takes shape, I'll be watching closely to make sure it's the flat tax that actually gets built — not just the one being pitched at podiums.
As always, I want to hear from you.
Reach out through ShaneKlakken.com or find me on social media.

title.after: Red Tape Is Killing Range Improvements — And Congress Already Said Fix It | Shane Klakken

added: top of page News Principles Calendar About Menu Close Donate Red Tape Is Killing Range Improvements — And Congress Already Said Fix It By Shane Klakken, Montana House District 37 July 30, 2026 Picture this: a rancher in central Montana wants to put in a stock water pipeline on his BLM allotment.
It’s a practical improvement — helps distribute cattle across the range, takes pressure off the creek, improves the land.
His grandfather probably built something similar with a shovel and a mule.
Today?
He calls the local BLM field office and gets told they’re years out from completing the environmental analysis required to approve it.
Years.
For a water pipeline.
This isn’t an isolated story.
It’s happening across the West, and the Montana Natural Resource Coalition of Counties put it in writing to federal officials in May of this year.

In a formal comment letter to BLM regarding National Environmental Policy Act procedures, MtNRC laid out the problem clearly: domestic livestock producers are being blocked from installing rangeland improvements not because anyone decided those improvements were bad, but because the federal environmental review bureaucracy simply can’t keep up.
Fences, wells, water pipelines, reservoirs, stock tanks, vegetation treatments — these are what the law calls rangeland improvements .
They’ve been prioritized by Congress for decades.
Under the Public Rangeland Improvement Act of 1978, the Secretary of Interior is directed to manage public rangelands with an intensive maintenance, management, and improvement program.
The Taylor Grazing Act itself explicitly authorizes fences, wells, and reservoirs on grazing districts.
FLPMA backs it up further.
Congress didn’t stutter.
These improvements are supposed to happen.
They benefit livestock, wildlife, and the long-term health of the range.
But the federal NEPA process — the environmental review framework — has become a wall between ranchers and the improvements their permits are supposed to allow.
The fix is straightforward, and BLM already uses it for other activities: a Categorical Exclusion, or CE.
A CE is a determination that a category of actions normally doesn’t have significant environmental impact, so it doesn’t require a full Environmental Assessment or Environmental Impact Statement.
BLM already issues CEs for certain forestry projects.
The MtNRC is asking: why not for rangeland improvements?
In fact, on March 31, 2026, the USDA and DOI signed a joint Memorandum of Understanding specifically directed at advancing grazing on Forest Service and BLM lands.
That MOU explicitly calls for using categorical exclusions as a tool to create “quicker pathways to opportunities for permittees” — including rangeland improvements.
Six days later, BLM issued a proposed revision of its NEPA implementing procedures.
But the revision only addressed forestry CEs.
Rangeland improvements weren’t touched.
The MtNRC called that out directly.
If the federal government just signed an MOU pledging to use CEs to advance grazing, and then issued a regulatory revision that ignored rangeland improvements entirely, something is wrong.
Either the left hand doesn’t know what the right hand is doing, or the commitment to ranchers isn’t as serious as the press release made it sound.

The coalition’s ask is specific: revise 516 DM 1 Appendix 2, section 11.9(D) to add a CE covering rangeland improvements — fences, wells, pipelines, reservoirs, stock tanks, vegetation treatments — when they’re consistent with an approved grazing permit or lease.
The criteria are already defined in statute and BLM policy.
This isn’t creating new law.
It’s applying existing law the way Congress intended.
Here in Fergus County, we understand what it means when infrastructure doesn’t get built.
A fence that doesn’t get fixed means cattle in the wrong pasture.
A water source that doesn’t get developed means overgrazing around the one creek that’s left.
These are real consequences for real families running real cattle on real land.
The environmental review process was never supposed to be a roadblock to practical range management.
It was supposed to be a safeguard against genuinely harmful projects — not a bureaucratic bottleneck that treats a stock tank like an industrial facility.
Congress has been clear about its priorities for public rangelands since 1934.
The improvements that keep this industry alive should not require years of federal paperwork.
BLM needs to catch up to its own stated commitments and give ranchers the tools the law has always intended them to have.

title.after: Save Our Kids…Save Our Country | Shane Klakken

added: top of page News Principles Calendar About Menu Close Donate Save Our Kids…Save Our Country By Shane Klakken, Montana House District 37 July 15, 2026 A few weeks ago I watched a piece of video that stuck with me for days.
A young man on the ground, in trouble, calling out for help, and the officers standing over him seemed frozen, unsure whether to act.
Commentators picked it apart for hours and never landed on a real answer.
But if you've spent any time around young folks lately, in a classroom, a church basement, or a 4-H barn, you already have a pretty good idea what's going on.
Those officers weren't unusual.
They're a symptom.

I've spent the last several years teaching Constitution classes and Biblical Citizenship courses right here in Lewistown, and I've had a front row seat to how a whole generation is being taught to see the world.
It isn't through algebra or American history the way we learned it.
It's through a lens that sorts every person, every event, and every institution into one of two buckets: oppressor or oppressed.
Once you're taught to see the world that way, right and wrong stop mattering as much as which bucket you or the other fellow falls into.
That's not an accident, and it isn't confined to the coasts.
It's in the textbooks, it's in the museum placards, it's in the algorithm feeding a fourteen-year-old's phone at midnight.
A kid can tell you three things happened in history and precious little else, but he can tell you exactly who was the villain in each one.
We used to raise kids on personal responsibility, hard work, and the idea that your word and your handshake meant something.
Somewhere along the way, a lot of us handed that job off to the schools, the screens, and the culture, and we assumed it would turn out fine because it turned out fine for us.
It didn't occur to us that raising a kid today is a different job entirely than the one our folks had.
I don't say any of this to scold young people.
I say it because we, the parents and grandparents, are the ones who let the job slide.
We were raised by a generation that didn't need to explain personal responsibility out loud, because the whole culture around us reinforced it.
Church, school, the co-op, the ballfield, all of it pointed the same direction.
That's not true anymore, and pretending otherwise is how we keep losing ground.

Here in central Montana we still have something worth protecting: a culture where a handshake counts, where a kid learns to work by actually working, and where right and wrong aren't up for renegotiation depending on who's involved.
But we can't assume that gets passed down automatically anymore.
It has to be taught on purpose, out loud, at the kitchen table and in the classroom, the same deliberate way you'd teach a kid to drive a tractor or throw a rope.

That's exactly why I keep showing up to teach these citizenship courses, and why I think every parent and grandparent in Fergus County ought to be having these conversations with the kids in their life, not waiting for someone else to do it.
The fix isn't complicated, even if it isn't easy.
Teach gratitude instead of grievance.
Teach that dignity comes from carrying your own weight, not from which group you belong to.
Teach forgiveness over score-settling, and love of country instead of contempt for it.
None of that requires a new law out of Helena or Washington.
It requires us to stop assuming somebody else is handling it.
Save our kids, and we save this way of life we've built out here.
That work starts at home, and it starts now.

title.after: The Grazing System Was Built for Ranchers — Let’s Make Sure It Stays That Way | Shane Klakken

added: top of page News Principles Calendar About Menu Close Donate The Grazing System Was Built for Ranchers — Let’s Make Sure It Stays That Way By Shane Klakken, Montana House District 37 August 5, 2026 There’s a principle embedded in the Taylor Grazing Act that doesn’t get talked about enough.
When Congress created the federal grazing district system in 1934, one of its explicit goals was to provide “the greatest extent of self-government to local stockmen.” Not Washington bureaucrats.
Not environmental organizations based in New York or San Francisco.
Local stockmen.

That principle matters today as much as it did ninety years ago, and it’s at the heart of what the Montana Natural Resource Coalition of Counties has been pressing BLM to honor in its latest round of regulatory revisions.

The MtNRC’s July comment letter to BLM Director Steve Pierce covered several specific regulatory proposals, and it’s worth walking through what the coalition supported — and where it raised concerns — because the details affect every permittee grazing on public land in central Montana.
First, the good news.
The MtNRC supports the proposed revision removing special use permitting requirements for indigenous animals .
The coalition notes, correctly, that there’s no statutory basis for that permitting requirement to begin with.
The TGA preference right system was built for people engaged in the livestock industry — farmers and stockmen — not as a vehicle for wildlife management schemes layered on top of grazing allotments.
Getting rid of a permit requirement that has no legal foundation is a straightforward win.
The coalition also strongly supports the overall direction of giving permittees greater flexibility to respond in real time to range conditions — weather, drought, available forage.
Anyone who has run cattle in central Montana knows that the range doesn’t follow a schedule.
A permit system rigid enough that a rancher can’t move cattle when conditions change isn’t managing land.
It’s managing paperwork.
The MtNRC is right to push for flexibility, and BLM should be listening.
Now the concern.
The proposed revision to the Office of Hearings and Appeals process would render a BLM decision inoperative — essentially suspended — as soon as it’s appealed.
At first glance that might sound like a protection for permittees.
But think through the implications.

If a rancher with a long-standing permit in good standing — meeting all rangeland health standards, paying his fees, doing everything right — gets his renewal approved, and someone files an appeal just to delay the process, that permittee couldn’t turn out on the range while the appeal grinds through the system.
That’s not protection.
That’s a new weapon for obstruction.
The MtNRC is asking BLM to think this through more carefully.
The coalition’s position is reasonable: an appeal shouldn’t automatically stay a decision when a preference right holder is in good standing and meeting their obligations.
There should be safeguards to prevent the appeals process from being weaponized against ranchers who’ve done nothing wrong.

Stepping back, what connects all of these issues — the TGA district mapping fight, the NEPA categorical exclusion fight, the permit flexibility and appeals process concerns — is a single underlying question: Who is the federal grazing system actually for?
The law gives a clear answer.
The Taylor Grazing Act was enacted to stabilize the livestock industry and the farming communities that depend on it.
FLPMA preserved those priorities.
PRIA reinforced them.
Montana went further than any other state by enacting the Montana Grass Conservation Act, creating state-level grazing district boards seated by stockmen to administer these lands locally.
Fergus County and Petroleum County exists because of ranching and farming.
So does most of central Montana.
Our customs, our economy, our communities — they’re built around the land and the livestock industry that depends on it.

When federal regulations make it harder to build a water pipeline, harder to see your allotment’s legal protections on a map, harder to get a permit renewed without an opponent grinding you down through appeals — those aren’t abstract policy problems.
They hit families and operations that have been on this land for generations.
The Montana Natural Resource Coalition of Counties is doing the work of making sure the federal government honors what the law already says.
That’s worth paying attention to.
And it’s worth showing up to support.
The grazing system was built for ranchers.
Let’s make sure Washington remembers that.

title.after: We're a Republic — And That's Not a Technicality | Shane Klakken

added: top of page News Principles Calendar About Menu Close Donate We're a Republic — And That's Not a Technicality By Shane Klakken, Montana House District 37 August 19, 2026 Remember these names: Dan Wilson, Kurt Alme and Troy Downing.

I've been teaching Constitution classes in Lewistown for a while now, and one thing I've noticed is that a lot of people use words like "democracy," "republic," and "federalism" interchangeably — as if they all mean the same thing.
They don't.
And the differences aren't just academic.
They matter every time someone in Washington or Helena tries to do something to you that they have no business doing.
Let's start with the one I get asked about most: What's the difference between a republic and a democracy?
The short answer is that in a pure democracy, the majority rules — period.
Whatever 51% wants, 51% gets.
The Founders had studied history carefully enough to know that never ends well.
James Madison laid it out plainly in Federalist No.

10: pure democracies have historically been "spectacles of turbulence and contention," incompatible with personal security and property rights, "as short in their lives as they have been violent in their deaths." John Adams was blunter still: "Democracy never lasts long.

It soon wastes, exhausts and murders itself." That's why they built us a republic instead — one where power derives from the people but is exercised by elected representatives operating under a fixed set of rules.
Representation, separation of powers, checks and balances, an independent judiciary, and explicit protections for minority rights.
The whole point was to slow things down, filter out mob passions, and protect individuals from being steamrolled by a temporary majority.
When Benjamin Franklin walked out of the Constitutional Convention and someone asked what they'd produced, he said: "A republic, if you can keep it." That "if" was doing a lot of work.
Now, where does federalism fit?
Federalism is the architecture — the blueprint for how power is divided between the federal government and the states.
The national government handles defense, foreign policy, currency, and interstate matters.
States handle education, local law enforcement, infrastructure, and the things closest to home.
Each level has constitutionally protected powers that the other can't just swipe away.
That's not an accident.
Federalism is a check on centralized power, and it's one of the main reasons Montana gets to be Montana instead of just a distant province of Washington, D.C.
Here in central Montana, we feel the tension between those two levels of government more than most.

When the federal government tells ranchers how to manage land their families have worked for generations, or mandates policies from a desk in D.C. that make no practical sense in Central Montana, that's federalism breaking down.

The Constitution didn't grant Washington unlimited authority — it granted specific, enumerated powers in Article I Section 8 of the US Constitution and left everything else to the states and to the people in the Tenth Amendment of the Bill of Rights.
There's one more concept worth understanding, and it comes up more than you might think: the “Fiction of the Law”.
A legal fiction is when the law deliberately treats something as true — even when everyone knows it isn't — in order to reach a practical result.
The most familiar example is corporate personhood: a corporation isn't a human being, but the law treats it as a "person" so it can own property, sign contracts, and be sued.
That's useful.
Legal fictions started in Roman law, were adopted into English common law, and exist today because sometimes applying rigid rules to complex reality produces unjust results.
But here's where I'd caution folks to pay attention: legal fictions can be used to expand power, not just achieve fairness.
When courts or agencies treat something as legally true that isn't factually true, it changes what they can do to you.
Jurisdictions get extended.
Rules get stretched.
Remedies get invented.
Jeremy Bentham, the English legal philosopher, called legal fictions "willful falsehoods" used by judges to quietly usurp legislative authority.
That critique still has teeth today.
“Fiction of the Law” has even stronger power in the false belief of the “separation of church and state”.
The reason I teach these things — and why I keep writing about them here — is simple.
A self-governing people can only hold their government accountable if they understand how it actually works.
Republic, federalism, legal fiction — these aren't words for lawyers and textbooks.
They're the vocabulary of self-defense for a free citizenry.
If you don't know the rules of the game, you can't call a foul when one gets committed against you.
Founding Father John Jay put it this way: “Every member of the State ought diligently to read and study the constitution of his country, and teach the rising generation to be free.
By knowing their rights, they will sooner perceive when they are violated, and be better prepared to defend and assert them.” Franklin said we have a republic, if we can keep it.
Out here in central Montana, I think we still want to keep it.
That starts with understanding what it is.
Reminder: Dan Wilson, Kurt Alme and Troy Downing.

title.after: Why Montana Can't Afford Amy Eddy on the Supreme Court | Shane Klakken

added: top of page News Principles Calendar About Menu Close Donate Why Montana Can't Afford Amy Eddy on the Supreme Court By Shane Klakken, Montana House District 37 October 7, 2026 I don't often weigh in on judicial races.
They're supposed to be non-partisan, but we all know they are not at all “non-partisan”.
All you have to do is take a look at the donor list of each candidate and investigate the donors themselves.

The race between Judge Dan Wilson and Judge Amy Eddy for the Montana Supreme Court is the most important thing on your ballot this fall — more important, frankly, than most of the legislative races people will spend their time arguing about.
Here's why: the Supreme Court has become the branch that overrules the other two.
When the Legislature passes a law — say, HB121, which simply keeps men out of women's bathrooms — it's the courts that decide whether that law survives.
Progressive judges around this state know it, too.
They can block a law they don't like, confident the Supreme Court has their back.
That's not how a republic is supposed to work, and it's exactly why this race matters more than the "non-partisan" label lets on.
Let's start with the primary.
Judge Eddy beat Judge Wilson by about 7,600 votes out of well over 270,000 cast.

That's close, and it should worry every conservative in this state, because Eddy has resources behind her that Wilson doesn't — the Montana Trial Lawyers Association chief among them, along with a long list of left-wing nonprofits I'll get to in a minute.
Judge Dan Wilson is the real deal.
Thirty-two years in the law — private practice, Justice of the Peace, District Court Judge — and he's won every office he's held at the ballot box, not by appointment.
His judicial philosophy is about as plain as it gets: apply the Constitution and the law as written, according to their original meaning, without inventing new law from the bench.
During COVID, when the Bullock administration tried to strong-arm five Flathead businesses over mask mandates, Wilson didn't cave the way so many did.
He ruled that the harm to those businesses and their employees had to be weighed too.
That's a judge who understands limited government isn't just a slogan.
Amy Eddy is a different story entirely.
She wasn't elected to the bench first — she was appointed by Democratic Governor Steve Bullock, and has run as an incumbent ever since.
Her campaign says she'll be "fair, impartial, and independent." Look at who's actually behind her and judge for yourself.

Every major endorser listed on her own website is a sitting or former liberal justice, or a hard-left advocacy group: Montana Conservation Voters (funded almost entirely by out-of-state foundation money, including a Seattle foundation bankrolled by a foreign billionaire), the public employee unions, Montana NOW, and groups pushing "reproductive rights" — which in plain English means abortion on demand.
She's a past president of the Montana Trial Lawyers Association, the same outfit quietly bankrolling her campaign while it goes unmentioned on her own website.
As a lawyer, Eddy argued the Montana Supreme Court had no choice but to seize control of emissions regulation statewide.
When the Court said no, she said the Court got it wrong.
That's not a woman who keeps politics out of the courtroom — that's radical environmentalism dressed up as legal argument, and it's a direct threat to how Montanans use their own land and resources.
I'll say this plainly: watch out for the dirty tricks.

A mailer went out in Billings calling Wilson "dangerous" for a plea deal from 2017-18, conveniently leaving out that the defendant got ten years, violated parole, and is sitting in Deer Lodge right now.
That mailer traces back to Eddy-aligned groups.
When your opponent's supporters have to lie about your record two days before you campaign in a city, that tells you something about how badly they need to change the subject.
Montanans, don't vote for a candidate just because of the letter — or in this case, the black robe — next to their name.
Look at who's funding them and what they actually believe.
Dan Wilson has spent thirty-two years earning the public's trust the honest way.
Amy Eddy has spent her career serving the interests of trial lawyers, radical environmentalists, and the abortion lobby.
This November, vote for the Constitution.
Vote Dan Wilson.

title.after: Your Grazing Rights Are Being Erased — Not by Law, But by Omission | Shane Klakken

added: top of page News Principles Calendar About Menu Close Donate Your Grazing Rights Are Being Erased — Not by Law, But by Omission By Shane Klakken, Montana House District 37 July 22, 2026 If you’ve ever had a map that left out your property line, you know the trouble that causes.
Now imagine that happening to millions of acres of grazing land across the West — not by accident, but through decades of administrative neglect.

That’s exactly what the Montana Natural Resource Coalition of Counties has been fighting to correct, and it matters directly to every ranching family in Fergus County, Petroleum County, and across central Montana.
Here’s the issue in plain terms.
The Taylor Grazing Act of 1934 created what are called TGA Grazing Districts — federally reserved lands set apart specifically for domestic livestock grazing.
These aren’t just lines on a map.
They carry real legal weight.
Under the TGA, the Secretary of Interior is required by law to adequately safeguard grazing privileges on these lands.
That’s not a suggestion.
That’s a statutory obligation.

But here’s the problem: BLM Resource Management Plans across Montana — the very documents that guide how federal land is managed — don’t include the maps or adequate descriptions of these TGA reserved districts.
They’ve been quietly left out.
Why does that matter?

Because when those districts don’t appear in planning documents, it becomes easier for environmental groups and federal administrators to treat grazing lands as if they’re available for repurposing — rewilding projects, biodiversity corridors, habitat conservation plans.
The legal foundation for grazing gets eroded, not through Congress changing the law, but through bureaucrats and activists simply pretending the maps don’t exist.
The MtNRC — which represents Fergus County and several other Montana counties — submitted formal comments to BLM Director Steve Pierce earlier this month making exactly this argument.
The coalition is pushing BLM to incorporate the official National TGA district dataset directly into federal regulations at 43 CFR 4100.

They’re also calling on BLM to build an interactive public web map on blm.gov showing full TGA district layers, allotment overlays, and classifications across all ten western states where these districts exist.
Montana is already ahead of the curve here.

Through the Montana Grass Conservation Commission and the State Library, Montana has digitally mapped its TGA grazing districts in a user-friendly viewer that layers state lands, BLM lands, Forest Service, and Wildlife Refuges all together.
BLM should be doing this nationally.
Instead, they’ve left a void that their opponents have been more than happy to fill with their own narrative.
The legal case for these districts is rock solid.

The Taylor Grazing Act established them as formal federal reservations — not temporary withdrawals, but lands set aside for a specific designated public purpose: protecting the range, providing orderly use by farmers and stockmen, and stabilizing the livestock industry.
When Congress passed the Federal Land Policy and Management Act in 1976, it explicitly left the TGA provisions intact.
A 2003 Solicitor’s clarification confirmed it plainly — Congress did not repeal or modify the grazing provisions of the TGA when it enacted FLPMA.
The classifications, boundaries, and mission remain legally sound.
Montana has an additional layer of protection that no other state can claim.
In 1939, Montana enacted the Montana Grass Conservation Act, establishing State Grazing Districts that work in cooperation with the federal system.
Local grazing district boards — seated by actual stockmen — were put in charge of administering these lands to protect the range and stabilize the livestock industry.
That’s local self-government at its best, exactly what these districts were designed to produce.
The bottom line is this: your grazing allotment didn’t appear out of thin air.
It rests on nearly a century of federal law, Montana statute, and administrative precedent.
But legal rights that aren’t visible on official maps are rights that can be chipped away — one planning document, one environmental review, one federal administrator at a time.
The MtNRC is doing the right thing by demanding BLM put these maps back where they belong — in black and white, in the official record, for all to see.
Ranching built this county.
The law is on your side.
But you have to make sure the government is forced to acknowledge it.

The Georgia General Assembly started the first day of the 2026 legislative session on Monday, January 12, 2026.
The House of Representatives along with the Senate, make up our state lawmaking body called the Georgia General Assembly.
MONDAY, January 12th The House celebrated the first day with a special performance by Audrey Kittila - Miss Georgia 2025.
Kittila delivered a violin rendition of “ Georgia on My Mind ”.
The performance was a great way to begin session and set the tone before the House took up the business for the day.
The House voted to adopt the Adjournment Resolution House Resolution 998 , establishing the 40-day legislative calendar for 2026 legislative session.
Georgia’s Constitution requires the Georgia General Assembly to convene for 40 non-consecutive legislative days.
The final day of this year’s session (known as “Sine Die”) is scheduled for Thursday, April 2, 2026.
TUESDAY Several bills received first readers on the House floor.
We also recognized Delta Sigma Theta Sorority, Inc., for 113 Years of Service and recognized January 13, 2026, as Founders Day.
The Sorority's first public act was its participation in the historic 1913 Women's Suffrage March in Washington, D.C., underscoring its legacy of civic engagement and social action.
WEDNESDAY Members of the General Assembly attended the Georgia Chamber of Commerce’s annual Eggs & Issues breakfast where Governor Kemp gave a preview of some of his priorities for the year.
THURSDAY A joint session of the House & Senate gathered in the House Chamber to hear Governor Kemp deliver his final State of the State Address .
We were also joined by the Justices of the Supreme Court & the Judges of the Court of Appeals.

Governor Kemp’s final address centered on lowering the cost of living for Georgians prioritizing education workforce training school safety strengthening retirement security for law enforcement intensifying efforts to combat human trafficking gang-related crime across Georgia.

VERDA COLVIN - Justice of the Georgia Supreme Court First African American woman to be named to either court by a Republican Governor FRIDAY At the Capitol, a celebration of service was held to honor the life and legacy of Dr.
Martin Luther King, Jr.
His legacy challenges all elected officials to lead with compassion and unity to ensure that our work at the Capitol continues to serve every Georgian.
Also, on Friday - along with union members, elected officials and others, I attended the Atlanta-North Georgia Labor Council annual Dr.
Martin Luther King, Jr.
Prayer Breakfast before the House gaveled in for session.
My colleagues and I will return to the Capitol on Tuesday, Jan.
20, to begin work on one of the most important responsibilities of this session -- the state budget.
During this “budget week,” we will hear directly from Governor Kemp and state agency leaders as they present their budget requests to the joint House and Senate Appropriations Committees.
The General Assembly will return on Monday, January 26, for Legislative Day 6.
I invite you to attend the legislative session and the committee meetings in person -or- watch the House live streams at https://www.legis.ga.gov/schedule/house .

Committees: Appropriations Health Judiciary Juvenile (Secretary) Transportation Ways & Means House Democratic Caucus (Deputy Whip) Women Caucus(Secretary) As your State Representative, I work on issues important to you, your family, our community and the state of Georgia.
I can author, sponsor, and vote on bills that may become state laws.
I will continue to work on behalf of our community and serve the needs of my constituents.

added: Skip to content Home About Issues Get Involved Home About Issues Get Involved Donate Donate Issues Categories Affordability AI and Data Centers Education Environment & Public Lands Healthcare Search Recent Posts A Neighbor, Not a Career Politician Endorsed by Planned Parenthood Advocates of Montana Three Times in Five Years, Montana Kept the Right to Bargain A Neighbor, Not a Career Politician Your ballot arrives this week.
Before you open it, here is what I would like you to know.
What I did this year I have lived in the Heights for more than twenty-five years.
This year I knocked on [FILL: door count] doors here.
Most of them belonged to people who will not vote for me.
I knocked anyway, because that is the job.
Every door I missed got a postcard in my handwriting saying I came by and I would still like to hear what is on their mind.
Some people wrote back.
A few invited me for coffee.
One or two argued with me for half an hour on their own front step and then shook my hand.
That is a neighborhood.
It is the thing worth having, and we still have it.
What I heard Property taxes that keep climbing, and relief that came with a form some people never found.
A school where the bullying is not getting handled, and a parent who called and emailed and asked a specific question about their own child and never got an answer.
A power bill people are watching nervously while a company from out of state asks for thousands of megawatts, with the contract blacked out and the decisions moved to Helena.
A clinic too far away, and a wait too long.
A promise to a retired teacher that somebody in Helena would like to quietly forget.
An elderly neighbor going hungry.
A disabled worker, “laid off” and overlooked on new applications.
None of that is a Republican problem or a Democratic problem.
It is a Heights problem.
And all of it has solutions.
Why me I fix things for a living.
I have run a small business here since 2001, which means twenty-five years of making payroll, keeping promises that cost money, and getting told no on a Tuesday.
I serve on a disability-led board where the people affected direct the work, and where I am regularly the least expert person in the room.
That has been good for me.
I am working with the Heights Business Association to build a TIF district, so this part of town stops getting skipped when the money gets handed out.
None of that is a political résumé.
It is the reason I think I can do this job.
What the job actually is I will not promise you outcomes.
One legislator is one vote out of a hundred, and anyone telling you otherwise at your door is hoping you will not check.
What I will promise is the part that is entirely mine to give.
I will listen first.
I will show up.
I will tell you when I disagree with you, at your door, to your face, the way I have all year.
Solving one person’s problem is a good day.
Figuring out what keeps causing it and fixing that is a better one.
That is the whole reason I want this job.
Either way Whether or not you vote for me, I will still be your neighbor on November 4, and you will still be my constituent.
That does not change based on how you fill out a ballot.
Government belongs to us.
We reclaim it when we show up.
Your ballot is in the mail.
Please fill it out, sign the envelope, and send it back.

removed: Skip to content Home About Issues Get Involved Home About Issues Get Involved Donate Donate Issues Categories Affordability AI and Data Centers Education Environment & Public Lands Healthcare Search Recent Posts Endorsed by Planned Parenthood Advocates of Montana Three Times in Five Years, Montana Kept the Right to Bargain Endorsed by Western Native Voice Action Fund Go Check Your Homestead Enrollment A neighbor in the Heights told me this summer that property taxes seem to change every year, but even with rebates, she still pays more every time.
Some version of that has come up at more doors than anything else I have heard this year.
So I went and read what the Legislature actually did about property taxes last session.
Two things happened… 1.
Created a special rate for data centers The Legislature cut property taxes for data centers.
It created a new tax class for them, set a lower rate, and wrote it into the code.
Nobody had to go find out about it.
Nobody had to fill anything out.
It simply applied.
Lowered property taxes… for those who know how to get it The Legislature also cut property taxes for homeowners, through the homestead reduced rate on primary residences.
That relief is real, and for most Montana homeowners it lowered the bill.
It arrived differently, though.
To get it, a homeowner had to know it existed, find their property’s 17-digit geocode, and file an application by a deadline.
Most people were enrolled automatically, and that happened only because they had already applied for the 2025 rebate, which was its own form with its own window.
Anyone outside that group had to go get it themselves.
And this spring, the state extended the deadline by nearly three weeks because so many people filed at the last minute that the online portal ran into intermittent technical problems.
That extension was the right call.
It is also the whole point.
One kind of relief was written into the code and applied on its own.
The other came with a form, a deadline, and a way to fall through.
A person who misses a form loses the money just as completely as a person who was never offered anything.
The bill on the counter looks the same either way.
Enroll for the Homestead reduced rate Here is why I am writing this in August instead of next February.
The enrollment window for the 2027 tax year is open right now.
It opened May 4 and it runs through March 1, 2027.
If your house is already enrolled, you keep the reduced rate and there is nothing for you to do.
It stays with the property until something actually changes, like a sale or a move.
If it is not enrolled, you can fix that today at homestead.mt.gov .
Check it even if you are certain.
It takes about a minute.
You will need your property’s geocode, which you can look up through the Montana Cadastral site, and the state’s verification tool will tell you where you stand.
If it turns out you are not enrolled, the Department of Revenue call center at 406-444-6900 can help, and so can the local field office.
What I will advocate for in Helena Relief that arrives on its own.
If the state decides a primary residence should be taxed at a lower rate, the state already has the information to apply it.
Montana knows who owns the house and who lives in it.
Making enrollment automatic and permanent, so a homeowner keeps the rate until something actually changes, is a straightforward fix and I will vote for it.
A circuit breaker for fixed incomes.
Relief that scales to what a household can actually pay, so a retired couple in a house they paid off in 1994 never loses it to a tax bill.
This is the most direct protection available and Montana should have a stronger version of it.
Large industrial property paying its own way.
That includes the projects asking for thousands of megawatts.
Welcome the jobs, make them pay their own way, and let the people who live nearby have a say before anyone breaks ground.
A homeowner in the Heights should not need a tax attorney to get what the Legislature already voted to give them.
Before you close this tab Go check. homestead.mt.gov .
About a minute.
I would rather you get the money than agree with me about anything.

added: alt://instagram.fsdv2-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t39.30808-6/698939189_1369571168328892_6271675812844713660_n.jpg|Redistricting is one of those issues people often consider “inside baseball” until they realize it shapes almost everything else. Who gets heard. Whose communities stay intact. Whose votes carry power. And ultimately… who government believes it is accountable to. For the third time since 2021, the majority party in the Georgia General Assembly will be redrawing district lines now that Governor Kemp has called for a special session beginning June 17th. The maps drawn in this process will not just shape elections. They will shape political power, public policy, and representation for years to come. This moment is another reminder that democracy is not guaranteed by tradition alone. It depends on participation, vigilance, and the courage to stay engaged even when the process feels frustrating or predetermined. And, it requires a willingness to tell the truth about what is happening in plain sight. Langston Hughes once wrote: “O, yes, I say it plain, America never was America to me, And yet I swear this oath—America will be!” That tension — between what this country has been and what it has the capacity to become — is part of the unfolding American story. Georgia has always stood at the center of the struggle for representation, voice, and democracy. And once again, we are being reminded that fair representation does not defend itself. People, pay attention. Ask questions. Speak up. And know that I’ll be fighting for fair representation and our voting rights under the Gold Dome. Because the map is never neutral. And it is never just a map.

alt://instagram.fsdv2-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t39.30808-6/727864803_1399445155341493_4782010524670662717_n.jpg|Juneteenth reminds us that freedom is not just a moment in history but a responsibility we carry forward.

alt://instagram.fsdv2-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t39.30808-6/728664217_1401602785125730_5328628331734526883_n.jpg|Back at the Capitol and in committee meetings early this Monday morning. One of the most important pieces of legislation passed and signed into law this year is the Georgia Early Literacy Act of 2026, which will place literacy coaches in K-3 schools across our state. As a member of the Senate Education & Youth Committee, I can’t overstate how important the work we’ve done on literacy over the last three years has been. Today, only about 30% of Georgia third graders are reading at grade level. We can do better than that. And we will. Because when a child learns to read, they gain the foundation to learn, grow, and succeed in every subject that follows. Every child deserves that chance.

alt://instagram.fsdv2-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t39.30808-6/729069127_1402389708380371_4739887556392488066_n.jpg|More explanation on why I voted NO on these tax bills which swaps property tax relief for a new sales tax.

alt://instagram.fsdv2-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t39.30808-6/729414176_1401118195174189_8642219699021418361_n.jpg|Today, I’m grateful for the fathers, grandfathers, stepfathers, mentors, and father figures who show up with love, wisdom, patience, and strength. The ones who guide, encourage, protect, and help shape who we become. To those celebrating, remembering, missing someone, or carrying on their legacy—wishing you peace, love, and meaningful moments today. Happy Father’s Day.

alt://instagram.fsdv2-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t51.71878-15/705451056_1048815681139964_3171737461591848021_n.jpg|Too many hardworking Georgia families are doing everything right and still finding it difficult to keep up with rising costs. That’s why affordability remains one of my top priorities. From conversations at the Capitol to ongoing work with colleagues across state government, I remain focused on solutions that help families afford housing, access quality healthcare, support their children, and build financial stability for the future. Public service is about improving everyday life for the people we represent. I’ll continue fighting for policies that put working families first and ensure every Georgian has the opportunity to thrive—not just get by. Thank you for allowing me to be your voice under the Gold Dome. Together, we will keep moving Georgia forward. #SonyaSays #Sonya4Ga

alt://instagram.fsdv2-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t51.82787-15/683483692_18105941546312458_6041532980430484482_n.jpg|For weeks now, I’ve been feeling a mix of emotions leading up to my son’s high school graduation. Pride. Gratitude. Nostalgia. Excitement. And if I’m being perfectly honest… a little (sometimes a lot of) sadness too. This is my middle child, my second son, so this is not my first time watching one of my children graduate from high school. And somehow, that makes the passage of time feel even more real. You would think the second time around makes it easier…but in many ways, you become even more aware of how quickly childhood gives way to adulthood. I mean one moment you are packing lunches, fussing about missing assignments and messy rooms, and helping with homework. Then suddenly, you are watching them prepare to step into adulthood with their own voice, their own dreams, and their own path ahead. I am so incredibly proud of the young man my son has become — thoughtful, resilient, kind, curious, and grounded in the values that matter most. This past weekend was about his accomplishment but it was also about possibility, About one chapter closing and another beginning as he heads off to college — a journey that will bring new lessons, new growth, and new opportunities just waiting to be discovered. To Nathaniel: never lose sight of who you are. Carry your integrity with you. Treat people well. Stay open to learning. And know that no matter how big this world gets, there will always be a place where you are loved, supported, and cheered on unconditionally. What a gift it is to be your mother. 🎓❤️

alt://instagram.fsdv2-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t51.82787-15/696261565_18105000680312458_79262261711059663_n.jpg|To all of the amazing mothers across Georgia — Happy Mother’s Day! 💐 Today, we celebrate the strength, love, sacrifice, and wisdom that great mothers bring to our families, communities, and future generations every single day. Your impact is truly immeasurable, and Georgia is stronger because of you. Thank you for all that you do and all that you are. Wishing you a beautiful day filled with the love you so deeply deserve. ❤️ Tag a Mother! #HappyMothersDay #GeorgiaMoms #MothersDay #CelebrateMothers #GeorgiaFamilies

alt://instagram.fsdv2-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t51.82787-15/702982607_18105969650312458_7704255354311971770_n.jpg|Tomorrow is Election Day, and your voice matters more than ever. As your State Senator, I want to encourage every eligible voter to make a plan, know your polling location, and understand your rights before heading to the polls. In Georgia - a place with so much to offer and a history of setting powerful examples for the rest of the country - we can and must do better. I am committed to finding real solutions to the problems we face. Thank you for trusting me to be your voice under the Gold Dome! Voters can use several forms of acceptable ID, including a Georgia driver’s license, state ID card, U.S. passport, military ID, tribal ID, or voter identification card. Don’t let confusion or misinformation stop you from participating in our democracy! Voting is more than a right — it’s a responsibility and an opportunity to shape the future of our communities, our families, and the next generation. Educate yourself, encourage someone else to vote, and make your voice heard tomorrow. 🗳️🇺🇸 #Vote #GeorgiaVotes #UseYourVoice #Democracy #Sonya4GA

alt://instagram.fsdv2-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t51.82787-15/703633314_18106194053312458_4116125814918551635_n.jpg|Thank you, District 39. The work continues— I am focused, committed, and rooted in the needs of our community!!! ✔️🩵 #SonyaSays #Sonya4Ga #ThankYou #Community #District39

alt://instagram.fsdv2-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t51.82787-15/708088294_18107057414312458_5967760545517148167_n.jpg|May has been nothing short of eventful — filled with conversations, community, advocacy, and action. But through every meeting, event, and challenge, one thing remains the same: my dedication to serving my state. Being your senator is a responsibility I never take lightly, and I’m committed to continuing the work that moves our communities forward every single day. Thank you for trusting me to lead, listen, and fight for what matters most. #SonyaSays

alt://instagram.fsdv2-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t51.82787-15/714871101_18108118709312458_5629928560102886075_n.heic|The last couple of days have given me a chance to reflect on something I’ve come to appreciate throughout my time in public service: Georgia’s success is built through partnership. I’m here at the Georgia Chamber’s Spring Meeting, where I’m honored to have been recognized as Senate Legislator of the Year. The issues facing Georgia families and the issues facing Georgia businesses are often more connected than we think. A strong workforce, affordable housing, access to healthcare, reliable infrastructure, and economic opportunity matter to both. We may not always agree on every policy solution, but we do share a common interest in making and keeping Georgia strong. I’m grateful for the opportunity to work alongside business leaders, community partners, and colleagues across the state to help create a Georgia where both people and businesses can thrive. Economic growth and quality of life are not competing priorities—they rise and fall together.

alt://instagram.fsdv2-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t51.82787-15/780520381_18117495725312458_5924328307879087969_n.jpg|You're Invited! Join us next Thursday, August 26th, at 6:00-7:30 p.m. for the 2026 Southwestern Athletic Conference (SWAC) Commissioners Reception at the Commerce Club. This unique event will open the door for the community to connect with SWAC leaders across eleven colleges and various corporations. I encourage everyone to attend this night of culture, celebration, and unforgettable SWAC energy! I hope to see you all there.

alt://instagram.fsdv2-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t51.82787-15/782511189_18117604865312458_1646928453014674285_n.jpg|Atlanta's small businesses and artists are the backbone of this city's economy. Last week I got to stand with @byronamos and @councilmanlewis at the 13th Annual Biz Savvy Artist Competition to celebrate the work and impact of our local entrepreneurs and creatives. As an entrepreneur who's also worked alongside art organizations before I ran for office, this work matters to me. Thank you @bizsavvyartist for building community and creating real opportunity for Atlanta businesses.

alt://instagram.fsdv2-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t51.82787-15/786492803_18118004366312458_4131569903522336952_n.jpg|Happy 84th birthday to my beautiful mom! There are some people whose influence on your life is so deep, it’s hard to put into words. My mom is one of those people for me. She has taught me so much about strength, grace, family, faith, and showing up for the people you love. And the older I get, the more I understand just how much of who I am began with what I saw in her. Mom, I’m so grateful for your love, your example, and for the blessing of celebrating another trip around the sun with you. 84 looks pretty fabulous on you. I ❤️ you!

alt://instagram.fsdv2-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t51.82787-15/795068462_18119363774312458_263542338700642106_n.jpg|@atlutd has officially launched its 25th soccer field! The GA 100 project, apart of the Atlanta United Community Fund , is an initiative committed to making soccer more accessible to the communities who need it most by building 100 new soccer pitches across Georgia. This one is especially meaningful to me. As the State Senator representing this community and a proud board member of the YMCA of Metro Atlanta, I couldn’t think of a better home for this new pitch than the Andrew & Walter Young Family YMCA. The Y has spent generations creating places where young people can learn, play, grow, and discover what they’re capable of. And now, this field gives them one more place to do exactly that. The measure of what we build isn’t just what it means today. It’s what it makes possible for the next generation. Thank you to the Atlanta United community and everyone who helped make this happen. I can’t wait to see the soccer stars — and the leaders — who get their start right here. ⚽

alt://instagram.fsdv2-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t51.82787-15/838219126_18123406094312458_3168602444421833367_n.jpg|November 3rd’s Midterm elections are fastly approaching. alt://instagram.fsdv2-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t51.82787-15/838715048_18123539342312458_2783950269080230588_n.jpg|Atlanta is moving forward, and @Glydways is proud to be part of the conversation about the future of public transportation in our city! 🚝 Last week, Atlanta’s Community Improvement Districts hosted an Automatic Transit Network demonstration, offering community leaders and partners an inside look at what’s possible. As @andreforatlanta often says, “Atlanta is a group project.” This gathering was a great example of that spirit in action, bringing people together, sharing ideas, and working collectively to move our community forward. The new track will span half a mile around the Georgia International Convention Center, with three convenient stations designed to help connect people to where they need to go. The future of transportation is being shaped together, and we’re excited to be part of Atlanta’s journey. 🍑

alt://instagram.ftlv23-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t39.30808-6/704367010_1373870971232245_9093196896951057183_n.jpg|3 votes cast today — including my first-time voter. ❤️ Watching my kids step into their civic responsibility will never grow old. A reminder that democracy is not abstract. It is personal. It is generational. And it only works when we participate. Georgia, there is less than 1 hour left to vote in today’s primary election. If you are still in line by 7 PM, stay in line. Your voice matters. Your vote matters.

alt://instagram.ftlv23-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t39.30808-6/724598292_1396864692266206_7491307811334795185_n.jpg|Hey Georgia! Hey Fulton County! It’s Election Day and it’s your last chance to vote in these runoff elections. I got my peach sticker! 🍑 Go get yours. And while you’re at it, let’s keep our democracy strong by making our voices heard.

alt://instagram.ftlv23-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t39.30808-6/725440018_1397686355517373_6996259346694652865_n.jpg|BREAKING NEWS: Back at the Capitol for special session and here’s a first update. Republicans have announced that they will NOT be redrawing maps during this special session. There’s no question that every call, every rally, everyone who has showed up on these days leading to the start of session and here at the Capitol today have made it clear that disenfranchising black and brown voters is not what the people of our state want. And it's not what we will tolerate. Today, the people won. BUT we must continue to keep the pressure up so maps remain off the table. Round 2: November. Eyes wide open!

alt://instagram.ftlv23-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t51.71878-15/689393031_2181606912587624_3218313443040261390_n.jpg|The cost of living is hitting families harder than ever. Groceries are through the roof, health insurance premiums keep rising, and too many people across District 39 and all of Georgia are being forced to choose between basic necessities. I see it, I hear it, and I’m committed to speaking up for the people who feel overlooked and unheard. We deserve leadership that fights for affordable healthcare, lower everyday costs, and real solutions that help working families thrive — not just survive. I will continue using my voice to advocate for our communities, our seniors, our parents, our small business owners, and every Georgian working hard to make ends meet. #District39 #Georgia #CommunityFirst #AffordableHealthcare #CostOfLiving

alt://instagram.ftlv23-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t51.71878-15/788966064_2297828984378140_4486292939109961078_n.jpg|Whew… I blinked and my middle is off to college. Somehow, all those years of growing, learning, laughing, pushing boundaries, and finding his way brought us here. Move-in. Convocation. A few last hugs. And then the moment you realize it’s time to let him go make this next chapter his own. But not before shedding a few tears…okay, maybe more than a few. There’s so much I could say, but mostly I just want him to know how proud we are of the young man he has become—and how excited we are for all that is ahead of him. Go learn. Go explore. Go make some new friends. Take some chances. Make some mistakes. Call home. Definitely call your mom. 😏 And most of all, enjoy becoming more and more of who you are. The world is waiting for you. And we’ll always be just one call away. ❤️

alt://instagram.ftlv23-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t51.71878-15/814800512_1419565056772601_1237319889168188743_n.jpg|A look back at the @ga_blackcaucus and @gacoalitionofblackchambers BlackPrint Prosperity Convening!⁠ ⁠ On day two, I had the opportunity to lead a great conversation with @boodieforga, @sandra.l.williams3, and Rep. Al Williams on infrastructure and what it takes to build lasting economic prosperity.⁠ ⁠ I started the conversation with a simple premise: infrastructure is about more than roads and bridges. It’s the physical, digital, financial, educational and institutional systems that make prosperity possible.⁠ ⁠ But opportunity alone doesn’t create prosperity. The real test is whether people can participate, advance and build something from it—and whether our communities are stronger because of it.⁠ ⁠ That’s the work ahead. From rural Georgia to our urban centers and everywhere in between, we have to keep asking what we need to put in place so that more people, businesses and communities can thrive.⁠ ⁠ And the conversation doesn’t stop with the convening. I’m looking forward to continuing it—with more voices at the table and more ideas we can turn into action as we work toward a more prosperous Georgia.⁠ ⁠ #Sonya4Ga #BlackPrint #EconomicProsperity #GaInfrastructure

alt://instagram.ftlv23-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t51.82787-15/696266575_18105584096312458_4169641146848533924_n.jpg|I don’t operate from excuses, I operate from execution. I’ve never been the one to say “we don’t have the votes” and stop there. I do the work anyway — building relationships, finding common ground, and pushing ideas forward until they become results. That’s what leadership requires. So imagine what I can do with even more trust, more opportunity, and a stronger mandate to lead. Imagine what’s possible when I’m fully empowered to govern and deliver for the people I serve. I’m ready to do the work — not someday, but now. #sonya4ga #SonyaSays

alt://instagram.ftlv23-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t51.82787-15/733271341_18111611996312458_6878008467114591255_n.jpg|The measure of leadership isn’t what we build for ourselves — it’s what we leave behind for others. The institutions we lead belong to the American people, and our responsibility is to strengthen them and leave them better than we found them. As we celebrate America’s 250th anniversary, that reminder has never felt more urgent. From the Kennedy Center to our classrooms to the halls of Congress — we are in a moment that will test whether our leaders remember they are stewards, not owners. I wrote more about this for Common Dreams this week. Link in bio. 🔗 Today, let’s celebrate how far we’ve come, honor those who’ve expanded freedom and opportunity, and commit ourselves to doing the same. Happy Independence Day. Here’s to continuing the work of building a more perfect union. Better days are ahead. #July4th #Independence250 #BetterDaysAhead #SonyaHalpern #gapol

alt://instagram.ftlv23-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t51.82787-15/779002152_18117113351312458_4440478631369301382_n.jpg|Last Tuesday, I toured Fulton County’s Emergency Management facility with representatives, lobbyists, and leaders working to keep Fulton strong. 💙 As Chair of the Fulton County Senate Delegation, I helped organize this visit to see firsthand how our Emergency Management and Service teams like 911 work and how they prepare for unexpected disasters like earthquakes and infrastructure failures for example. Thank you to the Fulton Emergency Service and Emergency Management teams for protecting us behind the scenes. I’ll keep showing up to support the work that keeps us safe. #FultonStrong #CommunityFocused#Thankful #Sonya4Ga

This guide covers Georgia’s voter registration process, different ways to register, checking your registration status, helping others through the process, and protecting your personal information from unverified sources. Save this guide, share it with your family and friends, and pass it along to your neighbors!
